author: Unknown
title: Danny Evans - ‘Ultra-left’ anarchists and anti-fascism in the Second Republic
content:
Author

: Danny Evans

Title

: ‘Ultra-left’ anarchists and anti-fascism in the Second Republic

Date

: 2016

Source

:

International Journal of Iberian Studies

, 29: 3, pp. 241–56, doi: 10.1386/ijis.29.3.241_1


ABSTRACT


 This article investigates the anarchist understanding of fascism during the Second Republic, and particularly during the abstention campaign of 1933, when the practice of radicals in the National Confederation of Labour (CNT) has been described as ‘ultra-left’ in view of its sectarianism and insistence on the need for an insurrectionary response to the threat of the right. The article explores the comparison made to the German Communist Party (KPD) during the so-called ‘Third Period’, and the lessons that anarchists in Spain attempted to draw from the rise of Hitler.


INTRODUCTION


 The Spanish general election of November 1933 resulted in the formation of a centre-right government presided over by Alejandro Lerroux with the support of the Spanish Confederation of Autonomous Right Wing Groups (CEDA). Thus began the so-called ‘bienio negro’ of the Second Republic, characterized by the reversal of the reforms of the previous two years and the repression of left-wing and labour organizations. The elections had been preceded by a campaign orchestrated by the anarcho-syndicalist union, the National Confederation of Labour (CNT) which called on Spanish workers to abstain from voting. Following the elections, that same organization initiated a short-lived and disastrous uprising, which left over a hundred dead. This marked the beginning of a period of repression in which thousands of CNT activists were jailed and the day to day functioning of the organization was jeopardized.


 Understandably, the historiography has not been kind to the CNT in this period. Its actions have been considered a consequence of ‘impatience and revolutionary mysticism’ (Gómez Casas 1973: 172), its propaganda dismissed as ‘the radical discourse of a minority’ of anarchists within the organization (Casanova 2005: 46). Thus the abstention campaign and the rising of late 1933 have generally been considered to be consequent upon the internal dynamics of the CNT, and the culmination of the process of radicalization within the organization during the first bienio of the Second Republic (1931–1933). This radicalization had already produced two uprisings, in January 1932 and January 1933, and the December revolt has been considered the closing act of a ‘cycle of insurrections’. In contrast to the Asturian insurrection of October 1934, the anarchist revolt of late 1933 is not normally considered a response to the increasing perception of an international and domestic fascist threat. On the contrary, the CNT’s insistence on pursuing a lonely insurrectionist tactic has been taken as evidence of ultra-left indifference among radicals as to the specific danger posed by fascism. According to Chris Ealham, anarchist radicals in this period ‘downplayed the danger of the far Right’, and acted in a sectarian manner that undermined attempts at anti-fascist unity:


 Playing an ultra-leftist, divisive role that had much in common with the German Communist Party (KPD) prior to Hitler’s electoral triumph, the radical anarchists argued that there was no difference between the various electoral options, even suggesting that fascism was already in power […] like the KPD, the CNT and the FAI [the Iberian Anarchist Federation, a federation of anarchist affinity groups] blocked united anti-fascist action, directing their fury against what they regarded as the ‘fascism’ of their enemies, be they treintista [moderate syndicalist], socialist, republican or bloquista [dissident communist], all of whom were regarded as variants of authoritarianism. (2010: 134)


 Using this suggestive comparison as a starting point, in this article I examine the roots of the commonalities between the approaches of the KPD and the CNT, specifically their sectarianism and revolutionary maximalism, while also fleshing out the differences that marked the anarchist approach to fascism in theory and in practice.


 The ‘anti-fascist epic’ (Southworth 1996: 310) was finally won in 1945 by an alliance of imperial, Communist and democratic forces. This alliance contrasted with the ‘divisions and ineffectiveness’ of those who had opposed Hitler in Germany, identified as a contributing factor in his accession to power (Bullock 1973: 253). As such, the ‘object lesson’ of the rise …

author: Unknown
title: Эррико Малатеста - Цели и средства (компиляция Вернона Ричардса)
content:
Автор

: Эррико Малатеста

Название

: Цели и средства (компиляция Вернона Ричардса)


 Цель оправдывает средства: об этом принципе говорят много негативного. На самом же деле, это является универсальным ориентиром борьбы.


 Можно сказать лучше: каждая цель имеет свои средства. Нужно искать мораль в самой цели; средства же в любом случае её оправдают.


 Предполагаемый результат, полученный произвольно или по необходимости, важнейшая проблема жизни состоит в том, чтобы отыскать средства, которые, соответствуя обстоятельствам, с наибольшей вероятностью и с наименьшими затратами приведут к ожидаемому итогу. Способ решения той или иной проблемы зависит (настолько, насколько он в принципе может зависеть от человеческой воли) от того достигает ли индивид или партия с его помощью своих целей, принесет ли он пользу своему делу или, сам того не желая, послужит делу врага. Найти подходящие средства – вот и весь секрет великих людей и великих партий, оставивших свой след в истории.


 […]


 Цель иезуитов – для мистиков слава Божия, для остальных же – могущество ордена. Поэтому они должны стремиться оглуплять массы, держать их в страхе и подчинять их.


 Цель якобинцев и всех авторитарных партий, которые мнят себя обладателями абсолютной истины, – навязать свои идеи массе непосвящённых. Для этого они должны стремиться захватить власть, подчинить себе массы и уложить человечество на прокрустово ложе своих концепций.


 Что касается нас, то тут совсем другое дело: наша цель принципиально иная, соответственно средства её достижения должны быть совершенно другими.


 Мы боремся не за то, чтобы самим занять место сегодняшних эксплуататоров и угнетателей, и не за триумф пустой абстракции. Мы не похожи на того итальянского патриота, сказавшего: «Какое значение имеет то, что все итальянцы падают в обморок от голода, если Италия будет великой и славной!» Не больше мы похожи и на того товарища, который признался, что для него оправдано убийство трех четвертей человечества, при условии, что оставшиеся будут свободными и счастливыми.


 […]


 Для нас всё, что стремится уничтожить экономическое и политическое угнетение; что служит поднятию морального и интеллектуального уровня людей, чтобы дать им сознание своих прав и своих сил, и убедить их самим вести свои дела, - всё, что вызывает ненависть к угнетению и любовь между людьми, приближает нас к нашей цели и потому есть благо, подчинённое лишь количественному расчёту, дабы при данных силах получить максимум полезного эффекта. Напротив, злом является всё, что стремится сохранить нынешнее состояние или принести человека, против его воли, в жертву торжеству какого-либо принципа.


 Мы же хотим торжества свободы и любви.


 Получается, ради этого мы отказываемся использовать насильственные средства? Совсем нет. Наши средства – те, которые позволяют и навязывают нам обстоятельства.


 Разумеется, мы не хотели бы причинить никому вреда – даже волоса с головы у кого-нибудь не сорвать; мы хотели бы осушить все слёзы и не заставить пролиться ни одной. Но нам приходится бороться в мире, каков он есть, под угрозой остаться бесплодными мечтателями.


 Придёт день – мы твёрдо в это верим, – когда можно будет делать людям добро, не причиняя зла ни себе, ни другим. Сегодня это невозможно. Даже самый чистый и кроткий из мучеников, тот, кто дал бы вести себя на эшафот ради торжества добра, без сопротивления, благословляя своих гонителей, как Христос из легенды, – даже он причинил бы немало зла. Помимо зла, которое он причинил бы себе, а это тоже должно что-то значить, он заставил бы пролить горькие слёзы всех, кто его любит.


 Стало быть, всегда, во всех жизненных поступках, речь идёт о том, чтобы выбирать меньшее зло, стараться причинить как можно меньше зла ради как можно большей суммы добра.


 […]


 Разумеется, революция произведёт немало бедствий, немало страданий; но если бы она произвела их и в сто раз больше, она всё равно была бы благословением по сравнению с тем, что терпят сегодня

[1]

.


 […]


 Были и всегда были во всей политико-социальной борьбе усыпители двух видов.


 Есть те, кто считает, что время никогда не наступает, что требования слишком велики, что надо ждать и довольствоваться постепенным продвижением – за счёт мелких улучшеньишек… которые то получают, то теряют, так ничего и не решая


 И есть те, кто напускает на себя презрение к малым делам и требует, чтобы никто ничего не предпринимал, если нельзя получить всё, и кто, предлагая вещи, может быть, прекраснейшие, но …

author: Kate Sharpley
title: An anarchist in the archive : Remembering Barry Pateman
content:
For over seven decades, Myanmar was consumed by the world’s longest civil war, but the Intha (Insaku), the "Children of the Lake/The People of The Lake," remained a peaceful exception. Nestled among high mountain peaks in Shan State, they lived peacefully with nature on the still waters of Inle Lake, famous worldwide for their stilt houses, floating gardens (ye-chan), and iconic leg-rowing fishermen, or at least that's what the state and tourism agency’s narrative for their brand image. The iconic leg-rowing fishermen have become a brand of Myanmar's tourism campaign since 1996, when the military was promising market reform and democracy.


Author


Al Wine


    Submitted by

heinhtetkyaw

 on October 17, 2026


Although recognized as one of Myanmar's 135 distinct indigenous groups, the Intha remain a "minority within a minority" in Southern Shan State, distinct in language and history from their Shan, Pa'O, Lisu, Taungtha, Kareni, and Danu neighbors, and their language is a branch of Widely accepted theories suggest their ancestors migrated from Lower Burma, Dawei, a long time ago, or a group of Tibeto-Burman who were still left behind. At the same time, the rest moved forward to the Irrawaddy Valley. Applying James C. Scott’s concept of “Zomia,” which describes upland societies that historically avoided centralized state control, the Intha experience can be understood as a form of aquatic adaptation. Rather than escaping into mountains, they survived on an economically marginal lake environment surrounded by hills. Their oral histories and religious traditions contain accounts of resistance against local feudal authorities. Even during British colonial rule, the region was viewed less as a profitable administrative center and more as a scenic recreational area.


This delicate socio-ecological balance began to shatter after the 2010 political reforms. Under President Thein Sein’s administration, military-tied tycoons and international investors targeted the lake's eastern shore for a massive "Hotel Zone" project. The infrastructure building has leveled hillsides, drained wetlands, and seized land with minimal compensation for the local population, leading to severe ecological damage, driving local fish populations toward extinction, and destroying traditional livelihoods.


Although Inle Lake was designated Myanmar's first UNESCO Biosphere Reserve in 2015, the surrounding Inlay Lake Wildlife Sanctuary had already been recognized as an ASEAN Heritage Park in 2003. It was later designated Myanmar's fifth Ramsar Wetland of International Importance in 2018. Despite these international conservation recognitions, environmental degradation driven by deforestation, unsustainable agriculture, tourism development, and weak conservation governance has continued. One of the most controversial cases involved Myanmar Naing Group Co., Ltd., owned by U Tun Naing Shwe, son of former military ruler Than Shwe, which proposed to construct a luxury hotel on land that had previously been part of the Inle Lake Wildlife Sanctuary. The proposal sparked widespread opposition from local communities, environmental organizations, and government agencies, becoming a prominent example of the conflict between tourism development and environmental conservation around Inle Lake.


Many farmers and fishermen lost their way of life; many were forced to migrate abroad for work. Those who stayed were pushed into minimum-wage work in construction and the hospital sector. Some local activists and scholars have criticized the commercialization of Inle Lake’s cultural practices, arguing that activities such as staged leg-row fishing and ethnic performances risk transforming living traditions into tourist spectacles rather than preserving their original social meaning.


The commercialization of agriculture and watershed degradation has intensified the ecological crisis at Inle Lake. Historically, the lake’s unique wetland ecosystem allowed the Intha to develop floating-garden agriculture, with tomatoes becoming one of the region’s most important economic crops. However, expanding domestic and regional markets encouraged increased use of chemical fertilizers, pesticides, and commercial seeds, contributing to nutrient pollution and ecological stress.


 At the same time, state land policies allowed customary lands in Shan State to be classified as vacant or wasteland and allocated to large-scale investors and military-linked companies. Many Environmental …

title: the reason why you don’t see women raping or sexually exploiting men as often as the other way…
content:
the reason why you don’t see women raping or sexually exploiting men as often as the other way around, isn’t because women have the divine aura of femininity that prevents them from thinking rapist thoughts, or because cis women lack the Evil Rape Organ or whatever. it is because rape isn’t really purely individual form of violence, but a systemic one. it is also not necessarily done only for personal sexual gratification, but a reassertion of social position through violence.

women hold a lower position compared to men within patriarchy. if you hold a position lower than someone else, then violence against them is not typically something you can get away with, nor can you assert your power over them if you don’t have it.

this is also why the vast majority of cases of women raping or sexually exploiting men are done when a woman holds a higher social position than the man in question. you see this with disparity in class, age (in the case of women sexually abusing children), between white and racialised, and between imperialist and imperialised. most notable examples are the women abusing and torturing prisoners in Abu Ghraib as much as their male colleagues, or the female Israeli prison guards torturing Palestinians.

and of course, women sexually exploiting or abusing other women is done on similar grounds. it is more common for cis women to sexually exploit or abuse trans women than the other way around for example.

author: Patrick William Kelly
title: The Person They Never Asked About
content:
A

fter lights out at the state forensic hospital, a worker would peer through my door’s square window every fifteen minutes. He would quickly flick the overhead light on and off—just long enough to record whether I was breathing and in what position I was sleeping. Sometimes I could hear him whispering the data aloud to a partner making rounds alongside him, recounting our bodily orientations like buried bodies in a graveyard:


Left side. Right side. Back.


They knew the position in which my body slept every fifteen minutes for ten months. But they rarely asked me a personal question about my life.


I spent fourteen months in county jails and a state psychiatric hospital after accepting a not-guilty-by-reason-of-mental-disease plea on eight felony stalking charges arising from a psychotic manic episode. I had a doctorate from the University of Chicago and a book with Cambridge University Press. I had also been misdiagnosed by four different hospital systems, prescribed the wrong class of medications for four years, and carried an undetected neurosyphilis infection that inflamed my brain while every clinician I encountered looked somewhere else. By the time I arrived at Mendota Mental Health Institute, Wisconsin’s forensic psychiatric hospital, in January of 2025, the system had demonstrated an extraordinary capacity to observe and document me and an almost total incapacity to know me.


The maximum-security units were arranged in a hub-and-spoke design. A central core provided sightlines into four radiating wards, each terminating in a nurse’s station enclosed in tinted glass from which staff monitored and documented; from the dayroom, we could often see them behind the glass looking down at their phones. Exchanges with psychiatric care technicians (PCTs) occurred only through a narrow request portal, whose hours had shrunk over the years to ten or fifteen minutes per hour. The portal was a test: could you wait and follow the rules? Could you manage your frustration with the demands of bureaucratic order while practicing the skills of emotional regulation? These were the questions the watchtower was built to answer. Whether you were suffering, or confused, or intellectually alive, or desperately lonely—these were questions the watchtower had no room for.


Goffman argued in

Asylums

 that total institutions mortify the self through a process in which “all acts of resistance by the so-called mentally ill” become “just further evidence, in the eyes of the staff, of their mental incompetence and illness.” Mendota was not a mid-century asylum—it was cleaner, better staffed, and far more humane. But the structural logic Goffman recognized had not vanished; it had just been refined. I intend this less as a polemic than as an honest portrayal—a careful account, from the inside, of a system that has developed a more sophisticated capacity to measure a human being than to know one.


II.


Through the wall of my room at Mendota, my neighbor Johnnie—a man with schizophrenia—was the conductor of a full symphony of voices no one else could hear. In one movement alone, he shifted seamlessly from polite dialogue to laughter to verbal combat. Then came the machine-gun of counting: “One-one, two-two, three-three”—up to twenty, silence, followed by another cartridge. Each number landed twice, as if repetition could nail it to the fabric of reality. In a world where thoughts bled into voices and voices blurred into persecution, counting seemed to provide Johnnie with an anchor—a metronome to ward off psychic freefall. What looked like madness from the outside was, from within, a courageous effort at coherence.


He often cornered me in the hallway to announce an epiphany, “Vocationally, spiritually, politically, logistically, the zebra is the outright leader of the animal kingdom—correct, Patrick?” I learned that polite agreement was the kindest response. Johnnie called me by name, and the institution did not always manage that.


In a psychology group one afternoon, our therapist asked us why it was so hard to be happy. We sat in a semicircle—six men adjudicated dangerous to themselves or others, parsing the nature of happiness like students in a high school ethics class. At the end of the session, Johnnie shot up his hand. “I’d just like to say it’s important to remember the following: we’re not sick, we need a sheikh!” The room burst into scattered laughter. And for a brief instant, the cage dissolved.

 Η Οργάνωση Εξωτερικού της Κομμουνιστικής Απελευθέρωσης διοργανώνει ανοικτή διαδικτυακή συζήτηση για τις πρόσφατες εξελίξεις στην Ισπανία και στη Γαλλία.


 Με αφορμή την έξωση της Μαρικάρμεν, ο λαός στην Ισπανία βρίσκεται στο δρόμο, με συνεχείς κινητοποιήσεις για να υπερασπιστεί το δικαίωμα στην στέγαση, έχοντας μπροστά την πρώτη πανεργατική απεργία μετά από 14 χρόνια. Στη Γαλλία, το αρχικό μπλοκάρισμα των σχολείων για τη διεκδίκηση μίας καλύτερης παιδείας έχει μεταδοθεί και σε άλλα κομμάτια της κοινωνίας, με την πρόσφατη απεργία στο δημόσιο να βάζει στο στόχαστρο την ακρίβεια και τον προϋπολογισμό λιτότητας, με μαζικές κινητοποιήσεις σε όλες τις γαλλικές πόλεις.


 Για να πιάσουμε το νήμα των εξελίξεων αυτών, να μεταδώσουμε τις εμπειρίες από τις χώρες αυτές, μέσω των μελών της ΚΑ που εργάζονται και δρουν σε αυτές, και να συζητήσουμε συλλογικά τις εξελίξεις στην Ευρώπη συνολικά, η Οργανωση Βάσης Εξωτερικού της Κομμουνιστικής Απελευθέρωσης καλεί σε διαδικτυακή ανοικτή συζήτηση την Δευτέρα 19 Οκτώβρη, 19.00 CEST (20.00 Ελλάδος).


 Ως Οργανώσεις ΚΑ-νΚΑ Θεσσαλονίκης διοργανώνουμε προβολή της εκδήλωσης στη Λέσχη Αναιρέσεις (Πελοποννήσου 4) στις 20:00

title: Fransa’da kitlesel eylemlerin ardından gözaltılar 2 bini aştı
content:
Fransa’da lise öğrencilerinin eğitimde eşitlik talebiyle başlattığı protestoların yüz binlerce kişinin katıldığı bir toplumsal harekete dönüşmesinin ardından, bugün hükümetin güvenlik politikaları, polis müdahaleleri ve sendikaların talepleri ülkenin gündemindeki yerini korudu.


17 Ekim’de ülke genelinde düzenlenen 110 gösteriye katılım, sendikalara göre 800 bine, İçişleri Bakanlığı’na göre 550 bine ulaştı. Yürüyüşlerin büyük bölümü barışçıl geçerken Paris, Marsilya, Lyon, Toulouse ve Limoges başta olmak üzere çeşitli kentlerde çatışmalar, yağma ve kundaklama olayları yaşandı.


İçişleri Bakanı Laurent Nuñez’in bugün yaptığı açıklamaya göre, gözaltı sayısı 2 bini, yaralanan polis, jandarma ve itfaiye personelinin sayısı ise 600’ü aştı.


Fransa: Öğrenci isyanı toplumsallaşıyor, 800 bin insan Cumartesi sokaktaydı


Bugün  00:34


Gözaltı bilançosu büyüyor


17 Ekim akşamı yaklaşık 400 olarak açıklanan gözaltı sayısı, gece boyunca süren polis operasyonlarının ardından hızla yükseldi.


Paris Emniyet Müdürlüğü’ne göre yalnızca başkentte 855 kişi gözaltına alındı. Yetkililer bu sayının tek bir gösteri günü için olağanüstü yüksek olduğunu belirtti.


Nuñez, kamu binalarına yönelik saldırılarla mağaza yağmalarından “aşırı sol” olarak nitelendirdiği grupları sorumlu tuttu.


Hükümet cezaları ağırlaştırmak istiyor


Başbakan Sébastien Lecornu, gösterilerin ardından yaptığı açıklamalarda şiddet olaylarına karışanların daha ağır yaptırımlarla karşılaşacağını söyledi.


Hükümet, gösteriler sırasında ortaya çıkan maddi zararın sorumlularından tahsil edilmesini amaçlayan ve kamuoyunda “zarar veren öder” (casseurs-payeurs) adıyla bilinen yasa tasarısının görüşmelerini hızlandırıyor.


Senatonun resmî takvimine göre tasarı 27 ve 28 Ekim’de Genel Kurul gündemine gelecek. Düzenleme, kamusal alandaki şiddet ve tahribat nedeniyle ortaya çıkan zararların sorumlularından karşılanmasına ilişkin yeni hükümler öngörüyor.


Lecornu, Adalet Bakanı Didier Migaud’un yarın (19 Ekim) başsavcılarla bir araya gelerek gözaltılar ve soruşturmalar kapsamında uygulanacak adli politikaları değerlendireceğini de açıkladı.


Cumhurbaşkanı Emmanuel Macron ise bu akşam Fransa saatiyle 20.00’da (TSİ 21.00) halka seslenecek. Élysée Sarayı, Macron’un konuşmasından önce hükümet üyeleriyle bir güvenlik toplantısı yapacağını duyurdu.


CGT: “Hükümet toplumsal taleplere yanıt vermeli”


Hükümetin güvenlik ve cezalandırma odaklı açıklamalarına karşı Genel Emek Konfederasyonu (CGT), 17 Ekim gösterilerinin geniş katılımını hatırlatarak toplumsal taleplerin gündeme alınmasını istedi.


CGT, yaklaşık 800 bin kişinin katıldığını belirttiği eylemlerde öğrencilerin eğitim koşullarının yanı sıra alım gücündeki düşüş, hayat pahalılığı, emekli aylıkları ve kamu hizmetlerine ayrılan kaynakların yetersizliğinin de protesto edildiğini vurguladı.


Halkın kitlesel ve barışçıl biçimde dile getirdiği taleplere ısrarla kulak tıkayan hükümet, bugün şiddetin tırmanmasından siyasi olarak sorumludur.

–CGT, 17 Ekim 2026


CGT, hükümete öğrenci ve çalışan sendikalarıyla müzakere çağrısı yaparken, gösterilere katılımı engelleyen polis müdahalelerine de karşı çıktı.


5 Kasım’da ülke çapında grev


Fransa’da sendikalar, hükümetin sertleşen güvenlik politikalarına karşın toplumsal taleplerini gündemde tutmayı sürdürüyor.


CGT’nin yanı sıra Fransız Demokratik Emek Konfederasyonu (CFDT), İşçi Gücü (FO), Birleşik Sendikalar Federasyonu (FSU), Ulusal Özerk Sendikalar Birliği (UNSA) ve Dayanışma Sendikaları Birliği (Solidaires), 5 Kasım'da kamu ve özel sektör çalışanlarının katılımıyla yeni grev ve gösteriler düzenlemeyi planlıyor.


Sendikalar, ücretlerin ve emekli aylıklarının artırılmasını, kamu hizmetlerine daha fazla kaynak ayrılmasını ve hükümetin 2027 bütçesindeki kemer sıkma politikalarından vazgeçmesini talep ediyor.


Lise öğrencileri açısından ise öğretmen açığının giderilmesi, kalabalık sınıfların azaltılması, okulların fiziki koşullarının iyileştirilmesi ve yükseköğretime erişimde eşitlik talepleri gündemdeki yerini koruyor.


Kaynaklar: AFP, Associated Press, CGT, Le Monde, Reuters

author: paradox-a
title: Kollaps. Chaos? Faschismus. Neuanfang!
content:
GESCHICHTSPHOLISOPHISCHE UND GESELLSCAFTSTHEORETISCHE GEDANKEN ZU EINER UNTERGEHENDEN ZIVILISATIION


„Hurra, die Welt geht unter“, so sangen es 2015 K.I.Z. mit Henning May. Eine andere Band mit drei Buchstaben – R.E.M . – wurde mit Song „It’s the end of the world as we know it (and I’ll feel fine)“ von 1987 bekannt. Im Jahr 1968 wurde das Musical „Hair“ uraufgeführt. Der erste Titel propagiert „This is the dawning of the Age of Aquarius“. In der popkulturell-esoterischen Bezugnahme auf das sogenannte „Wassermannzeitalter“ durch die Hippies kommt sowohl die tiefgreifende Entfremdung von der bestehenden Gesellschaftsform, als auch die Hoffnung auf eine grundlegende Erneuerung zum Ausdruck. Doch schon Ende des 19. Jahrhunderts, in der Phase des sogenannten Fin de Siècle, zeugen zahlreiche literarische Texte von einer pessimistischen Endzeitstimmung. Für diese wurde ein Jahrhundert zuvor der romantische Ausdruck „Weltschmerz“ geprägt, der an die – ebenfalls romantische und sehr deutsche – Vorstellung von „Sehnsucht“ anknüpft.


Das Zeitgefühl, eine umfangreiche Zivilisationskrise zu erleben, ist zunächst einmal das: Ein Gefühl. Es entwickelt sich unter bestimmten gesellschaftlichen Rahmenbedingungen und ihren unabsehbaren Veränderungen. Dabei scheint die Angst vor Schmerz, Leid, Verfall und Tod merkwürdig verknüpft mit der Erlösungshoffnung auf eine umfassende Erneuerung zu sein. Ein solches Krisenbewusstsein haben Menschen zu verschiedenen Zeiten entwickelt. Wenn heute zunehmend von „Kollaps“ gesprochen wird, deutet dies auf eine Bewusstwerdung über den unhaltbaren Zustand der Gesellschaft beziehungsweise ihrer prognostizierte katastrophale Entwicklung hin. In verschiedenen sozialen Milieus sind Zeitgefühl und Bewusstsein unterschiedlich ausgeprägt. Sie hängen beispielsweise damit zusammen, ob Leute von den angenommenen Rahmenbedingungen profitieren und aufsteigen oder von ihnen bedroht werden und verarmen. Diese Aspekte gilt es zu berücksichtigen, wenn man das empfundene Krisengefühl sinnvoll verstehen und einordnen will, um in sich verändernden und verunsichernden Umständen handlungsfähig zu werden.


Allerdings gibt es einen wesentlichen Unterschied zu allen uns bekannten Zivilisationskrisen wie etwa dem Zerfall des Weströmischen Reiches im 4. und 5. Jahrhundert: Durch die menschengemachte Klimaveränderung spitzen sich die Verteilungskämpfe um fruchtbares Land und Wasser zu und werden die Lebensbedingungen für einen großen Teil der Menschheit zunehmend unwirtlicher. Parallel dazu verschärfen sich geopolitische Auseinandersetzungen, sodass Nationalstaaten zu neofeudalen Imperien mutieren. Seit den 1970er Jahren konzentriert sich die Eigentumsverteilung ungebrochen bei der Elite, während öffentliche Institutionen und Kommunen aufgrund der Privatisierung von Gewinnen erodieren. Infolgedessen erweisen sich Versprechungen von Absicherung und entspanntem Rentenalter, von Aufstieg und gesellschaftlichem Status, Konsum und Selbstverwirklichung, für immer mehr Menschen als Illusion. Dabei bilden jene Versprechungen die Grundlage des gesellschaftlichen Zusammenhalts: Sie sind die Voraussetzungen dafür, sich in nervtötende, hierarchische und schlecht bezahlte Lohnarbeitsverhältnisse zu begeben, sich konform und gesetzestreu zu verhalten, ökonomische, soziale und politische Ungleichheiten zu akzeptieren und bei der Lösung gesellschaftlicher Herausforderungen auf die jeweilige Regierung zu vertrauen.


KOLLAPS


Im Zuge der Desillusionierung der Klimabewegung nahm das Nachdenken über Kollaps an Fahrt auf: Obwohl sie weltweit Millionen von Menschen auf die Straße brachte, eine ganze Generation politisierte und sich zahlreiche Gruppen im Zuge der Auseinandersetzungen um die Begrenzung der Klimaerwärmung bildeten, zerstreute sich diese Bewegung wieder. Die Engagierten mussten feststellen, dass die Regierungen ihren Forderungen keine Beachtung schenkten und trotz wissenschaftlicher Erkenntnissen weiter auf Profitwachstum durch die Verbrennung fossiler Energieträger setzten. Zudem verschwand das Thema im Zuge der Covid-Pandemie, der Kriege in der Ukraine und Palästina, sowie dem Aufstieg des Neofaschismus weitgehend von der politischen Agenda. Die daraus resultierenden ökologischen Folgen sind bekannt: Anstieg des Meeresspiegels durch das Abschmelzen von Polkappen und Gletschern, zunehmende Waldbrände und Hurrikans, die Verwüstung trockener Gebieten, massenhaftes Artensterben, die Vernichtung von Leben im Meer etc.. author: Mada Masr
title: Parliament puts off vote on authorizing Sisi to send troops to Saudi Arabia until Tuesday
content:
After a closed session on Sunday that ran for nearly three hours, the House of Representatives postponed a vote on authorizing President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi to send troops on a combat mission to defend Saudi Arabia, putting it off until after Monday’s and Tuesday’s sessions.


Sisi had called for an emergency parliamentary session during the Egyptian Military Academy graduation ceremony on Saturday, asking lawmakers to authorize him to take any measures necessary to protect Saudi Arabia against Houthi attacks “if we are asked to do so.”


The delay came after MPs demanded details of the Armed Forces’ role in Saudi Arabia beyond the National Defense Council’s

statement

, asking that every MP get a chance to express their views on the matter, according to three lawmakers who spoke to Mada Masr.


MP Ehab Mansour, the Egyptian Social Democratic Party parliamentary bloc head, told Mada Masr after the session that members were instructed not to share details of the discussions with the media.


“We are not looking for a role to play, but it makes no sense whatsoever for us to allow any harm to come to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, its security or its stability,” Sisi said during the graduation ceremony.


He appealed to “everyone in the Gulf” to stop the war. “Regardless of this appeal, whether it is heeded or not, Egypt, in line with His Majesty King Salman and Crown Prince Mohamed bin Salman’s directives, will carry out any measure to protect and defend you,” he added.


Sisi stressed that he is not speaking “in order for us to fight anyone or attack anyone. We are speaking only in defense.”


Following Sisi’s remarks, House Speaker Hesham Badawy called an emergency plenary session for Sunday morning.


Article 152 of the

Constitution

 requires the president to consult the National Defense Council before declaring war or sending armed forces on combat missions outside the country. It also requires approval from two-thirds of the members of the House of Representatives, voting in a closed session under Article 130 of the House’s bylaws.


Before Parliament convened, the presidential spokesperson

announced

 three points agreed upon by the National Defense Council at a meeting chaired by Sisi earlier on Sunday morning. The council declared Egypt’s full solidarity with Saudi Arabia, out of a belief that Saudi national security is tied to Egyptian and Arab national security, and pledged to provide the country with all necessary and available forms of support to defend its security and stability, protect its resources and territorial integrity and safeguard Islamic holy sites.


The council also called for continued and intensified political and diplomatic efforts, coordinated with relevant regional and international parties, to de-escalate tensions across the region and peacefully resolve the crisis affecting it.


A senior judicial source criticized the wording of the presidential request. “No state takes directives from another state,” he told Mada Masr on condition of anonymity.


The source explained that the Constitution requires Parliament’s approval before troops are sent on combat missions outside the country, meaning the president must specify the nature of the mission, its strategic value to the country and the number of soldiers needed to carry it out. That “authorize me and I’ll handle it” matter, the source said, is “unconstitutional.”


In a video

posted

to his personal Facebook account, MP Reda Abdel Salam, an economics professor at Mansoura University, laid out his view of the president’s authorization request, saying he was unable to express it during the session as each MP was allotted only two minutes. “If Egypt takes part in defending Saudi Arabia, it is only defense, with no Egyptian soldier sent onto Yemeni soil and no Egyptian strike or bullet fired at brotherly Yemen,” he said. “We are defending, alongside Saudi Arabia, the property, wealth, vital sites, airports and water and power stations. Egypt’s participation is defensive only, while mediation efforts continue.”


An MP with military background who spoke to Mada Masr on condition of anonymity expected Egypt’s involvement to be limited to deploying air defense forces and missiles, while also replacing some Saudi units with Egyptian forces and carrying out limited airstrikes against naval targets, without deploying troops in ground combat.


The source said that Egypt’s military doctrine since former President Gamal Abdel Nasser’s …

author: Mzi Velapi
title: ‘End hunger, stop climate harm’: protesters take demands to Parliament
content:
About 200 residents and activists marched through the streets of Cape Town on World Food Day, calling for the government to end hunger and stop climate harm. Organised by the Climate Justice Charter Movement (CJCM) and the South African Food Sovereignty Campaign and allied partners, the protesters handed the memorandum to parliament where they called for the adoption of the People’s Sovereignty Act No 1 of 2024, a People’s Sovereignty Policy and an immediate ban on pesticides.


At least 14 to 15 million people in South Africa live below the food poverty line and experience regular food insecurity, while 11,000 children die due to malnutrition every year, and 10-million tonnes of food go to waste every year, according to Unite Against Hunger.


A recent report by the International Panel of Experts on Sustainable Food Systems (IPES-Food) found that nearly 1.4-billion people in the world work in the agrifood sector, including farmworkers. Despite their number and the vital role they play, they are among the most exploited workers in the world.


Speaking to

Elitsha

, Kara Mackay from Women on Farms Project said that women farmworkers bear the brunt of lack of access to food because of the unequal power relations that govern their relationship with farm owners. “The issue of poor wages and the high prices of food is linked to unequal power relations where the farmer is seen as the producer and the farmworkers as merely consumers,” she said.


Retired farmworker, Magrieta Prins from De Doorns said that farmers deny workers the opportunity to grow their own food by controlling their access to water. “Farmworkers do not have land to grow their own food but even in instances where they are allowed to do so, the farmer controls their use of water and in most times just deny them access to water,” Prins said.


A seasonal farmer from Ceres, Charmaine Lynx said that not having access to water impacts on their ability to produce their own food. “The social grants play a crucial role during off season. I have to look after my daughter and family during off season as I share my AllPay grant with them. Some have to resort to recycling as a means to put food on the table for their families,” said Prins.


One of the demands of the protesters is the implementation of the climate emergency social contract, that requires the government and the corporations which promote and profit from fossil fuels, pay the price.


Communities on the coastal areas of the Western Cape are experiencing severe weather that has impacted on their ability to feed their families. Fisher woman from Buffels Baai in the Southern Cape, Sarah Niemand said that the weather patterns have resulted in cold waters and fish migrating away. “For the past two months we struggled to get fish because they are scarce because of the bad weather,” she said.


Addressing the protesters outside of parliament, activist and academic, Vishwas Satgar said that southern Africa is heating at twice the global average rate, pushing the region toward an estimated 3°C of warming as global mitigation targets face severe shortfalls. “We are here to tell this government that we are not going to pay the price for their failure of leadership to prepare this country. Climate signs are telling us that El Niño is coming and the last El Niño resulted in collapsed food systems and pushed the food prices up as a result,” Satgar said.


Responding to the memorandum, Mfuneko Toyana said that the government will announce additional funding to respond to El Niño, when the minister of finance tables the Medium-Term Budget Policy Statement next week.


Satgar responded to this news: “It does not add up, this is the government that is squeezing the working class and the poor in this country. They are driving austerity meaures, and this is just a modest gesture given that the problem is big and El Niño is coming.”

author: Yasmine Benabderrahmane
title: Is "khawa khawa" a North African myth?
content:
In the haze of

el ghorba

 — the strangeness and alienation of living abroad — I gravitate toward the Maghrebi diaspora. For a moment, we relax our tongues from the unnatural twists of Arabic dialects foreign to us and speak in the Maghrebi

darija

s. Desperate to latch onto whatever whispers of home exist elsewhere, we claim that we are

khawa khawa

.

Among the Algerians, Moroccans, and Tunisians,

khawa khawa

 is an official nod to an unofficial alliance, loosely translating to

brotherhood

. It is an ode to our shared cultures and history in the face of North African identity discourses.

But what began as a salve for colonialism was lost in the monotonous chants for brotherhood.

Before the 19th century, North African states were “undefined” to European cartographers and authorities alike. Hence, like the concept of the Middle East and the Sahel, the Maghreb was prone to imperial invention. Unsurprisingly, this coincided with the Scramble for Africa — when the insatiable greed of European colonial powers took interest in dividing the African continent among themselves.

Encompassing other colonial legacies, the borders born out of the Scramble engineered the ethnic rivalries that persist in Africa today. Through the newly devised borders and the infamous “divide and conquer” regimes, the Maghreb was branded as distinct.

Despite the existing racial diversity of the region, the French colonial regimes rebranded the Maghreb as a biracial society: Amazigh or Arab. While the Amazigh identity was mislabeled in proximity to the whiteness of Europe, the Arab identity became an accusation of settler colonialism. North Africa became a geographic body for the Francophonie world, distanced from its neighboring regions’ cultures, politics, and society.

In 1962, Algeria — the last of France’s Maghrebi colonies — declared independence. In the years that followed, the Maghrebi people looked inwards and toward rebuilding the identity of North Africa. Thus,

khawa khawa

 was born and reinforced by the diaspora that fled their homes in the wake of political instability. It became a card dealt in moments of desperation to bond to something, or someone, that vaguely resembled home.

Khawa khawa

, and the brotherhood that blossomed with it, became the means to redress an identity obscured by European colonialism.

True

khawa khawa

 culture demands communal harmony void of ego. But when politics becomes inevitably entangled in the national identity of communities, the culture of Maghrebi brotherhood falls flat.

Shortly after 1962, newly independent Algeria and Morocco fell into border disputes. The following decades spiraled into attempted land grabs, fits of cultural monopolies, and accusations of expansionist ambitions. In response, the people cried out

khawa khawa; our governments do not define our brotherhood

!

But too often, the politics override the social bonds of Algerians and Moroccans (and occasionally, Tunisians). With the rise of the internet, discourse shifted, and social media became a useful mirror for the abstractions of the Maghrebi identity.

Most recently, the

khawa khawa

 culture was dramatically pronounced dead on social media platforms, following the 2025 African Cup of Nations (AFCON). Almost overnight, the football tournament became a litmus test for Algerian-Moroccan relations and spiraled into a warped perception of North African relations. A futile online back-and-forth that began as shared banter turned into personal attacks and political scrutiny.

The post-AFCON

guerre

 between Algerians and Moroccans — which coincided with the recent

UN support

 for Moroccan plans over the Western Sahara, disapproved by the Algerian government — is a recurring phenomenon of how Maghrebi culture wages war parallel to the political tensions of its respective countries. Despite the adamant denial, online Maghrebi communities fall into the habit of using our governments to verify the authenticity of

khawa khawa

.

The problem rests in the fact that both communities — Algerian and Moroccan — fall into the habit of claiming the minority of hateful comments as the consensus among the entirety of both nations. We see assertions made that we cannot prove, except that they are too insulting and their wounds far too inflicting to recover from. It has become a pattern of malice between both nations that resurfaces regardless of how loudly

khawa khawa

 is chanted.

Perhaps the fault is also in the fragility …

author: Francis Annagu
title: Nigeria has not decided how to regulate Chinese businesses. Who will decide?
content:
In mid-September 2026, traders in the auto spare parts section of the Lagos International Trade Fair Complex

protested against Chinese traders who sell directly to customers

. One protester

said

 the Chinese had ‘built warehouses, rented shops and are now selling as we do as retailers.’ Police called the protesters

‘a few miscreants’

.


Nigeria already has rules for foreign businesses. But the government has not said what it wants from Chinese businesses, or who will carry out the policy. In the two weeks after the protest, the police, a market board, a minister’s aide and a governor all spoke. None said whether the rules will change. Mining shows the same gap. In both, a policy question is being handled as a policing problem.


Competition over one supply chain


Retailer John Chidebere

told Premium Times

 that goods from China take two to three months to arrive and leave him little profit. Meanwhile,

Chinese businesses can sell directly

 to local customers at wholesale prices. Nigeria imported

N11.01 trillion

 of goods from China in the first half of 2026, nearly 40 per cent of its imports, according to National Bureau of Statistics data.

SBM Intelligence

 says the trade deficit is ‘substantially a symptom of Nigeria’s broader industrial and macroeconomic environment, not a cause in itself.’ Commentator

Martin Beck Nworah

 said: ‘once the wholesaler becomes the middleman, the retailer is edged out.’ So this is a fight inside one supply chain, not only Nigerians against Chinese competitors.


Protesters rally outdoors in Nigeria, October 2020


What the traders are asking for


Newsclick

 reported placards reading ‘The Chinese must go.’ But Chief Osigwe told Premium Times that Chinese traders should leave the market and trade elsewhere,

not leave Nigeria

. Trader Clement Ebere said: ‘I’m not saying the Chinese should leave, but it should be negotiated.’ The association’s president,

Nnamdi Ngozi Emechebe

, said asking the Chinese to leave Nigeria was not an option.

Some of the Chinese wholesalers

 approached by Premium Times declined to comment. So the slogan and the demand did not match. The traders want Chinese businesses out of retail, not out of Nigeria.


The law allows it


A

BusinessDay legal explainer

 says the Nigerian Investment Promotion Commission (NIPC) Act lets foreigners invest in most businesses.

The Act’s short list of banned areas

 covers arms and ammunition, narcotic drugs, and military and paramilitary clothing, plus anything the Federal Executive Council adds. Retail is not on it. Foreigners still need visas,

business permits and expatriate quotas

. So the legal question is whether these businesses have the right permits. The political question is bigger: does Nigeria want foreign companies in retail at all?


The

Centre for the Promotion of Private Enterprise

 and a

Daily Trust editorial

 of 2 October both ask for the rules on foreign retailers to be reviewed. Neither asks for a ban. The rules exist. What is missing is a decision on whether to change them.


Institutions have spoken, but no decision taken


Police Area Commander ACP Chike Oti said the protesters had

been cautioned

 and arrests would follow, but

no arrest had been reported

 in the coverage I found. Veronica Ndanusa, who heads the

Lagos International Trade Fair Complex Management Board

, a body under the Federal Ministry of Industry, Trade and Investment,

told traders to stay calm

 and said foreign investors who

follow the law

 would be protected.


Ms Ndanusa spoke about investors, not about whether foreigners should be in retail. I found no public statement on that question, or on the protest, from the Nigerian Investment Promotion Commission, the trade ministry itself, or the Lagos State Government. The nearest Lagos voice was the governor’s new-media aide, Jubril Gawat,

sharing a video of a police officer

 speaking about arrests.


Political comments filled the gap. Lere Olayinka, an aide to FCT Minister Nyesom Wike,

mocked the protesters on X

. Abia Governor Alex Otti, on 29 September, said Igbo traders were

‘moving from the market to manufacturing’

. Actor

Joseph Okechukwu

 claimed the federal government brought Chinese people in to destroy Igbo businesses. The report quoting him gave no evidence.


The same gap in mining


Local gold miners at work in Kano State, Nigeria, August 2022.


On 3 September 2026, Premium Times reported that Niger State’s commissioner had asked …

author: Soreti Kadir
title: Finfinnee is the Third Space
content:
At the end of 2010, I took a trip to Ethiopia to visit my family. At the time, my parents worked in Bole, the commercial centre of Addis Ababa. Being only 16, my movements were more or less regulated by my parents, which meant that I would travel with them into the city each day, after which it was the extent of my curiosity and creativity (and pocket money) that determined what I did until evening, when I would head back to our house on the outskirts of the city. Slowly, interactions with the staff at a nearby cafe, just a few hundred meters from the building where my family worked, became routine. 


Over the two months that I was in Ethiopia, with much of this time spent in Addis Ababa, we spent most of our lunch breaks together, hanging out on the steps of the cafe, sharing stories to pass the time. One day, the conversation of our relationship to ‘Ethiopia’, as a national identity, came up. It’s important to note that I was raised in the Oromo diaspora, a community that, in the years my mother and I migrated to Australia, was made up mostly of political refugees who fled the country after the adoption of the “Transitional Period Charter of Ethiopia” and the official establishment of a transitional government. 


This eventually led to the Tigrayan People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) monopolizing power within the Ethiopian People’s Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF), a process that resulted in the isolation of those seeking political power within the EPRDF through the ballot. Given the size and economic importance of the Oromia region, it was the Oromo Liberation Front (OLF), amongst others, that became a key target of political violence, creating political communities in exile exactly like the one that I grew up in.


I inherited a different definition of Ethiopia, coloured by memories and experiences of violence and displacement that informed my relationship to the state as a place of unbelonging for those who shared my identity. The day that the conversation with these two new friends wandered into political territory, we all engaged passionately, striving to reflect the extent of both our personal experiences and hopes for our country. They found my reflections to be overly nostalgic and antagonistic towards the country’s future.  Unconcerned for the good of the future. I found their insistence that we shared a national identity to be inaccurate and offensive. We agreed on little, and I found it exhilarating. 


That evening, I was restlessly anticipating the opportunity to tell my mother about what I thought was the most exciting experience of my trip to date. In recounting the story, I almost gave my mother a heart attack. Angry, afraid, and in shock, my mother warned me sternly against ever engaging in such conversation in public again. She asked me many questions about who these men were, how I knew them, and if we’d ever had such conversations before. What I was blind to, and what was the daily lived experience of my parents, was that Addis Ababa, primarily but not exclusively, was a heavily surveilled city, the State looking for the people doing exactly what I found myself doing that day – discussing the political reality of our country. Thereafter, I was careful, out of curiosity more than fear (being 16 with a high risk tolerance will do that), and refrained from fully-fledged conversations, opting for quiet enquiry when the opportunity presented itself. Although our conversation never veered down the road of politics again, I continued to visit my friends every day and remember rushing to say a heartfelt goodbye on the day I was due to fly back to Australia. 


For this piece, I will centre the discussion on Ethiopia’s capital, Addis Ababa, as opposed to extending the conversation to other parts of the country which exist with their own nuances and political realities, requiring more space for analysis than I have here. I share the introductory anecdote to forward the idea that, in Ethiopia, to nurture spaces of connection, community-building, and care, we must first invest in collective repair of the damage wrought by decades of state surveillance that has defined the range and breadth of relational life the city space can hold, and from the legacy of what can only be defined as settler colonialism. ‘Where’, figuratively and literally, can this process of repair take place? I argue that it must take place in Finfinnee, geographically the same location as Addis Ababa, but sociologically and …

author: AfricanFeminism
title: Morocco’s First Woman Prime Minister and the Terms of Freedom
content:
Something changes when a woman occupies an office men have treated as their natural inheritance. Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri’s

appointment

 on 29 September 2026 makes that change visible in Morocco. For women whose competence is routinely scrutinised, the pleasure is neither naïve nor trivial.


But the woman forming a government and the woman labouring in the fields, raising children without pay and denied an equal share of her inheritance encounter power differently. Representation changes who governs; emancipation changes what all women have the power to do. That distinction shifts our attention from PM Mansouri’s gender to the politics of the centre-right

 Party of Authenticity and Modernity (PAM

)

, which she leads. Will its programme redistribute the resources and rights on which women’s freedom depends?


The history beneath the headline


Calling women’s leadership foreign to Morocco requires forgetting its history. Historian Osire Glacier

documents

 women’s authority long before the contemporary premiership. Kenza al Awrabiya, the Amazigh mother of Idris II, helped secure the Idrisid dynasty, founded in the late eighth century in what is now Morocco. Zaynab al Nafzawiyya influenced eleventh-century Almoravid politics around Aghmat, near Marrakech. Sayyida al Hurra governed Tétouan, a city in northern Morocco, during the sixteenth century. Khnata bint Bakkar intervened in eighteenth-century dynastic politics.


Across the region,

Dihya

 is remembered as an Amazigh queen who led resistance to the Arab conquest in the Aurès, in present-day Algeria, during the late seventh century. Tuareg oral tradition remembers

Tin Hinan

 as a queen and founding ancestress of noble lineages in the Ahaggar, in present-day southern Algeria.


These histories expose how male authority is made to appear natural. Fatima Mernissi’s

The Forgotten Queens of Islam


challenges that selective memory. Colonialism also reorganised authority: French Protectorate administrators

reshaped

 customary courts around imperial priorities. What survives as tradition can carry the history of political intervention. 


Religious interpretation can give exclusion another claim to permanence. Islamist and other conservative opponents invoke this

hadith

 against women’s political authority:


«لَنْ يُفْلِحَ قَوْمٌ وَلَّوْا أَمْرَهُمُ امْرَأَةً»


Usually translated as saying that a people governed by a woman will not prosper, it becomes a prohibition irrespective of her competence. Asma Lamrabet, a

Moroccan Islamic feminist thinker

, questions turning a

narration linked

 to Persia’s dynastic succession into a universal ban. She reads it against the Qur’anic Queen of Sheba, whose judgement demonstrates capable leadership. Her argument contests male authority’s claim to divine necessity.


PAM’s promises and its record


Women have long contested how authority is distributed within the family. Fatima Sadiqi

documents

the Union de l’Action Féminine’s 1992 million-signature campaign to reform the Moudawana, Morocco’s family code. The 2004 reform abolished wives’ duty of obedience but retained unequal inheritance and exceptions to the marriage age of eighteen. Proposals announced in December 2024 left fundamental equality demands unresolved. In October 2025, more than sixty civil society organisations and public figures

joined to call for comprehensive reform

. Rights in Morocco have advanced through organised demands, not the gender of an officeholder.


PAM, a centre-right party founded in 2008,

advocates

 social modernisation and positions itself against the Islamist Justice and Development Party (PJD). It entered government in 2021 alongside the National Rally of Independents and conservative nationalist Istiqlal. Opposition to Islamist conservatism, however, does not itself entail reforming the laws and economic conditions that subordinate women.


PAM’s

2026 programme

 promises improved widow pensions, childcare, safe transport, a women’s enterprise fund and labour inspection. The commitments leave inheritance equality, abortion reform and decriminalisation of consensual same sex relations unaddressed. Mansouri called for

banning child marriage

 without exceptions in 2024, yet PAM’s electoral programme

omits that commitment

. Employment can support independence, but a wage does not cancel criminalisation or unequal property rights. The programme leaves those constraints intact.


Even PAM’s narrow promise to increase …

author: WoMin
title: Press Release | Women’s Climate Assembly strengthens Pan African solidarity, women-led resistance and the struggle for a just future
content:
“

Empowering women is a radical way to transform the world!

” –

Ivorian activist


The fourth regional

Women’s Climate Assembly

 (WCA), held in Yaoundé, Cameroon, from 5–8 October 2026, concluded with a powerful reaffirmation of African women’s determination to defend their lands, territories, livelihoods and communities, and to demand climate justice and reparations.


Under the theme, “

Our lands, our voices: African women united for climate justice and reparations!

”, the Assembly convened over 75 women community leaders, activists, feminist organisations, civil society groups and allies from twelve countries including Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Guinea-Conakry, Liberia, Namibia, Niger, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, Senegal and Zambia.


The gathering provided a vital space for women on the frontlines of the climate crisis, extractive industries, land dispossession and environmental destruction to share their experiences, strengthen relationships across borders and build collective strategies for change.


As the Assembly closed, one message rang clear: African women are not merely bearing the costs of the climate crisis. They are leading the struggle for solutions, defending their communities and shaping the future they want.


“

There’s an adage in my village that women cannot build a nation. The Women’s Climate Assembly has proved that women build nations. We counter this adage with the unity and solidarity of African women!”

 –

DRC activist-participant


Turning shared struggles into collective power


From communities confronting oil and gas expansion and destructive mining to women defending forests, seeds, water sources and ancestral lands, participants brought forward the lived realities of communities too often excluded from decisions about their territories and futures.


Through collective reflection, popular education and movement-building, women connected struggles that may take place in different countries but are rooted in common systems of exploitation, inequality and environmental destruction.


Designed by women activists and members of the WCA Steering Committee, the thematic teach-ins explored a range of political concepts, questions and practices, including:


The erosion of farmers’ seeds

: A challenge for building resilient and sustainable food systems. What solutions are there for preserving our seed heritage?  


Nature Commons

: The defence of the Congo Basin’s forests.


Counting the Costs of Mal/Bad Development and Demanding reparations

: The case of the African Development Bank campaign.


Fighting some of the false solutions to the climate crisis

: Gas extraction, enclosure of our forests and lands for carbon trading, green conservation and more.


Building democratic, accountable, ‘loving’ leadership

: Why are these principles so important to feminist leadership? What else do we feel is critical to leading as feminists?


Lessons on organising and movement building

: Growing National/sub-regional grassroots movements.


Building knowledge from what we know

: Building feminist popular knowledge as the basis for Building Women’s Power. How can we go about doing this locally in our communities and beyond that.


The WCA celebrated the knowledge, resistance and organising power of rural, Indigenous, peasant and working-class women. The

Each One, Teach One

 sessions embodied this spirit of knowledge-sharing, collective learning and liberation. On Day Two, participants exchanged practical skills, crafts and tools, sharing techniques for making baobab candies, producing eco-briquettes from cassava and creating seed bricks to cultivate and protect Indigenous seeds. Weaving, cloth-dyeing, beadwork and other practices also featured, affirming the value of knowledge held, practised and passed down through generations of women.


The gathering reaffirmed the importance of strengthening a Pan African ecofeminist movement that recognises the connections between the climate crisis, extractivism, gender injustice, food insecurity and the loss of community control over natural resources.


It also reinforced a fundamental principle: communities must have the power to determine their own futures, including the right to say NO to destructive development projects that threaten their lands, livelihoods and ways of life.


Climate justice means reparations, not empty promises

author: ROAPE
title: African Labour and Liberation
content:
African Labour and Liberation

 brings together the experiences of workers, trade unions and labour movements across the continent to ask what they can tell us about work, power and liberation today. We assembled this collection because of the surprisingly few recent accounts of the emergence of a class politics on the continent. Labour is central to understanding the present political economy of Africa.  More than 90 percent of Africa’s 500 million workers work in informal and precarious jobs in a labour force that will grow rapidly in the next three decades.


The social and political mobilization of workers in multifarious contexts across the continent is imperative to improving their socio-economic conditions. It is necessary to situate Africa’s workers at the centre. This collection starts from the premise that labour struggles are essential to improving the conditions of work and stamping out poverty and inequality that the confronts most African workers today and form the basis for building new forms of collective power.


This heterodox collec­tion finds six primary patterns prevalent in the struggle for the working class liberation in the post-independence era.


1. Most governments in Africa are comprador-bureaucratic regimes beholden to foreign capital and imperialists’ interests to protect and maintain unequal exchange of trade and the attenuation of demands by the masses for national control over natural resources and production. Comprador-bureaucratic regimes remain loyal to their post-colonial powers and pay fleeting attention to national sustainability, the rights of women, natu­ral ecology, and the ever-growing needs of the masses for health care, education, housing, infrastructure, water, and electricity.


Government legislation to defend popular interests that have been enacted by national assemblies are rarely fully implemented and are likely to be opposed by international banks and lenders, predominantly from the West through structural adjustment programs that undermine evanescent attempts to ameliorate the most significant challenges.


2. Diverse workers’ movements form to resist t the comprador-bureaucratic political economies which formed in the colonial era which most often extract surplus value from workers and natural resources from the continent  through what  Arghiri Emmanuel  identified as

unequal exchange of trade

, and despoiling, and plundering African nations. Control is maintained by local elites attached to state power who are beneficiaries of rentier capitalism. These national elites have welcomed Western powers to establish military bases osten­sibly to establish peace and order.


In most instances, the emergence of violence and disorder were generated by Western military intervention. However, as Samir Amin shows, workers and peasants drive the enduring imperative for the formation of national projects for popular sovereignty, which are often imperfect and challenged by imperialists seeking to maintain the unequal exchange of trade.


3. African states are ruled by comprador state-centric bureaucratic elites who maintain rentier capitalism as the primary source of revenue rather than investing in productive technology. The historical pattern is opposition to the redistribution of wealth and income to the masses.


This process, in which bureaucratic elements seek to transform themselves – sometimes successful sometimes not, but nearly always drawing links to imperial­ism and thereby fusing the bureaucratic and comprador elements – can be seen nearly everywhere. Unquestionably, compliant and often corrupt political elites provide the patina of legitimacy for all practical purposes, for the expansion of inequality.


4. In Africa, racial justice must include an anti-imperialist per­spective which acknowledges the legacy of European colonialism and the protracted nature of imperialism which sustains racial subordina­tion. Markedly, South Africa, a semi-peripheral mineral-rich state, did not redistribute wealth and property with the end of political apartheid and the development of a superficially democratic state. Black South Africans, composing over 80 percent of the country’s 65 million popu­lation, remain marginalized through the 1994 accords, which did not include a redistribution of wealth and resources – causing higher levels of poverty and inequality and impeding the working class from improv­ing its living standards.


5. Women constitute a large proportion of the …

author: Caleb Okereke
title: Matthew Blaise wants to be your friend and neighbor
content:
Matthew Blaise and I must have been in our mid teens when we first met. I don’t remember the exact year, but I remember that it was on Facebook. It did not take long for that online connection to become a real friendship, and it is one that has persisted despite life carrying us in different directions.   


When we sit down for this conversation in September, I am in Philadelphia and Matthew is in Brazil. He is preparing for

Friends and Neighbors

, a new art and literary festival in Lagos built around a deceptively simple question: What responsibility do we have to the people we call our friends and our neighbors?


It is a question that makes our own friendship an interesting place from which to begin. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 


Caleb:

 Something I find provocative about the title “Friends and Neighbors” is that you also seem to be making a statement about the ways queerness shows up in the ordinary. I’m thinking about this song, “Your driver could be LGBT, your friend could be LGBT, your neighbour could be LGBT.” Was that part of the conceptual framing?


Matthew:

 Actually, that’s another way to see it. When I thought of this concept, I thought of proximity within our community. A trip from Lagos to Europe is cheaper than a trip from Lagos to Abidjan, which is a neighboring country. For me, that’s a metaphor for what a lot of friendship within the African continent, especially around queerness, has been due to bad policy, homophobia and criminalization.


Queer people within Africa are not so familiar with themselves. And in that sense, we really haven’t constructed what queer Africanness is because we are still not so close to ourselves. But I find it interesting that you also see it from the point of everyday life, where people you come in contact with could be of this community or could possess these identities without you knowing.


Caleb:

 That’s what immediately came to my attention. Even when you say, “Hello, friends. Hello, neighbors,” you’re talking to all of us, right? It’s not “queer friends and neighbors.” The implicit read is that even if you’re straight, queer people are all around you. They’re your friends. They’re your neighbors. They might not tell you that they’re queer, but they’re there.


Matthew:

 From the perspective of bell hooks, societies should be built on love and friendship. This very important foundation of love has been taken away from queer people, or we’ve not been given that due to our queerness. Governmental policies and criminalization also make us live our lives in isolation. What it means to be friends right now is also very transactional, especially for queer people.


Caleb:

 One thing that has defined our friendship, at least for me, is honesty. There are things I can tell you that I can’t tell anybody else, obviously, so a sort of radical honesty. And as you were talking about transactional relationships, it made me think, what is the place of honesty in friendship, especially in a context where being honest about yourself can carry consequences?


Matthew:

 I think you don’t owe everyone that truth about yourself. For those who I truly trust, I owe them that responsibility of truth. And I do believe, for every friendship, there has to be that investment in honesty.


Caleb:

 But friendship in and of itself is a risk. I don’t think we realize that, but every friendship is a risk.


Matthew:

 Yeah, friendship sometimes, I mean, it’s not a constant state of feeling a certain way. It’s a roller coaster of emotions. It’s a journey. It’s an adventure. So you encounter a lot of things on the way.


You stretch your hand to someone and they actually bite your hand, then you know they are not really having that good intention towards you. So you can decide to stretch your hand again or push them away. But for me, I think it’s important that we’re able to stretch our hands and bring people together and do the work of educating them until we just know they’re irredeemable.


Caleb:

 Yeah…


Matthew:

 What responsibility do you think you owe me as your friend?


Caleb:

 You are now the one asking me questions. But no, I mean, I think you owe your friend loyalty. That’s one of the things that I’m non-negotiable on. I mean, there are many other things you owe your friend.


Matthew:

 You owe them honesty also?


Caleb:

 You owe them honesty. You also owe your friends grace. I give grace a lot. Maybe it’s not even grace. I’m also like, oh …

author: Hassan Alnaser, Mohamed Alagra, Mashair Idris
title: Govt scrambles to solve fuel crisis without clear end in sight, divided on fava bean import ban; Quintet tries to balance competing political initiatives; RSF continues Blue Nile push; Military sets sights on Darfur
content:
Subscribe to our Lens on Sudan newsletter

 here

.


The struggling wartime economy took center stage this week in Sudan with a pair of issues at the heart of daily life.


The first is a fuel crisis that has grown increasingly worse in recent weeks as gas stations have become makeshift campsites and prices have skyrocketed. While the government has projected an outward image of assurance, behind closed doors, the wheels are turning to try to bring fuel to the nine states under military control.


The plan has two axes, sources informed of the discussion told Mada Masr. The first is essentially a triage: tighten fuel allocations and movement to where it is needed. Various government bodies have tried their hand at centralizing authority to better streamline decision-making, but Sudan’s fractured executive apparatus has seen more attempts than results.


The second part of the plan would require solving the issue at its source: bringing in new supplies to offset the non-performing domestic oil sector. For this, Transitional Sovereignty Council chair Abdel Fattah al-Burhan is holding talks with Saudi Arabia. But as an informed TSF source told Mada Masr, the government cannot commit to a timeline to end the crisis until external agreements are finalized and the necessary financial guarantees are in place.


Alongside the fuel crisis, more potential trouble looms on the horizon, and this one is of the government’s own making. At the beginning of October, the Agriculture Ministry announced it would implement a prime ministerial decree banning fava bean imports in order to bolster domestic production and save foreign currency. In the last two weeks, the move has come in for fierce public criticism, which has been mirrored by criticism from the government and traders, sources in both arenas told Mada Masr.


The concern centers on whether a domestic agriculture sector strained by war and the fuel crisis can realistically carry the burden of producing enough supply of the daily food staple. Government sources told Mada Masr that the process in announcing the decision was flawed, and the Cabinet does not have the required data to ensure the ban won’t have disastrous effects. State-level administrative officials and traders chimed in to argue that the timing of the decision hasn’t given farmers enough time to adjust this season’s production plan to bolster supply.


While a source in Prime Minister Kamel Idris’s office projected confidence that the Agriculture Ministry has the necessary data to back up the soundness of the ban, a source in the ministry said that officials are already discussing contingency plans.


The political front this week saw yet another spin on the merry-go-round of political initiatives. The Quintet — which comprises the African Union, the United Nations, the Arab League, the European Union and the Intergovernmental Authority on Development — is trying to carefully engage with all competing political initiatives without endorsing any. This comes amid increasing divides between civilian political groups and the preparatory committee leading the government-sponsored internal dialogue over who gets to set its terms and who gets to participate. Both sides of the divide are trying to influence the AU to gain a leg up.


On the military front, the Rapid Support Forces continued this week to push for greater control of the Blue Nile locality of Wad al-Mahi. The military was able to push the advance back in a counteroffensive on October 9.


On the western front, the military launched airstrikes on RSF positions as it looked to translate its control of North Kordofan into a stronger position in West Kordofan to take the strategic city of Nuhud. Control of Nuhud would open the door to North Darfur, on which they already have their sights set, military sources told Mada Masr.


From within Darfur, the military made strategic gains this week, with the joint forces advancing from their remaining garrisons in the north of the region down into West Darfur, where they seized control of the agriculturally rich area of Bir Keleikil.


***


Burhan takes direct control of oil file amid worsening fuel shortages


Crowded gas station in Khartoum, September 27. Courtesy: Nepta Petroleum CO.LTD via Facebook.

author: Shalina Chatlani
title: “No Kings” Shifts Focus to Midterms With Early Voting Day of Action
content:
Over 5 million ballots have been cast, according to an estimate, as Trump faces a historic low in approval ratings.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Organizers launched more than 2,500 No Kings events across all 50 states and the District of Columbia Saturday, this time focusing their efforts on the midterm elections.

From roadside rallies to letter-writing campaigns and protest songs, this round of demonstrations aimed to get people to the polls early.

In the bustling and diverse neighborhood of Jackson Heights, Queens, where Bangladeshi street vendors whip up fuska — crispy, potato-filled shells — and Mexican taquerías serve up al pastor and carne asada, volunteers gathered at a popular local restaurant called The Queensboro. The organizers are part of the Jackson Heights chapter of Indivisible, one of the many grassroots organizations that have made No Kings demonstrations happen.

Arianne Mayer, 49, cofounded the chapter about two years ago after President Donald Trump was elected to his second term. On this “No Kings: Vote Early Day of Action”, she hands out pens and paper to volunteers to write letters to voters in battleground states, encouraging them to get out and cast their ballots as early as possible.

“The practice of mobilization of bodies is really helpful, especially in New York City, where you’re trying to mobilize many thousands of people,” Mayer said. “When you see those thousands of marches, you understand people everywhere are not OK with this, but it’s nice to have a different approach for this event. ”

Mayer, like many people here, said she was deeply frustrated and “disgusted” by the presence of federal immigration agents targeting her neighbors. Many people also said the federal government is implementing increasingly authoritarian policies.

Since summer 2025, the No Kings movement has held multiple massive demonstrations across thousands of sites around the country, attracting millions of people to protest against what they consider to be an overreach of government under the Trump Administration.

This time around organizers shifted their focus, understanding that the midterm elections will determine which political party controls Congress. If it’s the Democrats, they could put up roadblocks to Trump’s agenda. Organizers are hoping the day of early voting could not only increase the pool of voters, but also ease the burden on poll workers on Nov. 3, Election Day.

Voting is in full swing across dozens of states, with over 5 million ballots cast, according to the University of Florida’s Election Lab. Trump faces a historic low in approval ratings.

In Minnesota folk musician Emmett Doyle took to a stage in downtown Minneapolis to perform Lluís Llach’s “L’Estaca,” written in the 1960s in protest of Francisco Franco’s dictatorship in Spain.

Doyle is one of 15 defendants facing federal felony conspiracy charges stemming from protests against U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s crackdown in Minnesota.

“When I was getting pulled out of my truck by federal agents a couple months ago, one of the first things I asked them was, ‘Hey, is this about the songs?’ And they told me, ‘No, it’s about resisting ICE,’” Doyle said to the crowd of about 1,000. “I told them, ‘Well, you’re going to have to arrest all of Minneapolis if you want to hit me for that.’”

Diane Komsky, 67, drove an hour to the No Kings protest in Sioux Falls, South Dakota, because of the “madness in the White House,” she said.

“I want to give peace a real chance for families in the United States,” she said.

Mark Lyons of Centennial, Colorado, said he hadn’t been involved in much political activism or organizing before last year. Saturday’s protest was his fourth No Kings event.

With the midterms approaching, Lyons is hopeful that Democrats will take control of Congress and “put all kinds of checks and balances” on the Trump administration.

“They’ve been stealing the country blind for the last two years,” he said. “There has to be accountability, and it can’t be business as usual.”

At an event in the nation’s capital, 25-year-old Octavia Clapp said using her right to vote especially matters as Trump attempts to wield authority over voting. The Trump administration has spent more than a year in court battles with dozens of states and voting rights groups seeking to force states to provide sensitive voter data and curb voting by mail.
