author: Charlotte Morritt-Jacobs
title: Treaty rights and voting access at centre of Alberta referendum
content:
As Albertans prepare to vote on the province’s future in Canada, Siksika Nation Chief Samuel Crowfoot says the separation debate raises questions about who would honour First Nations treaties and protect the rights they guarantee.


“There’s too many unanswered questions and there’s been no consultation with First Nations, and that’s a requirement as protected by the Constitution.” Crowfoot said.


Crowfoot’s great-great-great-grandfather, chief Crowfoot, was an original signatory of Treaty 7, which established a relationship between the Blackfoot people and the Crown. That treaty predates Alberta’s entry into Confederation in 1905.


The Oct. 19 referendum will ask Albertans whether the province should begin the process of separating from Canada. For First Nations, the question extends beyond provincial politics to treaty obligations, sovereignty and the Crown’s responsibility to uphold agreements protected by the Constitution.


Chief of Siksika Nation, Samuel Crowfoot poses for a photo in his traditional homelands close to where Treaty 7 was signed. Photo: Charlotte Morritt-Jacobs/APTN.


Siksika Nation, Piikani Nation, the Blood Tribe and Athabasca Chipewyan First Nation challenged the decision. On May 13, the Alberta Court of King’s Bench ruled that Alberta breached its duty to consult First Nations in the process leading to the approval of a citizen-led separation petition.


Crowfoot says it’s because of First Nation’s taking legal action that the vote is non-binding, meaning it would not itself make Alberta independent, but it could influence the next steps in the separation debate.


The province and the petition organizer appealed the ruling.


Carly Fox, a lawyer and member of the Kainai Nation, emphasized to APTN News how Alberta had hired outside private practice counsel to handle the appeal rather than relying on Alberta Justice.


“That shows that they’re really interested and willing to put a lot of effort and public money into this, which I think is really upsetting,” Fox said.


Voter Information sessions raise questions 


Fox has been holding information sessions for Siksika Nation and other members of the Blackfoot Confederacy to explain the referendum questions and their potential implications.


“Even though treaty rights are a collective entitlement, I think as an individual, to me, it was important for me to vote and to defend my treaty rights,” Fox said.


She said the referendum questions about immigration could leave voters with a misleading impression of existing rules around access to public services.


“There’s rules for eligibility for income support and for education and for health care,” Fox said. “It’s not a free-for-all, but the way that the questions are framed makes it seem like that.”


Carly Fox is a lawyer and member of the Blood Tribe who has held information sessions to answer questions and create discussion around the referendum and its potential implications for Indigenous communities.  Photo: Charlotte Morritt-Jacobs/APTN.


Crowfoot said the referendum’s questions about immigration also raise concerns for the Blackfoot Confederacy, whose members have family and cultural ties on both sides of the Canada-U.S. border.


The Confederacy includes Siksika Nation, Piikani Nation and the Kainai Nation, also known as the Blood Tribe, in Alberta, as well as the Blackfeet Tribe in Montana.


“Those discussions about immigration don’t take into account First Nations and the unique position that we’re in. And so we have concerns about that,” Crowfoot said.


He said many Siksika members are married to members of the Blackfeet Tribe in Montana, raising questions about how potential changes to immigration rules could affect their ability to cross the border.


“Is that something that can be seen as another obstacle to keep them from their traditional homelands?” he said.


Referendum street signs along the Trans-Canada highway in Calgary. Photo: Charlotte Morritt-Jacobs/APTN.


Federal Responsibility


Prime Minister Mark Carney attended a Forever Canadian Rally in Calgary on Friday and urged  Albertans to vote to keep Canada united, but there was no mention of recognizing treaty rights and the role First Nations played in challenging the separation petition.


Fox called the rally a missed opportunity to build a stronger nation-to-nation relationship.


“I think it would be really nice for him to fully understand First Nations rights and understand our sovereignty and understand why …

author: Andrea
title: ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑐᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᑦ ᐃᓕᓴᖅᓯᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᖁᕕᐊᓲᑎᖃᕐᑐᑦ ᓯᐅᕗᓕᐅᕐᑎᐅᕙᒃᑐᓂᒃ, ᐃᑲᔪᖅᑎᐅᕙᒃᑐᓂ
content:
For the English version of this story, please see

Nunavut Sport and Recreation awards gala honours leaders, volunteers

.


ᓯᕗᓕᐅᕐᑎᐅᓂᖅ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᑎᐅᕙᖕᓂᖅ ᐃᓕᓴᕆᔭᐅᓯᒪᓚᐅᕐᑐᑦ ᐅᕙᓂ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑐᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᑦ ᐃᓕᓴᕆᔭᐅᔾᔪᑎᓕᕆᑎᓪᓗᒋᑦ ᐃᖃᓗᖕᓂ ᐅᕙᓂ ᐊᕐᓴᕐᓃᑦ ᑐᔪᕐᒥᕕᒃᒥ ᐅᒃᑑᐱᕆ 3-ᖑᑎᓪᓗᒍ.


ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑕᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᒥᕐᖑᐃᕐᓯᕐᕕᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᑦ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᖏᑦ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᑐᙵᓱᒃᑎᑦᑎᔨᐅᖃᑕᐅᓚᐅᕐᑐᑦ ᐅᑯᓂᖓ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑐᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᓐᓂ ᐊᒻᒪ ᓄᓇᕗᑦ ᒐᕙᒪᒃᑯᑦ ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑐᓕᕆᔨᖏᓐᓂ.


ᓄᕗᐊᓕᐊ ᑭᐅᕆᐅ ᑭᙵᕐᓂ ᓄᓇᖃᕐᑐᖅ ᐃᓕᓴᕆᔭᐅᔾᔪᑎᑖᖅᑎᑕᐅᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ ᐆᒥᖓ ᑳᒻ ᐃᐅ ᐃᓅᓱᒃᑐᓂ ᓯᕗᓕᐅᕐᑎᐅᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᓵᓚᖃᖅᖢᓂ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᕆᕙᒃᑕᖏᓐᓄᑦ ᐊᐅᔭᒃᑯᑦ ᑲᒪᔨᐅᓪᓗᓂ ᐊᒻᒪᓗ ᐊᖓᔪᖅᑳᕆᔭᐅᓕᖅᖢᖢᓂ ᕼᐋᒻᒪᓚᒃᑯᑦ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕌᓂᒃᑳᖓᑕ ᖃᓄᐃᓕᐅᕈᑎᖏᓐᓄᑦ.


“ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑐᓕᕆᓂᖅ ᐱᒻᒪᕆᐊᓘᒻᒪ ᐃᓅᓱᒃᑐᓄᑦ ᓲᖃᐃᒻᒪ ᖃᓄᐃᑦᑕᐃᓕᓂᒃᑯᑦ ᐱᕈᖅᐸᓪᓕᐊᓂᕐᒨᖓᓂᖓᓄᑦ, ᐃᓱᒪᒃᑯᓪᓗ ᐋᖅᑭᒃᓯᒪᓂᕐᓴᐅᔾᔪᑎᐅᓪᓗᓂ ᐊᒻᒪᓗ ᐊᔪᕈᓐᓃᕐᓴᕈᑎᐅᓪᓗᓂ ᐃᓅᓯᕐᒧᑦ ᐊᑐᕈᓐᓇᖅᑐᓂ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐃᓅᖃᑎᒌᖕᓂᕐᒧᑦ,” ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ ᑭᐅᕆᐅ ᕙᐃᔅᐳᒃᑯ ᐅᒃᑑᐱᕆ 8-ᖑᑎᓪᓗᒍ.


ᐅᓇ ᐊᕐᕌᒍᓕᒃ 18-ᓂ ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑎ ᑲᒪᒋᔭᖃᖃᑦᑕᖅᑐᖅ 40-ᖏᓐᓃᑦᑐᓂ ᓱᕈᓯᕐᓂ ᐊᕐᕌᒍᓕᖕᓂ 5-ᓂ 12-ᓄ 4:00 ᐅᓪᓗᒃᑯᑦ 6:00 ᑎᑭᓐᓇᓱᖕᓂᖓᓂ ᐱᓇᓱᐊᕈᓯᐅᑉ ᐃᓗᐊᒍᑦ ᐃᓅᓱᒃᑐᒃᑯᕕᒃᒥᑦ.


ᑐᓴᕐᓈᖅᑕᐅᔪᑦ ᐅᑯᐊ ᐃᙱᖅᖢᑎ Black Eyed Peas ᐊᒻᒪ ᐊᓯᖏᑦ ᐃᙱᕐᑏᑦ ᑐᓴᕐᓈᕈᑎᒃᑯᑦ ᓂᐱᑭᓵᓯᒪᓪᓗᓂ, ᑭᐅᕆᐅ ᑖᒃᑯᓂᖓ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕐᕕᐅᓪᓗ ᐊᖏᕐᕋᖏᑦᑕᓕ ᐊᓯᐊᒎᖓᓂᒃᑯᑦ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖃᕋᓱᒃᖢᓂ.


ᐃᒡᓘ ᐃᓗᐊᓂ ᖃᓄᐃᓕᐅᕈᑎᐅᔪᓐᓇᖅᑐᓂᒃ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖃᕋᓱᒃᖢᓂ ᐃᓱᒫᓘᑎᖃᕋᓂ “ᐃᓐᓇᕐᓄᑦ ᐱᒡᒍᓴᐅᑎᐅᓇᔭᙳᐊᖅᑐᓂᒃ.”


“ᖃᓄᐃᓕᐅᕈᑎᐅᔪᑦ ᓲᕐᓗ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕐᕕᖕᒦᖅᑰᔨᓐᓇᕈᓐᓃᖅᑎᓪᓗᒍ ᓱᕈᓰᑦ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᓂ ᑲᒪᒋᔭᖃᕐᓂᕐᓴᐅᓕᖃᑦᑕᕐᒪᑕ,” ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ.


ᐅᑯᐊ ᑮᓇᐅᔭᓕᐅᕋᓱᒐᑎᒃ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᖑᔪᑦ ᖁᕕᐊᓲᑎᖃᓚᐅᕐᒥᔪᑦ ᑭᙵᐃᑦ ᐃᓅᓱᒃᑐᓂ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᑎᐅᖃᑦᑕᖅᑐᓂ ᐊᕐᕌᒍᒧᑦ ᐃᓕᓴᕆᔭᐅᔾᔪᑎᓕᕆᓪᓗᑎᒃ.


“ᐃᑲᔪᖅᑐᐃᔨᐅᕙᒃᑐᑦ ᐆᒻᒪᑎᒋᔭᐅᒻᒪᕆᒃᑐᑦ ᓄᓇᓕᖏᓐᓂᒃ,” ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᑦ ᐊᐅᓚᑦᑎᔨ ᑐᑭᒧᐊᖅᑎᑦᑎᔨᖓ ᐃᐅᕋᓐ ᕌᐱᓐᓴᓐ ᐅᖄᓚᐅᑎᒃᑯᑦ ᐊᐱᕐᓱᖅᑕᐅᑎᓪᓗᒍ ᐅᒃᑑᐱᕆ 8-ᖑᑎᓪᓗᒍ.


ᖁᓕᐅᓪᓗᑎᒃ (10) ᐃᓅᓱᒃᑐᑦ ᐊᕐᕌᒍᓖᑦ 13-ᓂ 19-ᒧ ᑖᒃᑯᐊ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᑦ ᒪᓂᒻᒪᐃᓯᒪᔪᑦ ᐅᓗᕆᐊᓇᙱᑦᑐᒥ ᐃᓅᓱᒃᑐᓄᑦ ᐅᐸᒃᑕᐅᕙᒃᑐᓂ ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ.


ᕕᕝᕗᐊᕆᐅᑎᓪᓗᒍ ᑖᒃᑯᐊ ᐃᓅᓱᒃᑐᑦ 200 ᐅᖓᑖᓃᑦᑐᓂᒃ ᕚᓚᓐᑕᐃᓐᔅ ᑕᐃᒥ (ᓇᒡᓕᒍᓱᖕᓇᒥ) ᐅᓪᓛᕈᒻᒥᑕᖅᑎᑦᑎᓚᐅᕐᓯᒪᔪᑦ, ᕌᐱᓐᓴᓐ ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ.


“ᐅᑯᐊ ᐃᓅᓱᒃᑐᑦ ᐃᓱᒪᒋᔭᖃᑦᑎᐊᖅᖢᑎᒃ, ᐱᓕᕆᖃᑎᒌᑦᑎᐊᖅᖢᑎᒃ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐱᒃᑯᒋᔭᖃᖅᖢᑎᒃ ᐱᓕᕆᖃᑲᑦᑕᖅᑐᑦ,” ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ. “ᐊᓯᖏᓐᓄᑦ ᐃᓱᒪᒋᔭᐅᑦᑎᐊᓕᖃᑦᑕᖅᑐᑦ, ᓄᓇᓕᖕᓂ ᐱᕈᖅᑎᑦᑎᕙᓪᓕᐊᓪᓗᑎᒃ ᐊᒻᒪ ᓴᖅᑭᑎᑦᑎᓯᒪᓪᓗᑎᒃ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᑐᐃᕙᖕᓂ ᐊᒻᒪ ᓯᕗᓕᐅᖅᑎᐅᕙᖕᓂᖅ ᖃᓄᐃᓕᖓᓂᖓᓂᒃ.”


ᐃᖃᓗᐃᑦ ᓄᓇᓕᐸᐅᔭᖓᓂ ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑐᓕᕆᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᑐᑭᒧᐊᖅᑎᑦᑎᔨ ᐳᕆᑕᓐ ᒪᒃᓂᐅᓪ ᑐᓂᔭᐅᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑐᓕᕆᓂᕐᒥᒃ ᓯᕗᓕᐅᖅᑎᐅᓂᖓᓄᑦ ᐊᕐᕌᒍᒧᑦ ᐃᓕᓴᕆᔭᐅᔾᔪᑎᒥ.


ᐃᓕᓴᕆᔭᐅᔾᔪᑎᓕᕆᑎᓪᓗᒋᑦ, ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑐᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᑦ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᖏᑦ ᕼᐋᑭᖅᑎᐅᓂᑯᕕᓂᕐᒥ ᔪᐊᑎᓐ ᑐᑐᒥ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐃᓅᔪᓐᓃᕐᓯᒪᓕᕐᑐᒥ ᐅᑭᐅᕐᑕᖅᑐᕐᒥ ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑎᒥ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐋᖅᑭᒃᓱᐃᔨᐅᖃᑦᑕᕐᓂᑯᒥ ᐊᑏᒪ ᕼᐊᓪᓚᕆᒥ ᐃᓕᓴᕆᔭᐅᔾᔪᑎᑖᖅᑎᑦᑎᓚᐅᕐᑐᑦ ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑐᓕᕆᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᐃᓕᓴᕆᔭᐅᔾᔪᑎᓕᕆᓂᕐᒧᑦ (Hall of Fame) ᑖᓐᓇᓗ ᐋᖅᑭᒃᑕᐅᓵᕐᓂᑰᓪᓗᓂ.


ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᑦ ᐊᒻᒪᓗ ᓄᓇᕗᑦ ᒐᕙᒪᒃᑯᑦ ᑐᓂᓯᓚᐅᕐᒥᔪᑦ ᐃᓕᓴᕆᔭᐅᔾᔪᑎᓂ ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑎᓄᑦ, ᐊᐅᓚᑦᑎᔨᖏᓐᓄᑦ, ᐊᒻᒪ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᑎᐅᕙᒃᑐᓄᑦ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ.


ᖁᙱᐊᖅᑐᑦ ᐃᓚᖃᓚᐅᕐᑐᑦ 100 ᐅᖓᑖᓂ ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑐᓕᕆᔨᒻᒪᕆᖕᓂ ᐅᐸᒍᑎᓯᒪᓪᓗᑎᒡᓗ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᑦ ᐱᓇᓱᐊᕈᓯᐅᑉ ᓄᙳᐊᓂ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᕆᔭᐅᔪᒥ.


ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᑦ ᐃᓚᖃᖅᖢᑎᒃ ᐅᑯᓂᖓ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᐹᔅᑭᑦᐹᓪ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᙱᓐᓂᒃ, ᕚᓕᐹᓪ ᓄᓇᕗᑯᓐᓂ, ᓄᓇᕗᑦ ᓵᑯᑯᓐᓂᑦ, ᓄᓇᕗᒥ ᐱᖕᐹᖃᑦᑕᖅᑐᑦ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᖏᓐᓂ, ᐃᖃᓗᒃᑑᑦᑎᐊᕐᒥ ᐅᓇᑕᖃᑦᑕᖅᑐᑦ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᙱᓐᓂ ᐊᒻᒪ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᐹᑦᒥᓐᑕᓐᑯᓐᓂ ᑐᙵᓱᒃᑎᑦᑎᔨᐅᓪᓗᑎᒃ ᐃᖃᓗᖕᓂ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕐᕕᖕᒥ ᐃᖃᐃᓕᓴᕐᕕᖏᓐᓂᒃ ᐅᒃᑑᐱᕆ 3-ᒥ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐅᒃᑑᐱᕆ 4-ᒥ.

author: Kevin Carson
title: Review. CLR James: Cultivator of the Popular Will, by Matthew Quest
content:
Matthew Quest.

CLR James: Cultivator of the Popular Will. A Study of the History and Politics of World Revolution

 (Brill, 2026).


As Matthew Quest notes in his appendix, “Top Ten Reasons We Don’t Know More about CLR James,” CLR James is a relatively obscure thinker even among the African-American left. This is doubly so on the left more generally. According to Quest, James’ thought occupies a marginal position on the left primarily because his fundamental orientation — an affinity for direct democracy and workers’ self-management — is fundamentally at odds with the centralized, mass-based politics of the Old Left, whether Marxist-Leninist or Social Democratic. He was hostile to the British Labour Party and Atlee, the US Democratic Party and FDR, and to post-independence African leaders who were lionized elsewhere on the left. He saw nation-states and vanguard parties as mostly destructive rather than helpful, and the history of nationalization by progressive governments as hostile to self-management. James also saw the class reductionism of the dominant currents of the left, with their neglect of racial and anti-colonial dimensions of struggle, as failing to meet the needs of the time.


Quest himself is a perfect fit for intellectual biographer of James, as a historian and critic of national liberation movements in Africa and elsewhere in the colonial and post-colonial world, as well as post-independence governments. James’ central values of direct democracy and self-governance resonate strongly with Quest’s hostility — which come through clearly in these quotes from his Preface — to self-serving establishments, Black, revolutionary, and/or “progressive.”


The search for identity and heritage, in all their proper cultural nuances, for those who have known scars, exploitation, and who are overcoming insecurity, cannot be permitted to be captured by those who define freedom as managing subordinate lives. This is how all who fatefully embrace the state define it. These are the facts of the long duration of post-civil rights, post-colonial existence.


…Hopefully, we have now learned that the challenge to respectability politics without opposition to elite representative government is a fraud….


We are living in an affirmative action empire and ethnically plural police state alongside subcontractors of guilt and activists for the government, funded by the white rich, talking about privilege. We have people lecturing us about the problem of ‘colour blindness’ who are not opposed to the police state; they are explicitly part of the boss class who murder, mass incarcerate, and get out the vote for those who exploit.


* * *


…[W]hen I questioned whether the working people of Cuba actually governed that country, many dedicated revolutionaries, socialists, and anti- imperialists replied that it did not matter. For most insulted by the historical denial of self-determination of conquered peoples and for most organising for some future socialism or communism, it did not matter whether ordinary people directly governed or not. This should shake those who are not Machiavellians to the core. We should not be so thirsty for empowerment that we will accept a half-made or second-hand society as a dwelling to sustain our search for liberation.


…No workers or youth to whom we were introduced asked questions about their contradictions. Surely, ordinary people in Cuba asked these questions but were not featured on the directed tours and cultural events. This raised questions about the democratic content and the political economy of the socialist future and the ethics of those who took part in such projects.


* * *


CLR James famously said: ‘Political treachery is not the monopoly of the white race’. He also said there are Black people who treat Black toilers like ‘colonial trustees’, and while they talk of desiring ‘independence’ and ‘power’ they already live a ‘delightful’ existence at the toilers’ expense.


James’ life (1901-1989) spanned the Russian Revolution, the rise and fracturing of Marxism-Leninism, and postwar national liberation movements, and intersected with them at numerous points.


Born in Trinidad, he lived in numerous countries over the course of his lifetime. His activist career was wide-ranging and global; as Quest writes, “James and his associates worked for an American revolution, a Caribbean revolution, African revolution, and world revolution.” He authored numerous historical works, including

The …

author: By Darren Thompson, Contributor
title: Mining in the Sacred and Stolen Black Hills, Then and Now
content:
The colonization of the Black Hills by the U.S. government is one of the most well-known land thefts in American history. Since gold was discovered in the sacred lands of Paha Sapa or Ȟe Sápa, also known as the Black Hills, more than 150 years of tragedy, land exploitation, and legal issues followed and continue to this day.


When rumors began to spread in the 19th century that gold was found in the Black Hills, U.S. Army General George Armstrong Custer led a 1,000 man expedition in 1874 to find out for himself. When the discovery became public, thousands rushed to the Black Hills — trespassing on Indian Territory — to also find out for themselves.


The Black Hills were then a part of the Great Sioux Reservation and belonged to the Great Sioux Nation as promised in the Fort Laramie Treaty of 1868 which reserved lands for the exclusive use and occupation by the Great Sioux Nation, including the Black Hills. Any cession of any part of the reservation required a new treaty executed and signed by at least three-fourths of all adult male Indians occupying the land.


One of the provisions of the 1868 Treaty was that white men were forbidden from stepping foot on the reservation, except for officials of the U.S. government. 


The discovery of gold led to thousands of white men trespassing in the Black Hills with the U.S. government rushing to colonize the area and take ownership.


Map of a reconnaissance of the Black Hills, July and August, 1874, with troops under command of Lt. Col. G.A. Custer, 7th Cavalry

via

 Library of Congress.


The Lakota — also known as the Great Sioux Nation — and the Cheyenne refused to cede ownership, resulting in many confrontations which ultimately culminated in the Battle of the Little Bighorn (also called Custer’s Last Stand and the

Battle of the Greasy Grass

).


On June 25-26, 1876, the U.S. Army’s 7th Cavalry — led by Gen. George Custer — was completely defeated by an encampment of thousands of Lakota, Cheyenne and Arapaho people along the Little Bighorn River in Montana.


Painting of the Battle of the Greasy Grass or Little Bighorn by

Martin Pate

 exhibited in Journey Museum in Rapid City.


After the U.S. defeat at the Battle of the Little Bighorn, Congress responded by cutting off all rations for the Sioux until all hostiles were terminated or imprisoned and the tribe would cede the Black Hills to the U.S.


The Indian Appropriations Act of 1876, enacted on August 15 of that year, was aimed at acquiring the Black Hills by sale or otherwise starve the people. In 1877, a new treaty was presented by a commission headed by George Manypenny, and some signed the treaty under the threat of starvation, with the Black Hills being taken.


“In any first-year contracts course, we teach that a valid agreement requires mutual assent (an agreement by all parties),” Danielle Finn told Unicorn Riot. Finn is Standing Rock Sioux tribal citizen and professor of Lakota Law at William S. Boyd School of Law at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas.


“What the Manypenny Commission presented to the Sioux in 1876 fails that test categorically,” Finn said, “the Fort Laramie Treaty — a binding instrument under the Supremacy Clause — required the signatures of three-fourths of all adult male Sioux to cede any portion of their reservation. The ‘agreement’ that was actually presented to the Sioux was signed by only 10% of the adult male Sioux population. No legitimate legal system would call that consent. The Supreme Court didn’t either.”


The taking of the Black Hills has been challenged several times in federal court by the tribes ultimately resulting in a Supreme Court decision that ruled in favor of the tribes’ claim.


Justice Harry Blackmun delivered the Supreme Court’s opinion in 1980,

United States v. Sioux Nation of Indians

, and wrote that the tribes were never fairly compensated for the taking of the Black Hills and that they should be. The tribes were entitled to an award of at least $17.5 million, without interest, as damages under the Indian Claims Commission Act of 1946.


“What all people must understand is that the Supreme Court’s holding here was not a gesture of sympathy, it was a constitutional determination,” Finn said. “When the Court confirmed that the 1877 Act constituted a ‘taking’ under the First Amendment, it was applying the same Takings Clause that protects any American property owner from government seizure without just compensation.”

author: Halie Moses
title: The Z Factor: Young Voters and the 2026 Midterms
content:
Generation Z voters (aged 18-29) are predicted to make a significant impact on the upcoming 2026 Midterm elections. This has not always been the case, as student and youth voter turnout has historically remained low. Only 47% of Americans aged 18-29 voted in the 2024 election. This year, 50 million Gen Z Americans are eligible to vote.

In October, a report by UCLA’s William Institute examined the political priorities and voting intentions of Gen Z adults ahead of the 2026 midterms. The study found that nearly 74 percent of respondents said they were likely or certain to vote. These numbers come as no surprise to those who work with students, spend time organizing on college campuses, or identify as Gen Z during the Trump Administration. Rising living costs, ICE raids, attacks on reproductive rights access, sexual assault cases, climate change, and unwanted wars have directly impacted their lives and are driving them to the polls with a passion for change.

Leela Strong, Director of CIRCLE, who works to empower the youth vote, reflected: “Young people are sending us clear signals, not only of dissatisfaction with our politics and deep economic concerns, but also of a strong desire to take action and drive change.” Organizations such as When We All Vote are working to engage young people by connecting their priorities with the issues and candidates on their ballots. Opportunities to participate alongside friends and classmates can also encourage young people to become more involved in politics.

Campus organizing is another part of these efforts. The Feminist Majority Foundation’s Feminist Campus program is actively working to get the student vote out. Students can help their peers register to vote, understand their ballot, and march to the polls in solidarity. These efforts are particularly important for first-time voters, who may need guidance.

Not only are young people planning to vote, but they are also planning to vote overwhelmingly Democratic. In the September Economist/YouthGov Poll, when asked who they will cast their ballot for, 54% of 18-29-year-olds said the Democratic candidate, compared with 22% who said the Republican candidate. The same survey found a sentiment among youth that reflects that the Republican Party is too extreme. When asked, “Do you think the Republican Party is too extreme?” 65% of 18- 29-year-olds replied yes. In contrast, only 29% believe the Democratic Party is too extreme. These results reflect the views of respondents at the time of the survey and do not necessarily predict how young people will vote in November.

These numbers are significant and show promising signs that young people are empowered to change the course of our political and social reality. Voter registration, accessible election information, and campus organizing can help young people navigate the voting process and participate in decisions that affect their futures. To learn more, head to vote411.org/feminist.

author: Aaron Hemens, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: As parts of the Nicola River run dry, a father fears what his children will inherit
content:
Brian Holmes, a councillor for the Upper Nicola Band, walks through a dry stretch of the Nicola River on Sept. 18, 2026, a few minutes downstream from his community of spaxmn (Douglas Lake) in the Nicola Valley, in B.C.’s southern interior.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


On this stretch of the Nicola River, Brian Holmes misses the sound of water. 


“This is heartbreaking,” he quietly says to himself as he prepares to park above a kilometre-long stretch where no surface water remains.


In the absence of the river’s flow, birds can be heard in the thick vegetation, their calls occasionally joined by a horse neighing in the distance or a car passing along Douglas Lake Road above.


The 44-year-old Upper Nicola Band (UNB) member and father of two leaves his vehicle and disappears into the bush separating the river from a small ranch below the road, a few minutes downstream from his community of spaxmn (Douglas Lake) in the Nicola Valley, in “B.C.’s” southern interior. 


He re-emerges from the bush and makes his way down a steep slope into the exposed riverbed, where large boulders rise from a channel that should be running with water on this warm mid-September morning.


The Nicola River winds roughly 210 kilometres through syilx and Nlakaʼpamux homelands. It flows from its headwaters on the Thompson-Okanagan Plateau, down through Douglas and Nicola lakes before passing through Merritt, and eventually joining the Thompson River northeast of Lytton at Spences Bridge.


But along this one-kilometre dry stretch between Douglas and Nicola Lakes, just around the corner from the community’s drinking water, the waterway resembles more of a meandering valley of rocks.


“I’ve been looking at it enough that it’s numb to me now. This didn’t happen yesterday. It’s been like this for the last month,” said Holmes.


He said that it’s tough to see dried-up sections of the river, especially “when you know there should be water.”


“It’s supposed to be the major river system in this watershed, but it doesn’t have any water flowing through it over the surface,” Holmes said.


“We’ve seen a little bit of a flow coming out of Douglas Lake, but it’s going to get sucked in by the groundwater now. There is a little trickle, but then it just disappears partway down. Any water that pops up anywhere is all groundwater.”


Just upstream, on a bend in the river, there’s a deep hole in the waterway that Holmes and his friends used as a makeshift natural swimming pool every summer when they were children.


Brian Holmes, a councillor for the Upper Nicola Band, stands near a deep hole in the Nicola River that he and his friends swam in as children, in his community of spaxmn (Douglas Lake) on Sept. 18, 2026.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


“I don’t know if you would swim in it now,” he said, citing health concerns from a buildup of harmful algae blooms in the water.


“I’m hoping by the time (my sons) get to my age, they can enjoy it. If we’re in these (drought) cycles — hopefully we can survive long enough.”


He walks across the dry riverbed, using the boulders as stepping stones, then stops for a moment and looks downstream to where water should be flowing.


Brian Holmes, a councillor for the Upper Nicola Band, walks through a dry stretch of the Nicola River on Sept. 18, 2026, a few minutes downstream from his community of spaxmn (Douglas Lake) in the Nicola Valley, in B.C.’s southern interior.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


“It’s like another world, man. It’s — I don’t know. It just makes me think about missing that sound of water flowing,” Holmes said.


“When you walk down a stream, and there’s no water, it’s like losing a relative, losing a part of you. It’s just hard to explain.”


A few dozen kilometres up the river from this spot, where the stream converges with Chapperon Creek before flowing into Douglas Lake, IndigiNews observed smaller dry patches along the waterway’s surface as well.


A dry patch of the Nicola River, at its confluence with Chapperon Creek northeast of Douglas Lake, on Sept. 18, 2026.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


The watershed entered the growing season with little room to spare. In March, “B.C.’s” River Forecast Centre

forecast seasonal inflows

 to the Nicola River and Nicola Lake at just 40 to 60 per cent of normal, citing low snowpack, dry weather and already-low flows.


By mid-June, the Nicola basin was a Level 4 on

the province’s drought scale

, the second-highest rating. It remained at that level in mid-July and had reached …

author: Admin101
title: Sanctuary as a Verb: Experiences and Directions from Transversal Organizing for Immigrant Defense
content:
Black Rose/Rosa Negra Anarchist Federation (BRRN) is excited to announce the publication of

Sanctuary as a Verb: Experiences and Directions from Transversal Organizing for Immigrant Defense

.


Drawing on organizing experiences of Black Rose/Rosa Negra members across the United States, this pamphlet explores how workers, neighbors, and communities are building collective resistance to ICE and defending their immigrant coworkers, classmates, and loved ones. By connecting struggles across workplaces, schools, and neighborhoods, the

transversal organizing

 approach we prioritize builds solidarity across different sectors of society to confront the interconnected structures of domination that shape our lives.


You can find a downloadable PDF version of the pamphlet at the end of this text.


Two Years of Trump II: Immigrants in the Crosshairs, Resistance Under Attack


Upon returning to office, Donald Trump wasted little time fulfilling his white supremacist campaign pledge of “Mass Deportations Now.” Via a flurry of executive orders and congressional acts his administration reinstated the reviled “family separation” policy; directed virtually unlimited resources to stop a fictitious “invasion” of the country’s borders; and sought to end birthright citizenship. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents blitzed Los Angeles in June 2025 with spectacular raids, followed shortly by similar operations in dozens of cities across the country including New York City; Chicago, IL; New Orleans, LA; and Durham, NC. This “shock and awe” strategy culminated in Operation Metro Surge, a months-long invasion of the Minnesota Twin Cities that deported over 2,000 residents. 


Meanwhile, support for the deportation machine plummeted as collective action against it swelled. Everyday people covered their cars, lawns, and lips with the slogan “Abolish ICE;” as of July 2026, nearly 50% of US adults support such a measure. Both May Days since Trump’s second inauguration centered immigrant defense in their celebrations. Rapid-response networks that keep watch for ICE, document kidnappings, and sometimes disrupt them spread wildly. Know-your-rights training flourished at worksites and community centers. Millions of Red Cards–wallet-sized cards outlining the holder’s constitutional protections around interactions with ICE and other police–were distributed at schools, churches, restaurants, and municipal buildings. Children and their parents caged in concentration camps went on hunger strike as constituents bombarded politicians’ hotlines and town halls demanding humanitarian treatment and release outside their walls.


Popular responses in St. Paul and Minneapolis demonstrate the possibilities of mass resistance. Like the Los Angeles Tenant Union’s community defense centers that countered ICE’s Southern California invasion, organizers reactivated dormant neighborhood networks from the 2020 uprising and began building new ones when word spread that Commander-at-Large Greg Bovino was bringing his paramilitary forces to town. Once Operation Metro Surge launched, everyday Minnesotans refined sophisticated systems to track, delay, and disrupt arrests. ICE agents retaliated by killing rapid-responder Renée Good and shooting Julio C. Sosa-Celis, a Venezuelan immigrant targeted for deportation. Instead of cowering from the naked clampdown, neighborhood networks coordinated with unions, churches, and other civil societal organizations to shut down their cities on January 23rd. In its wake, Trump ousted Bovino and immigration enforcement plummeted.


But July 2026 saw record high immigrant detentions since Trump’s return to office with little public opposition. What explains it? ICE’s tactical shifts undoubtedly played a role. Bovino replacement and “Border Czar” Tom Homan traded provocative street operations with quiet detainers at jails and prisons and “targeted operations” at sites protected from activist impediment like airports. Escalating repression has also raised the costs of resistance. ICE’s bevy of brutality has included intimidation, beatings, and shootings, culminating in murdering Good and rapid-responder Alex Pretti. Federal grand juries fish from the shadows for information about our movements, stoking fears of informants that slow our organizing. From the Prairieland defendants to the Minnesota 15 and more, indictments and convictions on flimsy charges could make prosecuting dissidents even easier. Evidentiary discovery in the …

author: Daniel Hunter
title: How Vermont shut down ICE
content:
This article

How Vermont shut down ICE

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


After Operation Metro Surge, the Trump administration moved to rein in the Bovino-style spectacle with its made-for-TV arrests. In an attempt to avoid another public outcry, Immigration and Customs Enforcement has quietly settled into a new rhythm.


Arrests have still increased month after month, reaching

a record high

 of roughly 51,000 people taken into ICE custody in August. This is part of a new surge — carried out in hospitals, courthouses and airports — with an intent to stay off the nightly news. As

The


New York Times


reported

, this phase is “captured mostly by grainy security camera footage, through cracked blinds and from behind closed doors.” 


This phase is also backed by a dragnet of data. At airports, ICE has been

running name matches with TSA to detain people

 at check-in counters and gates. It has found a backdoor into the country’s license-plate cameras: Records show local and state police

ran more than 4,000 immigration-related searches

 on Flock’s camera network in a single year. (Yet another reason

Flock cameras should not exist

.)


Perhaps surprisingly, much of the tech infrastructure driving ICE’s new surge is headquartered in … Vermont. The town of Williston, outside Burlington, is home to both ICE’s

Law Enforcement Support Center

, which houses the agency’s national tip line, and ICE’s National Criminal Analysis and Targeting Center, or NCATC, its social-media surveillance hub. 


Sign Up for our Newsletter


We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.


As ICE tries a new approach, this new phase of resisting ICE requires moving to more offense — and the people of Vermont are offering us some clear lessons. 


Vermont resistance


Resistance started with the fight over flights. Early in Trump’s second term, activists

documented

 ICE moving detainees onto commercial flights out of Burlington’s airport — more than 450 people as of mid-July 2025, by their count. They showed up in airports as witnesses and disruptors, sometimes aided by empowered flight attendants. They forced an ICE retreat: organizers say

ICE hasn’t moved detainees through the airport in more than a year

.


More recently they’ve gone after the hard infrastructure. Sit-ins at the White Cap Business Park in Williston, where the NCATC facility is located, have led to arrests for allegedly blocking the entrance to the ICE offices, including

11 people in February and 13 in July.


After those arrests came some unusual twists, which speak volumes about the courage it takes to refuse unjust orders and to continue protesting in the face of repression.


Complicity and noncooperation


Responses to authoritarianism are as old as a time — many of the same dynamics from Vermont show up in the ancient story of Pharaoh and Moses.


Undeniably the most powerful person in his land, Pharaoh was the ultimate authoritarian. His big trick was taking beautiful work and turning it evil. Take the work of midwives, whose job is to usher life into the world — he turned that work into ugliness by ordering the Hebrew midwives to kill every newborn boy. 


But we all have a choice. And famously, several of the midwives refused. Their act of noncooperation with an unjust order is the reason Moses lived.


We are living through a moment when institution after institution is being turned toward evil. Some, like the Department of Justice, were already a mixed bag. But now it is being turned against the very logic of due process it claims to serve, as we’ve seen recently with the

criminal indictment of whistleblower Cassidy Hutchinson

. Other institutions, like the Environmental Protection Agency and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, are being perverted, with

great resistance from insiders

 who cling to the key values that these agencies were founded on.


Previous Coverage


The movement to defend the Minneapolis 15


In Vermont, the local prosecutor, Chittenden County State’s Attorney Sarah George, faced her own choice. When asked to

That makes sense: No one was harmed, and the protesters have a strong necessity defense — the argument that they were preventing an even greater harm. Every minute that ICE isn’t taking part in abducting people is good for the country.

author: Unknown
title: The Encampment Movement against Evictions and Gentrification : A Report from Madrid and Barcelona
content:
On September 23, 2026, Spanish authorities violently evicted Maricarmen Abascal, a disabled 87-year-old woman, from her home in Madrid following her long judicial struggle with a real estate company named Urbagestión. She had lived there for 70 years, but could not afford the latest rent increases. In response, 10,000 people took the streets in protest that day. Three days later, a much larger demonstration established an encampment in the Puerta del Sol square, which had been the site of the

15-M movement

 in 2011, itself the trigger for the

Occupy

 movement in the United States.


Maricarmen Abascal passed away on October 7 as a consequence of the stress resulting from the eviction. Protesters have continued to occupy the squares in many cities across the Iberian Peninsula. A general strike has been called for November 11.


Here, our correspondents in Madrid and Barcelona offer a view from within the movement against evictions and gentrification that has spread across Spain and Catalunya.


Anti-fascists gather to defend the housing encampment in Madrid’s Plaza del Sol, 2026.


The housing movement in Spain has a long and complex history. For any period that we might choose as a point of departure, there always exists a prior precedent that could serve just as well—so where we begin depends on how we wish to make sense of what is happening today, how we wish to narrate this story that is still being written in the streets. What follows, then, is an attempt, however insufficient and incomplete, to tell this story, in hopes that you can learn or be inspired by something from it and, in this way, become part of this story and build upon it wherever you live.


We could perhaps begin with the

15-M movement

, which erupted a decade and a half ago as part of the sequence of uprisings that unfolded across the globe in 2011. Encampments spread across Spain much as they have today, full of people clamoring for “

real democracy

.”


Whereas elsewhere, repression often put these movements to an unresolved end, in Spain, this movement culminated with the formation of several far-left political parties, including Podemos, as well as strong municipalist movements in Madrid, Barcelona, and other cities. Today, these parties lie in ruins, while the municipalists have largely lost whatever power they once held. Ultimately, much like

Occupy Wall Street

 and the Arab Spring, the true legacy of this sequence remains ambiguous, contested, and open to interpretation. Perhaps the 15-M movement is not the beginning of the story we’re telling, but simply the ruins from which the current one is being told.


Riot police are covered in eggs and paint while attempting to evict a building in Barcelona, 2021.


The movement that is now swelling across Spain emerged as a result of strong and stable union-style organizations that operate apart from the official institutional structures that are otherwise so present and influential in political life here. These organizations were built to tackle the housing crisis using horizontal and grassroots power, while simultaneously driving widespread and popular mobilizations like those we are witnessing today. These unions are novel in that they don’t involve questions of work directly, but rather address the conditions in which we live. The movement’s most significant antecedents lie in the creation of organizations such as the PAH (Platform for People Affected by Mortgages), the first chapter of which was founded in Barcelona in 2009. Like the more recently created housing organizations, the PAH groups practice what we call “social unionism.”


The premise is simple: an individual problem like a person facing the threat of losing their home is transformed into a collective issue addressed through shared political action. A variety of union-style tactics soon began to emerge, leading to the halting of many imminent evictions.


A group of thirty or so people assembles in front of an apartment in the historic city center as the sun is rising. People cling to one another tightly, locked arm in arm, crowding in front of the door of the building’s entrance while several vans of riot police pull up and park nearby as scheduled. There’s an announcement from a police loudspeaker to the effect that people must disperse, but no one does. Eventually, the cops move in, struggling to pull each person away one by one, until finally everyone has been cleared. In the end, the eviction is successful, but it …

author: Valerie Anne
title: ‘The Body’ Is a Sapphic, Ritual-Gone-Wrong Teen Horror Show Coming to Netflix
content:
Do you ever feel like a show was made just for you using all your favorite media keywords? That’s how I felt when I first heard about Netflix’s The Body. I saw Catholic school, dancers, ritual-gone-wrong, horror and I was beyond sold.

And in case those words and phrases didn’t make it obvious: The story is also sapphic. Writer and creator Quinn Shephard (who acted in movies like The Miseducation of Cameron Post and wrote/directed episodes of Under the Bridge) started writing the show the year she came out. She says: “It’s satirizing some of the trauma of growing up queer and repressed and the confusion around that.”

A lot of the main cast of girls are relative newcomers on the scene (aka they don’t have Wikipedia “personal life” pages yet) so I’m not sure who among them are queer, but the show WILL feature lesbian reality star Gabby Windey in a recurring role as a coach. Also, almost all of the episodes have women listed as writers.

The show looks freaky and weird in all the best ways, and I can’t wait. I hope it’s just as fun as shows like Yellowjackets and even Mike Flanagan’s Carrie. May the teens-getting-into-supernatural-mischief genre never die.

The series drops next month and you can watch the full official trailer right now!

author: Elizabeth Weill-Greenberg
title: Tablets Make Communication Easier Behind Bars – But Deaf People Are Left Behind
content:
This story was co-published with


Truthout

.


Tablet computers have revolutionized communication inside prisons for hearing prisoners. Prison systems from across the country — including in

New York

,

California

, and

Illinois

 — have

distributed tens of thousands

 of tablets to incarcerated people, which they can use to call home, watch movies, message loved ones, or attend virtual classes (although they are often

charged predatory fees

 for accessing these benefits). As of 2022,

25 state prison systems

 had tablet distribution programs, according to the Electronic Privacy Information Center. 


But as the rollout of such tablets continues, many deaf incarcerated people have been left behind. 


Disability justice organization HEARD points out that

it’s

unknown

 how many deaf people are incarcerated in U.S. prisons, but a

2015 report

 by the Bureau of Labor Statistics estimated that 6.2 percent of incarcerated people in

state

 and

federal

 prisons have a hearing disability, which would equal about 71,000 people.


Daniel Valenzuela, who is deaf, is incarcerated at Danville Correctional Center in Illinois. Last year, the Illinois Department of Corrections (IDOC)

distributed tablets

 to all incarcerated people. But IDOC blocks videophone capabilities, preventing Valenzuela from communicating in his primary language, American Sign Language (ASL).  


In September, Valenzuela sued the IDOC director for violating the Americans with Disabilities Act.


“I have six kids, four grandkids, and one of my sons is in the military. I cherish and love my family so much,” said Valenzuela in a

press release

 announcing the lawsuit. “I just want to tell them happy birthday and I am so grieved when I can’t call because I don’t want them to think I forgot.”


There are at least three other deaf individuals at Danville who primarily use ASL to communicate, according to the

complaint

 filed by Disability Rights Advocates, Equip for Equality, and the law firm Much Shelist. 


“Across the Illinois Department of Corrections, people can use tablets to communicate with their loved ones, which has been a game changer in removing restrictions on communication,” Valenzuela’s attorney, Rachel Weisberg, the directing attorney at Disability Rights Advocates, told

Truthout

. “But for Mr. Valenzuela and other deaf people who use American Sign Language, that same access simply isn’t available.” 


IDOC did not respond to a request for comment by the time of publication.


Last year, in addition to distributing tablets to incarcerated people, IDOC

announced

 it would provide every incarcerated person with 775 free domestic phone call minutes per month. In a press release,

IDOC said

 that these initiatives, working in tandem, “enhance family connections and increase access to technology that supports rehabilitation.” 


But deaf prisoners are excluded from accessing these critical programs. 


Unlike hearing prisoners who can use their tablets to make calls from their cells, Valenzuela must get a guard’s permission to walk to another building to use the one videophone that’s available to him. In at least one instance, Valenzuela had to go out in the pouring rain to use the videophone, according to the complaint. 


“When prison officials don’t communicate with deaf/disabled people in ways they can understand, they may be written up for being ‘non-compliant.'”


The videophone is often unavailable because the unit itself breaks down, the prison is on lockdown, or a guard denies his request, according to the complaint. Last year, Valenzuela was unable to speak with his family during the holidays because the phone was not working for 54 straight days, from November 2025 to January 2026. However, if the tablets malfunction, there are several backup phones that incarcerated hearing people can use, the complaint says.


“We’re asking for equal access, as that’s what the law requires,” said Weisberg. “Equal access is not static — it must reflect the benefits currently offered to others and account for the needs of people with disabilities as technology and communication systems evolve.”


These issues are not limited to Illinois. Advocates say incarcerated deaf people have to contend with discriminatory communication practices in prisons throughout the country.


“In prisons where we’ve seen scores of deaf/disabled people, there may only be 2 videophones,” Kah Mendoza, the communications coordinator for

HEARD

, told …

author: Rizomatica
title: Comunidad María Colipi Viuda de Maril manifiesta su apoyo a los PPM David y Javier Mariñán Millahual
content:
Tirua 5 de Octubre de 2026


Carta de Apoyo David y Javier Mariñán


Sres.


A quien corresponda:


A través de esta carta, venimos a manifestar nuestro apoyo moral y respaldo a los miembros de nuestra comunidad, David Mariñán Millahual y Javier Mariñán Millahual, quienes han sido condenados por el Tribunal Oral en lo Penal de Cañete, a la pena de 84 años de prisión.


Los hemanos David y Javier Mariñán son miembros activos de nuestra Comunidad Indigena Maria Colipi Viuda de Maril, residen aquí desde su infancia y, hasta el momento de ser encarcelados, participaban cotidianamente de las actividades propias de nuestra cultura mapuche, destacando en su interés por las prácticas culturales tradicionales.


Es de destacar que, en el caso de David Mariñán, él llegó a presentarse al Tribunal de Cañete voluntariamente al enterarse que era requerido por una causa en la que salió unánimemente absuelto. Posteriomente, fueron notificados de esta nueva investigación en su contra, en el cual ambos fueron condenados de una forma poco transparente, pues su supuesta participación en los hechos se basa solamente en el testimonio de testigos protegidos.


La familia de los hermanos David y Javier Mariñán nos ha comunicado su decisión de acudir a tribunales internacionales si es que no obtienen justicia en Chile, lo cual como comunidad respaldamos, pues el año 2014 la Corte Interamericana ya condenó al Estado de Chile en un caso similar.


A través de esta carta saludamos a nuestros socios David y Javier Mariñăn Millahual, solidarizando con ellos y su familia en estos momentos difíciles que enfrentan.

author: CMI Argentina
title: Las puertas de la distopía tecnológica se cierran de golpe
content:
Hay un video que se ha vuelto viral en el que se ve a un grupo de jabalíes atrapados en una trampa de corral. Cuando la puerta se cierra de golpe, los pobres animales corren de un lado a otro presas del pánico, buscando en vano una salida.


Según el texto que acompaña el video, el cazador esperó pacientemente durante cinco días a que toda la manada se sintiera lo suficientemente cómoda como para morder el cebo y entrar en la trampa todos a la vez. La puerta no se cerró hasta que el último jabalí entró en el cerco.


Y, sí. Eso es más o menos en donde estamos ahora mismo.


Estamos ahí parados comiéndonos nuestro cebo, disfrutando de nuestros panes y de nuestros circos, felizmente ajenos al cazador que espera pacientemente el momento perfecto para cerrar la puerta de golpe y dejarnos atrapados a todos.


“Che, qué buena que es la IA”


“¡Miranos a todos como personajes de Miyazaki!”


“¡Dejé que ChatGPT eligiera mi ropa de hoy!”


“¡Escribí una canción con solo teclear un prompt! ¡Estoy haciendo música!”


“¡Ahora TODOS somos artistas!”


“¡Ay, carajo, la puerta se acaba de cerrar!”


“¡Están escuchando todo lo que decimos!”


“¡Mierda, hay drones de la policía por todos lados!”


“¡Le están poniendo armas a esos perros robot!”


“¡La IA estatal canceló mi dinero digital porque intenté formar un sindicato!”


“¡Dije “Palestina libre” y ahora no puedo acceder a Internet!”


Durante todo este tiempo han estado construyendo en silencio una jaula a nuestro alrededor con el fin de encerrarnos para siempre en esta distopía capitalista. Los oligarcas y los gerentes del imperio han estado desarrollando rápidamente tecnologías que facilitarán la vigilancia masiva y los sistemas de armas autónomas —que

ya se están probando en el terreno

 en lugares como Gaza—, que casualmente son exactamente lo que la clase dominante necesita para socavar y aplastar cualquier movimiento revolucionario que pudiera surgir en respuesta a los abusos y las desigualdades cada vez mayores del capitalismo.


El cazador nos está llevando pacientemente a aceptar la vigilancia masiva, el avance sin límites de la inteligencia artificial, los robots militarizados, los drones policiales, las monedas digitales, y la propaganda, la censura y la manipulación asistida por IA del flujo de información.


Y luego, cuando sea el momento adecuado, la puerta se cerrará.


En esencia, es una carrera entre la revolución y el totalitarismo de alta tecnología. Una carrera entre el despertar de la conciencia pública ante la urgente necesidad de un cambio revolucionario y la capacidad de nuestros gobernantes para impedir que ese cambio revolucionario llegue a ocurrir. Una carrera entre nuestra capacidad para empezar a usar el poder de nuestra cantidad para forzar el fin de los sistemas abusivos bajo los cuales vivimos, y la capacidad de los dominadores ricos y poderosos para usar la vigilancia, la robótica y los mecanismos de control asistidos por IA para anular todas las ventajas que tenemos sobre ellos.


Y en este momento nuestra mayor desventaja es que la mayoría de nosotros ni siquiera sabemos que estamos en esta carrera. Nuestros gobernantes lo saben, pero el ciudadano promedio no. La mayoría de nosotros seguimos mordiendo el cebo de la trampa.


Aún hay tiempo. La trampa todavía no se ha cerrado. Pero tenemos que despertar a los demás chanchitos del corral para que se den cuenta de la realidad de lo que esos bastardos han planeado para nosotros, y ayudarlos a comprender que la carrera ya está en marcha.


Caitlin Johnstone es una periodista australiana. Escribe sobre política, economía, medios, feminismo y la naturaleza de la conciencia.

author: Ed Wanderley
title: Master: Em mensagens, Vorcaro declarou lado sem margem para dúvida: “apoiamos a direita”
content:
Há um mês, uma pesquisa do instituto Datafolha mostrou que mais entrevistados acreditavam que o escândalo do Banco Master envolvia mais políticos de esquerda (34%) do que de direita (27%). Naquele retrato da opinião nacional, divulgado em 18 de setembro, havia ainda 13% do velho “tá todo mundo envolvido”.

A dúvida não parece ser a mesma quando quem fala é o próprio dono do Master,

Daniel Vorcaro

, ao trocar mensagens com um amigo pessoal

: “apoiamos a direita”, escreveu o banqueiro em conversas de WhatsApp interceptadas pela Polícia Federal (PF) às quais a

Agência Pública

 teve acesso.


Em uma conversa com o pastor e líder da Igreja Batista da Lagoinha, André Valadão, Vorcaro afirmou apoiar a direita brasileira. A declaração foi feita após o empresário demonstrar irritação com uma publicação do deputado federal Nikolas Ferreira (PL), em 27 de abril de 2024.


Daniel Vorcaro, que mantém uma relação próxima com André Valadão, encaminhou um link ao pastor e demonstrou insatisfação com uma publicação do deputado.

 A postagem compartilhada pelo parlamentar trazia a seguinte mensagem: “Ministro do STF, STJ e TSE silenciam sobre quem pagou suas despesas em Londres”. Na legenda, Nikolas classificou a reportagem como “interessante”.


“Nikolas repostou a Malu [Gaspar]. Loucura isso. Aliás, narrativa ruim pra ele mesmo”, escreveu o empresário. “Quem me mandou foi um blog de esquerda, que sabe que apoiamos a direita. Olha a bola de neve que pode virar”, disse.


“Eu apoio diversos eventos e debates, e nesse caso o apoio foi com a palestra do Tony Blair com quem tive um debate de altíssimo nível. No evento, várias pessoas de direita, apoiadores do evento inclusive vários que apoiaram ele [Nikolas], como nós. Acaba ficando ruim ele incentivar e propagar um ataque a mim, como fez agora. Só preciso saber se estamos do mesmo lado ou agora estamos um contra o outro”, finalizou o banqueiro.


Horas depois de afirmar ao amigo que conversaria com Nikolas Ferreira, André Valadão retomou o diálogo e informou que o deputado desconhecia que o evento mencionado na reportagem da jornalista Malu Gaspar havia sido organizado pelo Banco Master.


“Resumindo, ele [Nikolas] nem sabia sobre o banco e você, “palavras dele né“, e daí pediu perdão demais e vai contornar tudo. Deve te chamar também, ele me disse. Disse da gratidão com você e por aí vai.”


Em março de 2025, antes de pedir ajuda de Vorcaro, Nikolas encaminha áudio ao banqueiro, retoma o assunto e pede desculpa pelas publicações com críticas ao evento organizado pelo Master. “

Troquei ideia lá com o pastor Valadão naquela época, lá naquela postagem. Eu falei: ‘Pastor, eu não fazia ideia que era este o banco do Dani etc. e tudo, senão, obviamente, eu não teria postado, já teria conversado anteriormente’, mas, enfim, acabou que a palavra dita não tem como voltar, né?

 Mas espero que tenha sido esclarecido, enfim, depois vamos marcar de a gente se encontrar também, tá bem?”, disse Nikolas.


Apoio e reciprocidade


A relação do Banco Master vai além de críticas pontuais de um ou outro deputado e passa também por manobras no exercício de seus mandatos. Quando diz que “apoiamos a direita”, Vorcaro entende o ecossistema que se formou em torno de sua empresa (e família) e tem rastro de uso de seus recursos para isso.


Em 2022, por exemplo, Fabiano Campos Zettel, pastor da igreja Lagoinha em Belo Horizonte, casado com a irmã de Vorcaro e que muitas vezes atuava para resolver as missões financeiras do empresário, foi oficialmente o sexto maior doador das Eleições 2022. Em nome dele, como já

registrou

 a

Pública

, foram destinados R$ 2 milhões para a campanha de Tarcísio de Freitas (Republicanos-SP) ao governo de São Paulo e outros R$ 3 milhões para a campanha à presidência de Jair Bolsonaro, derrotado nas urnas.


Zettel segue preso, na mesma investigação de fraude nas operações do Master que investiga Vorcaro. As 54 empresas do grupo seguem sendo controladas por Natália Vorcaro Zettel, irmã de Daniel e esposa de Fabiano, com quem se uniu em regime de separação de bens, como também

apontou

 a

Pública

.


Do outro lado do balcão, o apoio se mostra mútuo, especialmente em momentos delicados de crise. No início das suspeitas de fraude de suas operações de crédito, a saída para o Banco Master foi a compra pelo Banco de Brasília (BRB), uma operação que envolveu o senador Ciro Nogueira (PP-PI), o dirigente partidário Antônio Rueda (União Brasil-RJ) e o então governador do Distrito …

author: Andrés
title: No soy amigo de los que cooperan, los quiero fuera fuera fuera
content:
La pierna de un jubilado que cae por el chorro de un hidramte


La decadencia moral y generalizada de un país se mide por la cantidad de recursos empleados en contra de la propia población, y de la vida misma. Que todo gobierno autoritario invierte onerosos recursos en las Armas es un hecho más que probado. De lo que se habla bastante menos es que en países donde el trabajo formal se viene erosionando desde hace tanto, los puestos en las policías y fuerzas armadas los ocupan en amplia mayoría las clases socioeconómicas más vulnerables. Y entonces la extorsión del trabajo estable opera sobre los sujetos al punto de quebrar todo principio, cortar los trazos democráticos y convertir a los “servidores del orden” en cómplices de un poder que no los quiere más que dentro de una institución cuyo funcionamiento mafioso los subordina, los presiona. Y en muchos casos termina descerebrándolos al punto en que ni siquiera pueden abrir los ojos ante la traición que cometen cada vez que apuntan un arma, empuñan un palo, empujan a un compatriota, golpean a un viejo, gasean a una niña, ahorcan entre varios a un hombre solo, disparan a un joven, lo esconden, gasean a la población y lastiman toda posibilidad de concordia. El todos contra todos y cada uno contra sí mismo está a la orden del día bajo esta gestión fascista.

Por Andrés Manrique (ANRed).


El  jubilado golpeado por la presión del hidrante, apuntado por la Policía Federal


Quienes cobran para ir a pegar, disparar y ahogar a estudiantes, a discapacitados, a viejos se cuentan entre lo más bajo de los traidores. Si era el último círculo, cuando además se detenta la fuerza física, se suma una vuelta más.


“Vos te pasaste al otro lado de la vereda”


Tirarle gas a un viejo de camperita, empujarlo.


Pegarle con el puño a toda carrera y por la espalda a un fotorreportero en la cara.


Echarle la moto de alta cilindrada a alguien que va en paz por la vereda.


La Policía Federal agolpeando con el hidrante al jubilado de espaldas


Acorralar a dos fotógrafos en un zaguán y dispararle a quemarropa: contra el abdomen, a las piernas, a la cabeza: en la cara y a los ojos.


Clavarte la rodilla en la espalda cuando estás en el piso, boca abajo, desarmado, reducido por el sobrepeso de aquel al que un trote lo haría infartar, mientras otro te lastima las muñecas con el precinto, y un tercero apoya todo su odio contra las vértebras de tu cuello.


Amedrentar con los escudos, con las tonfas, acelerando las motos, haciendo chasquear las  escopetas, con  bombas de estruendo, postas de goma y armas mal llamadas no letales, con las que no se cansan de matar o herir de gravedad. Revolear bastones, batiendo el aerosol de gas pimienta sobre la cara de una nena, de una anciana, de una vecina que pierde su  bolsa de compras.


“Esa es la diferencia entre la gorra y la visera”


Gasear a pibes con carteles, irse encima de discapacitados. Golpear con la escopeta, salir a cazar a compatriotas que protestan. Salir a cazar fantasmas en manada. Seguir órdenes, aunque vayan en contra de todos los principios. Golpear a alguien indefenso, lastimar entre muchos a uno solo.


Miserable soldadesca del brazo tilingo del poder que nos ahoga. Dése vuelta, reconozca dónde está su enemigo. Identifiquelo, usted sabe que la mano que le pone el sueldo es la misma que lo va a someter a la mazmorra cuando no sirva más.


¿Más traidor que un desclasado?


¿Peor traidor que alguien al que han entrenado para que se odie a sí tanto que odia a todo el que tiene a su alrededor?


Fotos: Andrés Manrique

author: Darío Aranda
title: Las cuentas no cierran en Vaca Muerta: la fuga de dólares que oculta el relato extractivo
content:
Por Natalia Concina


La explotación de Vaca Muerta permitió el ingreso al país de casi dos mil millones de dólares entre lo que vendió y lo que pidió como préstamo durante 2026. Lejos de quedarse en el país,

esas divisas volvieron al exterior y le permitieron a las empresas petroleras y de diferentes rubros fugar sus ganancias

. Un nuevo estudio del grupo de investigación EJES confirma que el yacimiento de petróleo no convencional permite hoy sostener la estabilidad cambiaria, pero

consolida a los sectores de poder concentrado y genera una millonaria deuda a futuro

.


Durante la primera parte del año, las empresas que explotan Vaca Muerta pidieron préstamos por 936 millones de dólares mensuales promedio, una cifra incluso superior a las divisas que generaron por las ventas al exterior de hidrocarburos (que rondaron en un promedio de 754 millones por mes).


Esta inyección de divisas extranjeras es la que garantiza hoy la estabilidad cambiaria, es decir, que el precio de la moneda estadounidense esté más o menos estable. Sin embargo,

los dólares que ingresan por el endeudamiento privado son un problema para toda la sociedad

 porque —a futuro— utilizarán los dólares que genera toda la economía. ¿Por qué? Porque para cancelar sus deudas la empresas comprarán los dólares disponibles en el Banco Central, que a su vez ingresarán por las exportaciones u otros mecanismo (como podría ser esta de toma de deuda).


En otras palabras, Vaca Muerta permite hoy la “sostenibilidad” del modelo a través de estos dólares de los que se nutren, además de las empresas petroleras, los sectores corporativos más concentrados de la economía local para remitir sus ganancias al exterior, un proceso que se intensificó desde diciembre pasado.

Una especie de puerta giratoria de dólares

, aunque las deudas quedan.


Foto: Martín Álvarez Mullally


Estas conclusiones son los pilares más importantes d

el informe “

¿A dónde van los dólares de Vaca Muerta”,


el tercer estudio realizado por el Enlace por la Justicia Energética y Socioambiental (EJES)”

, una articulación de organizaciones que desde 2024 analiza sistemáticamente los números del yacimiento no convencional en forma crítica, exponiendo sus implicancias ocultas detrás del supuesto boom energético.


“El análisis de los datos del Banco Central de 2025 y lo que va de 2026 permite consolidar dos miradas respecto a Vaca Muerta: por un lado, que su función es traer dólares y no se está pensando en eslabonar un conjunto de actividades económicas a partir del yacimiento; por el otro, que

lo único que dejará al país son deudas

”, asegura a Tierra Viva el economista Marco Kofman, autor del trabajo.


¿A dónde van los dólares de Vaca Muerta? - EJES


Récord de ventas


En los primeros cinco meses de 2026, el país exportó 314.000 barriles diarios de petróleo, acumulando un total de 3.773 millones de dólares, lo que da un promedio de 754 millones por mes. No sólo se aumentó la cantidad de crudo sino que coincidió con un precio internacional relativamente elevado.


De las diez primeras empresas que comercializan internacionalmente el crudo argentino, hay cinco que exportan más del 50 por ciento de su producción local. Respecto al gas de Vaca Muerta, se vende al exterior sólo entre el cuatro y el cinco por ciento.


Pese a la orientación exportadora, el informe destaca que en los últimos años Argentina disminuyó la importación de hidrocarburos drásticamente, parte por la producción de Vaca Muerta, parte por la crisis en la producción local. En ese contexto, la balanza comercial energética (diferencia entre la compra y la venta de petróleo y gas) es favorable para la Argentina, que pasó de estar en rojo a tener un superávit de 3.000 millones de dólares acumulado sólo en los primeros cinco meses de 2026.


“A este ingreso de dólares por ventas (dólares comerciales),

se le suman los dólares financieros, es decir los que ingresan por toma de deuda de las empresas


que funcionan como un respirador artificial del modelo de Milei

y le permite que el dólar se mantenga estable, sin tener que devaluar ni poner controles cambiarios”, explica Kofman.


Foto: Depositphotos


El trabajo de EJES explica que de los 22.617 millones de dólares que el sector privado ingresó al país por la vía del endeudamiento, 14.441 millones —casi el 64 por ciento del total— fueron aportados por las empresas energéticas; en los primeros cinco meses del año, ese endeudamiento fue de 936 millones de dólares promedio …

author: La Zarzamora
title: DESPEDIR A JUAN…
content:
Esta mañana nuestro compañero Juan Aliste Vega ha partido de su cuerpo, cuerpo que el poder mantuvo en encierro los últimos 16 años, cuerpo que practicó el conflicto y lo materializó en acciones armadas, que acompañó su vida en el álgido recorrido de ser él. Fue en el hospital penitenciario de Santiago, donde en compañia y calma, se fugó definitivamente.

Aún no podemos confirmar donde ni como será su despedida, ló que sí sabemos es que serán muchas, en muchos territorios, en las calles, en los puentes, en las jaulas, en avenidas y carreteras.

Juan Aliste es y será reivindicado, pese a los esfuerzos incansables de la prensa del enemigo y de sus múltiples intentos de desprestigiarlo, nosotrxs sus compañerxs sabemos que en este momento estamos despidiendo a un guerrero de gran envergadura. Pese a sus miserables conjunciones de palabras, el mundo sabe quien es Juan y en todos los territorios se levantará fuego en su memoria.

Que desesperanza deben sentir los poderosos, al saber que amamos pese a estar en guerra, que nuestra historia es escrita por nosotrxs, pese a sus asquerosos relatos oficiales, tan indignos como ellos mismos.

Hoy es un día de nuestra propia historia, hoy parte el guerrero combatiente que se alzó en armas contra la dictadura y la pestilente democracia de burgueses y traidores, el que no se dejó abatir, el que atacó y acertó, el que siguió compartiendo conocimientos y enseñanzas pese al encierro, el que enviaba notas y saludos, el que hacía llegar sus palabras a actividades y espacios.

Cada vez es más difícil despedir, esto no es una noticia, ni tampoco un comunicado, es nuestro adiós a un hermano…

A nosotrxs ahora nos quedará volver a mirarnos, tensionar el encierro de nuestrxs compañerxs, cuestionarnos y autocriticarnos, dejar de hacernos tolerantes al encarcelamiento, dejar de normalizar la sociedad carcelaria y hacer. Arduo camino nos dejas.

Juan que tu fuga sea eterna querido compañero.

Ternura y ataque frontal por ti y por todxs nuestrxs muertxs.

title: Revista Crítica Anticapitalista 6 – La Comuna, la clase y la lucha de clases
content:
PRESENTACION


¿Qué relación existe entre la Comuna como forma política de la emancipación social y la clase, entendida ésta no como categoría positivizada y sociológica, sino en su carácter dual y contradictorio? ¿Es la Comuna una manera de entender la clase y la lucha de clases en clave no identitaria, no positivizada? ¿La oposición entre Comuna y clase es algo derivado de una concepción anti-dialéctica de la lucha de clases? En ese campo ¿a qué dialéctica nos referimos? ¿A la dialéctica hegeliana orientada a la síntesis estatal como forma política de la identidad? ¿A la dialéctica negativa que la cuestiona? ¿La lucha de clases, entendida en clave dialéctica no-identitaria, permite entender la Comuna como proceso contradictorio de disolución de la clase? ¿Implica esto un desafío a nuestro concepto de proletariado y a la idea de revolución calcada en el canon leninista?

author: Kodao Productions
title: Philippines now in worst hunger crisis in 3 decades
content:
More Filipinos are experiencing hunger and even more admitted to being poorer in the third quarter of the year, a national survey reveals. Nearly a quarter of Filipinos said they experienced “being hungry and having nothing to eat at least once in the past three months.”


In a study conducted from September 21 to 27, survey firm Social Weather Station (SWS) said that 22.6 per cent of respondent families admitted to experiencing involuntary hunger, up by 2.3 points from 20.3 per cent in June.


It was the worse hunger rate in the country since 1998. This year’s hunger incidence is worse by 1.5 points above the record-high 21.1 per cent average of 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic


Where in the Philippines is hunger worse?


Hunger is worse in the capital region of Metro Manila at 27 per cent, the survey said, followed by Mindanao at 23.7 per cent.


Poverty is as bad in the rest of Luzon at 23.6 per cent while the Visayas region has fallen to 16.0 per cent.


This translates to an estimated 16.8 million Filipino families considered themselves poor in September, up from 13.6 million in June.


The September 2026 survey also found that 55 per cent of Filipino families rated themselves as “poor” while 9 per cent rated themselves as “borderline poor”


What does it mean to be poor in the Philippines?


SWS’ latest survey said 44 per cent of Filipinos rate themselves as “food poor,” eating simpler meals and less.


Food vendor Ramil said his customers had been buying his rice porridge less and less. He noticed that some of his customers who used to order twice a day now only eat once.


“Maybe because I had to increase my price by P5 per order,” he said, citing that cooking gas had increased by as much as 44 per cent since the war in the Middle East started early this year.


Ramil had also announced he is no longer giving credit to his customers. He sells at P50 per bowl.


In a nearby eatery, a basic dish with three small meat slices also increased to P80 while a small cup of rice sells at P20. “We give our customers extra spoonfuls of sauce to make it appear our servings have not shrunk. But everyone in this neighborhood knows the situation,” food vendor Joanna said.


Who’s to blame?


The SWS survey was conducted as the Philippines suffered its worst inflation rate for the second time since the start of the US-Israel war against Iran early in the year. Both April and September registered an alarming 7.2 per cent rate of increase in prices of goods and services.


Independent economic think tank Ibon Foundation squarely blamed the Ferdinand Marcos Jr. government’s “inaction” on inflation.


“The government is not using its national energy emergency powers to control domestic oil prices or to cap prices of basic goods, contended with giving dole outs to select groups,” Ibon executive director Sonny Africa said.


Africa said he hopes Marcos was informed of the September inflation rates last weekend, only to distract the Philippine president from fully enjoying the F1 Singapore Grand prix. #

(Raymund B. Villanueva)

title: PJAK spokesperson Awdanan: Opponents of democracy fear integration
content:
Rêbwar Awdanan, spokesperson for the Kurdistan Free Life Party (PJAK), issued a message targeting individuals and groups opposed to PJAK and pro-democracy forces. Awdanan addressed a range of issues, from the idea of democratic integration and society’s self-governance to the slogan “Jin, Jiyan, Azadî” and the achievements of the Kurdish people.


Oppnonents of democracy are thinking about getting a share of power


Stating that opponents of democracy are uncomfortable with the people’s democratic outlook, Rêbwar Awdanan said: “They are opponents of democracy and are extremely sensitive to the outlook embraced by the people. That is why we speak about democracy every day. They think only about the share of power they can secure for themselves. The establishment of a decentralized democratic republic and Iran’s diversity are sources of fear and terror for them. That is why we challenge this mindset every day and speak about a Democratic Republic of Iran.”


Democratic integration exposes fascist ideas


Criticizing groups opposed to the idea of democratic integration, Awdanan said this approach exposes their views and their attitudes toward peoples, continuing: “They are afraid of the idea of democratic integration because they are slaves to a thousand masters, and democratic integration exposes their fascist ideas and hostility toward peoples. That is why we speak about democratic integration every day.”


Stating that those who oppose society’s self-governance are driven by a desire to hold power, Rêbwar Awdanan said: “They oppose society’s self-governance because the desire to become masters has penetrated them to the bone. That is why every day we speak about the defeat of their dictatorship and the victory of society’s self-governance.”


'Jin, Jiyan, Azadî' everywhere


Rêbwar Awdanan continued: “They oppose the slogan ‘Jin, Jiyan, Azadî’ because it reminds them of reactionism and darkness. That is why we, too, repeat the progressive slogan ‘Jin, Jiyan, Azadî’ at all times and everywhere.”


Arguing that groups opposing the achievements of the Kurdish people act in pursuit of their own interests, PJAK spokesperson Rêbwar Awdanan concluded his message with these words: “They oppose the achievements of the Kurdish people. To obtain a few dollars or grab a share of power, they put on a mask of Kurdish identity and cling to false nationalism. That is why they conceal their true faces in a thousand different ways. They are certain conservatives who are remnants of the coup era, and they want to fight against the aspirations of genuine defenders of freedom. That is why we remind people of their defeat every day.”

The arrests of anti-mining solidarity struggle activists Dr. Randall Sequeira and Laxman Naik on October 16 on cooked up charges is part of the ceaseless violence and arbitrary arrests unleashed by the state government and mining corporate nexus since mid-2023.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Animal Rights Advocates Call for Referendum on Snare Traps
content:
ANIMAL RIGHTS ADVOCATES are currently campaigning for a referendum to be held on the use of wild boar snares.

In particular, animal rights advocates have long criticized wild boar snares as overly cruel. Such traps use spring-loaded mechanisms to tighten around animals’ limbs when triggered.

Nevertheless, such traps have also been criticized for ensnaring other species, as they do not distinguish. Endangered species such as Formosan black bears and leopard cats had also been killed by such traps, as have cats and dogs, sometimes resulting in their losing limbs if they survive.

Though claims had been made that Indigenous hunters used such traps as part of traditional hunting rights, animal rights groups have generally cited that this was rarely the case, in that Indigenous hunters generally do not use such traps. By contrast, such animal rights advocates state that Indigenous hunters more commonly use traps made from wood, bamboo and vines, and other natural materials. In the past, the Central Election Commission turned down calls for a referendum on the use of wild boar snares on the basis that the referendum was unclear as to whether it pertained to traps used by Indigenous hunters.

Otherwise, such traps are sometimes used by farmers as a means of preventing damage to their crops. Animal rights advocates have called on the government to provide electric fencing, protective netting, or other means for farmers to protect their livestock and crops.

The proposals called for by animal rights advocates are relevant to the use, display, and sale of wild boar snares, as well as their import and export. It is thought that China is a major source of some of the wild boar snares used in Taiwan.

It is unclear as to whether the Central Election Commission will approve the referendum currently called for by animal rights advocates. At the same time, without a major political party endorsing it as an issue, such a referendum is unlikely to gain traction. It is to be seen if either the DPP or KMT, or perhaps even both parties, throw their weight behind the proposal.

One notes that there have been cases of political bipartisanship between both major parties on the issue of animal rights in past years, as seen with politicians of both parties supporting enshrining animal rights in the constitution. Even so, such politicians ultimately did not prove serious about such promises outside of election campaigning, as a result of which neither the KMT nor DPP acted on claims in past election cycles that animal rights would see constitutional protection.
