title: The IITs: Tragic Failures That Beget More Tragedies
content:
From a social perspective, the IITs are tragic failures that beget more tragedies.

But you already know the IITs are the pinnacle of Indian aspirations, achievements, accolades, blah-di-blah, right? How about we celebrate by taking a closer look at the graduates, the faculty, and the institution?

The institutional charter, briefly. The IITs were conceived in 1946 to support the country’s industrial development and help meet the nation’s technological challenges. Parliament’s 1961 Act declares them institutions of national importance. It charges them with instruction and research, and with the advancement of learning and dissemination of knowledge. The same Act says every institute shall be open to persons of either sex and of whatever race, creed, caste or class, in admitting or appointing students and teachers alike. [1] Later laws reserve seats for SC, ST and OBC students, PhD seats included, and, since 2019, teaching posts at every rank.

Start with the product. As any IIT alum would confirm, a majority of IIT graduates wouldn’t be able to properly describe what ‘engineering’ is. Poorly educated and narrowly conditioned to chase status from a young age, most of them used to end up in finance or as middle management in US IT firms, but have lately diversified into mercenary ouroboros via IIT coaching and YouTube influencing. The institute’s own numbers: in IIT Bombay’s placement report for 2023–24, 29% of offers were in engineering and technology. The rest went to IT, consulting, finance, analytics and “other”. [2]

The defence is usually the famous founders. Let’s do the math. Seats went from about 2k a year in the 80s to about 20k now, so total grads ~400k. Unicorn founders ~117, high value startup founders maybe four thousand if you’re generous. So, 0.03% and 1%. [3, 4] Like unicorns, these founders are statistical anomalies. Sensible folks within the system will themselves readily acknowledge that their success is mostly despite it rather than because of it. And given the stated mission, funnelling billions in public subsidy into private equity accumulation for a minuscule minority is cause for shame rather than something to tom-tom about.

This is the deal then. Ruin your childhood to join an exclusive band of svayambhu achievers. Concoct jagatguru-brand gig economy “innovations” for exploiting cheap labor. Garland each other for contributions to the economic miracle of jobless growth and extractive digital feudalism. Parade your arrogant indifference or offer defensive apologies for the mockery of a social contract, dressed up in a lazy pragmatism argument about success.

By the way, who’s even there to teach them? Across all 23 IITs, 4,804 of 12,498 sanctioned teaching posts stood vacant in January 2026, or 38.4%. [5] It was 38.3% in December 2022. [6] In the nine IITs that disclosed the breakdown, about 60% of the empty posts were reserved ones. [5] Cryogenic sthiratva.

Sour grapes? I was there, eating them for four lost years. So chill. First week in the hostel, the rank was a common icebreaker question you asked people along with where they were from and in what department. Some hesitant answers made me stop asking. Only the rare, confident stud would openly declare he was SC, came through the preparatory course etc. The term in use was ‘schaddu’, and people would murmur in the early semesters, but soon some of them were ahead on GPA, and the murmurs lost voice. Years later, a friend who got a PhD mentioned feeling conflicted using reservations since their father was also a PhD and they went to good schools. Not long ago, an alum stated that even though they got in via reservation, everything after was earned by merit. I couldn’t make out if this was being defensive or proud. I don’t remember hearing of any campus suicides, and only learned about them from ‘The Death of Merit’ documentary. [7]

A decade after graduation and on another continent, the sourness still stung, in an interview by another pitiable alum. I was struggling for purpose and careening across career lanes. Unusual for an IIT grad, and he got suspicious… maybe I was a ‘category candidate’? So he asked for my rank, and then I asked for his, and then he said that’s not relevant, and then I agreed, and the interview went downhill. So, no chill.

Then the people who run the place. Do the IITs still hire blatantly sexist dogs as professors? It used to be de rigueur in several departments. A lot of the students were of a similar breed …

author: Sarah Raymundo
title: On liberal opportunism and the “purity” smear
content:
Photo from Naga City Tourism Facebook page

Accusing leftists and activists of demanding a “useless politics of purity” is a classic liberal defense mechanism designed to shift the burden of moral failure onto the critic.

Why did former Vice President and now Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo roll out the pink carpet for the Zionist war machine? When Robredo hosted Israeli Ambassador Dana Kursh for an official courtesy visit, she was not merely performing the routine gestures of local hospitality. She was actively welcoming and legitimizing representatives of the US-Israeli genocidal apparatus. This intervention centers an anti-imperialist analysis to dismantle the liberal apologetics surrounding this act. Rather than an isolated error in judgment, this diplomatic encounter exposes the persistent, foundational tension within the Philippine political landscape: the contradiction between liberal reformism and anti-imperialist national liberation.

Dismissing progressives’ critique of Robredo’s hosting of the Israeli envoy as mere “political purism” is politically and morally impoverished. The underlying mechanism demands a total, systematic critique. To understand why her defenders deploy the “politics of purity” accusation, and why that defense completely falls apart when examining real power dynamics and economic interests, we must lay bare both the liberal class position and the ideological sleight of hand at work.

To make sense of Robredo’s pivot toward imperial hospitality, we must look directly at the liberal class position. Her stance is neither an accidental misstep nor a personal failure of political intelligence but the direct expression of her class character and political alignment. Liberal reformism in the global periphery operates strictly within the legal, institutional, and geopolitical framework dictated by US imperialism.

While Robredo served as a focal point against the overt state terrorism of the Marcos-Duterte dynasties, her opposition was strictly intra-class—a feud over how to manage the neocolonial state, pitting rule-of-law decorum against autocratic violence.

Because her political legitimacy rests upon acceptance by the global capitalist order, her opposition stops at the border of imperial interest. When forced to choose between international solidarity with an anti-imperialist national liberation movement and alignment with the Washington-Tel Aviv axis, liberal reformists invariably side with the imperial core. They cannot critique the drain of value, the extraction of labor, or the military hegemony of US imperialism because their entire political project depends on remaining within that very apparatus.

This structural subservience explains why defenders deploy the “purity politics” weapon whenever that alignment is exposed. Accusing leftists and activists of demanding a “useless politics of purity” is a classic liberal defense mechanism designed to shift the burden of moral failure onto the critic. From a materialist standpoint, this argument relies on three ideological fallacies:

First, it replaces a materialist baseline with ideological absolution. Opposition to active genocide, ethnic cleansing, and imperialist aggression is not a performative or elevated ideological standard; it is the absolute baseline of human solidarity and anti-imperialist struggle. Labeling principled opposition to mass slaughter as “purity” redefines baseline morality as an unreasonable demand, attempting to pass off complicity as pragmatic maturity.

Second, it operates on the logic of liberal idealism, which treats political stances as abstract moral choices made in a vacuum. Political actions reflect concrete class interests. Shielding a public figure from accountability for legitimizing a settler-colonial state serves a specific political function: it conditions the middle forces to accept imperial violence as a routine, acceptable feature of global diplomacy.

Third, it trades scientific alignment for unprincipled unity. Transformative praxis distinguishes between principled unity—built on anti-imperialist struggle and mass interest—and unprincipled unity, which colludes with reaction to preserve electoral coalitions. Demanding that the progressive movement remain silent on international solidarity to protect a liberal politician’s image trades human rights and anti-imperialist consciousness for temporary electoral expediency.

This dynamic reveals the distinct role of the middle forces—segments of the …

author: chuang
title: “Every War Is a World War”: Interview with a Member of Taiwan Alliance for a Free Palestine
content:
The following is an interview with friends from Taiwan who have formed the umbrella coalition Taiwan Alliance for a Free Palestine (TWAFP). The interview includes an overview of the rifts in the Taiwanese left, and the frustration of TWAFP organizers carving out their place amid divisions between pro-unification and independence, or pro- and anti-American positions, in the contentious and highly polarized politics on the island.


The organizer recounts their efforts to confront Taiwan’s growing ties with Israel and direct support for the genocide in Palestine. They speak with sadness that, even as Taiwan is now the fourth-largest supplier of arms to Israel, surpassing mainland China, most Taiwanese care little for the distant genocide and the struggle in Palestine seems far away. And yet, TWAFP has led successful demonstrations, pulled together a broad coalition of disparate groups in support of Palestine, and conducted research to expose Taiwan’s complicity in the ongoing genocide.


Be sure to read their

report


from 2025, outlining specific pathways of material component support for Israel, including radar, armor, and an array of military hardware.


See also a recent

piece

 submitted to us, outlining Taiwan’s deepening ties with Israel under the DPP government.


–

Chuang


Q: To begin, let’s just set the stage. Over the last few years, the Taiwan Alliance for a Free Palestine (TWAFP) has helped to organize the largest mobilizations against the genocide in Palestine seen in Taiwan. Can you tell us a little about how TWAFP formed and maybe review some of the protests it has organized?


A:

Taiwan Alliance for a Free Palestine (TWAFP)

 was founded in April of 2024. Prior to this, Taiwan had already seen several groups doing Palestine advocacy work arise spontaneously, including Palestine Action Front, Taiwan Palestine Solidarity Network, and Parallel Government. As its name suggests, TWAFP is an “Alliance” that brings together groups that were already involved in initiatives related to Palestine. In addition to the three groups already mentioned, the alliance also includes a migrant worker organization, the

Taiwan International Workers’ Association (TIWA)

; the human rights organization, Taiwan Association for Human Rights; the cultural collective, Taiwan Rave & Punk Solidarity Front for Palestine; the gender issues group, Queer Margins; and the Christian group, Taiwan Olive Branch Peace Collective. From 2024 to today, we have organized one petitioning campaign, issued two open letters, held one candlelight vigil, hosted one book club meeting, staged five protest actions, held three press conferences, and organized three marches. In the future, we plan to engage in a number of other activities, many of which may be smaller in scale.


Q: TWAFP also did some very interesting research on material links between Taiwan and Israel. We can link to the report here, but can you briefly go over the main findings, and maybe go over any new information that you’ve found since that report was released? For example, have there been more details since then?

      


A: In September of 2025, we released our report,

Taiwanese Companies’ Complicity in Israel’s Ongoing Genocide

, which identified specific manufacturers assisting Israel in the production of military weapons, including via the production of components. For example: Gloria Material Technology Corp (GMTC) supplies superalloys and high-grade steel produced through electroslag remelting, while ADLINK Technology supplies embedded computing systems and industrial-grade computers. In another case, Transcom marketed its vertically integrated capabilities—spanning chip design to module production—to enter the Israeli defense supply chain and is now a key, long-term supplier of components for the EL/M-2084 multi-mission radar, which is a core element of the Israeli “Iron Dome” air defense system designed by Israeli defense company Elta.


Since the primary purpose of this report was to provide accurate information that could be used by media outlets and other organizations, who would ideally follow up with their own reporting and investigation, we were relatively restrained in our writing approach and did not engage in much interpretation or extrapolation. However, when I was conducting this research, I came across a number of findings that I want to share widely:

content:
with added reports from Jessica Obciana and Kline Vergara

“Homes are destroyed, livelihoods are lost, nations are lost by interests that are made far beyond our own borders. Even now, initiatives like Pax Silica, supply chains for critical minerals and semiconductors are being reordered around the needs of the US war machine, and countries like us [the Philippines] are being asked to serve as suppliers and now become their targets, rather than being allowed to decide our own development,” said Dr. Giovanni Tapang, convener of the Stop the US-Israel War on Iran Network.

Various anti-imperialist groups gathered for the webinar Updates from the Resistance: The Current Situation in Iran, Palestine, Venezuela, and Cuba, co-organized by BAYAN, the International League of Peoples’ Struggle (ILPS) Philippines, the Philippines-Palestine Friendship Association (PPFA), and the Stop the US-Israel War on Iran Campaign Network, to express people’s solidarity in lambasting US imperialism following its sanctions, blockades, military aggression, and other forms of intervention and coercion against the people.

“This is the war machine that we are fighting against. And as we listen to those who are on the front lines, we learn of their resistance, deepen our understanding, and together strengthen solidarity to defeat this war machine,” Tapang added.

“We have seen the case of Venezuela: how this warfare has been attacking the Global South, attacking the country, and in many, many aspects, not only the political one, military, economic, and cultural, and in social consciousness. Venezuela is under siege now,” said Richard Lobo, Venezuela’s Chargé d’Affaires.

Venezuela possesses the world’s largest proven crude oil reserves, estimated at around 303 billion barrels as of 2023, according to the US Energy Information Administration.

Lobo noted that US intervention in Venezuela extends beyond economic sanctions to political, military, economic, and cultural intervention.

In January 2026, the US launched Operation Absolute Resolve as a large-scale military operation in Venezuela framed around drug trafficking and national security that led to the capture of President Nicolás Maduro and First Lady Cilia Flores and their transfer to the United States. Such an operation also targeted Venezuelan military infrastructure across Caracas and other locations.

Months after Maduro’s capture, the US laid out an agreement to gain access and control over an estimated 65 billion barrels of oil reserves, mineral wealth, and other resources.

Meanwhile, Lobo emphasized that the situation has only amplified the resistance among Venezuelans in defending their sovereignty and their right to determine the country’s political and economic direction.

“Even though we have been under attack […] the people there in Venezuela have been resisting and have been struggling. And one thing that I can say right now is that even with the kidnapping of our president, they believe the government is still in power,” Lobo stated.

More than 5,000 civilians have been killed in the US-Israel aggression against Iran, including 168 girls who were killed when a school was struck in March this year.

“Iran is experiencing aggression by the United States and Israel since the 1979 revolution against a very corrupt government, the Shah’s government. author: Unknown
title: ‘Temporary’ for 41 years: Turkey’s village guard system
content:
When Turkey introduced the system of so-called temporary village guards on March 26, 1985, it was officially intended as a time-limited “security measure.” Forty-one years later, the armed structure remains in place. Tens of thousands of village guards are still on duty, even though the PKK has ended its phase of armed struggle and the Peace and Democratic Society Process now has a legal framework.


This brings a question back into focus: How should the armed civilian apparatus that the Turkish state built up over decades during its war against the Kurdish freedom movement be dismantled?


According to the Turkish Ministry of Interior, 48,365 village guards were still on duty as of October 31, 2025. Their number is likely to have since fallen to approximately 47,000–48,000 due to retirements and the suspension of new recruitment.


The system, originally established as a temporary arrangement, thus remains part of the state security apparatus in Kurdistan more than four decades later.


A temporary measure becomes a permanent institution


The legal basis was established in 1985 through an amendment to Article 74 of the Village Law. Initially introduced in 22 provinces, the village guard system was intended to support military operations against the PKK by recruiting armed forces from the local population. During the parliamentary debates, historical parallels were already drawn with the Hamidiye Regiments of the Ottoman Empire.


The system was further expanded following the declaration of a state of emergency in 1987. From 1992 onward, village guards began receiving state salaries, and by the following year, the organization was operating in 35 provinces. Their numbers rose from around 62,000 in 1995 to approximately 90,000 by the end of the decade. Between 1985 and 2009, a total of 123,476 people served as village guards.


The system’s originally intended temporary nature was also largely abandoned in legal terms in 2007. Under Law No. 5673, which was passed unanimously, village guards who retired at the age of 55 after at least 15 years of service became entitled to a monthly pension. At the same time, a standard personnel ceiling of 40,000 was established, which the government could increase by up to 50 percent. However, the corresponding implementing regulation was never made public.


What had supposedly been a transitional arrangement had thus become a permanently funded and institutionally entrenched armed structure.


Human rights violations and widespread impunity


The history of the village guard system is closely linked to serious human rights violations in the Kurdish provinces. According to a study by the Human Rights Association (IHD), village guards were held responsible for the deaths of 183 people and injuries to another 259 between 1990 and March 2009. The report also documented 38 cases of villages being set on fire, 14 village evacuations, 70 cases of robbery, and 454 cases of torture and ill-treatment.


Particularly striking is the low number of criminal convictions. According to official figures from the Ministry of Interior, crimes committed by 5,139 village guards were recorded between 1985 and 2006. Although 853 of them were arrested, only 264 were convicted. This represents approximately five percent of those whose crimes were recorded in the statistics.


State-issued weapons were also used in private disputes. In 2009, four people were killed outside a police station during a feud between two village guard families in Ergani. Prosecutors sought four counts of aggravated life imprisonment for each of the five village guards involved. The killings were allegedly carried out with state-issued Kalashnikov rifles.


That same year, the Bilge massacre in Mardin province once again brought the system under public scrutiny. Forty-four people were murdered in an attack on an engagement celebration. However, a parliamentary investigation commission subsequently stopped short of recommending the abolition of the village guard system, instead proposing its restructuring through training and stricter disciplinary measures. Akın Birdal, then a member of parliament for the BDP, criticized the report for downplaying the state’s responsibility.


The Human Rights Association also called for an investigation into possible links between the village guard system and the intelligence organization JITEM.


Forced displacement and obstacles to return


The consequences of the system extend far beyond …

author: groundxero
title: Another One Bites the Dust: Construction Workers’ Not So Quiet Battle For Survival Ahead of Delhi’s Long Winter
content:
The ‘annual ban’ on construction work through the winter seasons in Delhi that has become tradition over the last half a decade due to an acute air pollution crisis in the city, has this year, become a starvation sentence.


 


by

Mouli Sharma


 


15 October 2026, New Delhi:

 The rain falls in sheets on Thursday morning, ice cold and sudden like it can only get during mid-October weeks as Autumn bleeds into Winter. The wide, planned roads of Delhi’s Civil Lines region don’t flood quite so much as Shankar Road and its tributaries (or, god forbid, Gurgaon) but it’s enough to drench the lower halves of even the umbrella havers stuck underneath foot-over bridges and bus stops. 


 


Needless to say, the roads are abandoned. At the T-Point facing the DRDO office, a lone rickshaw puller stops abruptly, shivering as he holds the thin gamchha protecting his head tighter over him and runs to the shelter of the bridge. I stand there, too. Water has been steadily gathering at the top, and has now begun flooding down the stairs, soaking his sandalled feet and into my socks and shoes. When the rain slows, for a minute, I make to leave, aiming for the bus stop 50 metres away in case it starts up again.


 


The rickshaw puller warns me not to do that. I tell him I have somewhere to be. He asks me where I’m trying to go. I tell him there’s a protest today at Vikas Bhawan. 


 


“Look at the weather. No one’s protesting in the middle of this. Only a lunatic would be out there today.”


 


He is, of course, wrong. 


***


 


At Thursday noon, nearly 50 construction workers led a march from Vikas Bhawan to the Sushruta Trauma Centre, led by the AICCTU’s Building Workers’ Union, many of them travelling from faraway districts like Burari and Okhla. This was ahead of an announcement by the Delhi government that construction work in the city would be banned for a period of three months between November and January, ostensibly due to air pollution concerns, except the Supreme Court’s directions that such a blanket ban on work must be accompanied by the provision of minimum wages to aggrieved workers are not only nowhere close to being fulfilled, but are in fact being violated for a consecutive season since the Rekha Gupta led BJP came to power in 2025. 


 


“The Welfare board website has been down for nearly four months now,” said Ranjan Kuswaha, a mason and secretary of the local Burari unit of the Building Workers’ Union. “They said they were making a new one. And now that they have, they’ve already announced a seasonal ban less than two weeks away, beginning on November 1st and ending on January 31st. And till now this website is taking neither new registrations nor renewals. How on earth is the worker supposed to survive?”


 


Kushwaha further highlighted the plight of the migrant worker, so many of whom come to Delhi to work contractually on the many building and developmental projects undertaken here annually, who will now be left destitute. 


 


Advocate Surya Prakash Union said that a majority of the workers associated with the BWU hail from Supaul and Saharsa, two of Bihar’s poorest districts. 


“Most of our workers come from the poorest regions,” Surya Prakash, AICCTU; Infographic via BWU.


“We demand that this website be fixed at the earliest, and that registrations and renewals be completed as soon as possible and the workers be provided their labour cards,” Kuswaha said. 


 


There is also the matter of alleged gross corruption within this “welfare board” itself—the Delhi Building and Other Construction Workers Welfare Board (DBoCWWB), an organisation founded in 2002 in reference to the 1996 BoCW Act, which is apparently as much of a handful as it as a mouthful, according to the workers whose welfare it proclaims to oversee.


 


“On paper, the welfare framework for Delhi’s construction workers promises them wide-ranging support in almost all spheres of life: from maternity care, pension, housing, healthcare, education and even free daily commute on govt buses,” wrote Ishita Jairath for the Times of India in her scathing January 2026 report,

Hands That Build Delhi Brick By Brick Out Of Welfare Framework. 


 


The ground reality, however, was that the intended beneficiaries she asked about the schemes meant for them had nothing more than a “blank look”.


 


“Bitto, a marble and tile worker from Mangolpuri, didn’t know his children are eligible for education assistance,” Jairath wrote. “Preeti, a …

author: Brian Hioe
title: In A First, China Sanctions Ministers of Diplomatic Allies of Taiwan
content:
THE CHINESE GOVERNMENT has sanctioned two government ministers from diplomatic allies of Taiwan. These would be Belizean Foreign Minister Francis Fonseca and Paraguayan Minister of Information Gustavo Villate. Such sanctions prevent them and their family members from doing business in China.

China does not appear to have sanctioned ministers of Taiwan’s diplomatic allies in the past. This would be a new means, then, of pressuring countries to switch ties from Taiwan to China.

Taiwan is larger than all of its diplomatic allies, whether measured in terms of the size of population or economy. The main reason why Taiwan maintains ties with its diplomatic allies is so that they can speak up for it in international organizations in which Taiwan is not a member.

That being said, Taiwan has also long been accused of “dollar diplomacy”–paying off diplomatic allies through infrastructure investment deals or slush money to high-ranking politicians in return for recognition. Indeed, one notes that many of Taiwan’s diplomatic allies are countries that have questionable human rights records.

Though China offers much the same to such allies in return for switching recognition, Taiwan is unable to outspend China. China is, of course, much larger than Taiwan. Likewise, small states risk being shut ouf of the lucrative–and much larger–Chinese market if they retain ties with Taiwan.

At times, the question of whether to maintain ties with Taiwan or break them in favor of Taiwan is a dividing issue between the two major political parties of Taiwan’s diplomatic allies. Another question for such countries, however, is that of ties with the US. The US does not diplomatically recognize Taiwan either, but it has in the past sought to shore up Taiwan’s existing diplomatic allies, maintaining ties with it. Indeed, one notes that Taiwan’s existing diplomatic allies are often also closer to the US, rather than China, and this proves another means of the US extending its influence in Latin and Central America, or among Pacific states.

The Chinese government has sanctioned American government officials such as Marco Rubio in the past, over hawkish stances on China, criticism of China’s human rights record, and support for Hong Kong. It may not be surprising to see China targeting government officials of countries that express support for Taiwan, then. This would follow up on how sanctions on Taiwanese government officials may in themselves be ineffective, seeing as such individuals and their family members may already know better than to do business in China. But it is not impossible that some of those that China eventually targets do, in fact, have business holdings in China. As such, it is to be seen whether this proves an effective means of pressure on diplomatic allies of Taiwan.

author: Barry York
title: From student activism to Pentridge and beyond: the life of Barry York
content:
Barry York was a leading student radical at La Trobe University at the height of the movement against the Vietnam War. In 1972, along with two other student activists, Barry was arrested and held in Pentridge Prison for his anti-war activity. He recently self-published a memoir of his time in Pentridge as a political prisoner which will soon be available at Red Flag books.

The La Trobe struggle was part of the wider student movement opposing the Vietnam War, conscription and apartheid in the late 1960s and early 1970s. On campus, we challenged the university’s ties to political and economic power, including Chancellor Sir Archibald Glenn’s association with ICI (Imperial Chemical Industries, renamed Orica Limited in 1998), which had contracts with the government linked to the Vietnam War. ICI’s parent company also had links to the munitions and chemicals industries in apartheid South Africa. We opposed La Trobe’s rule barring students suspended elsewhere from enrolling, and questioned its possible cooperation with the Joint Intelligence Organisation. At the heart of these campaigns was a basic question: whose interests should a university serve?

At a mass student meeting in April 1971, attended by about 1,000 people, students endorsed demands for action on these issues. It must be noted that, at that time, La Trobe was a small campus and probably only had about 1,500 students on campus at any time. The campaign involved meetings, leafleting, debate, occupations and demonstrations. In July, students blockaded the university governing body, the Council, inside its chambers. The action had been endorsed at a student meeting, but it prompted a heavy police response and intensified the conflict between student activists and university authorities. Several activists were suspended and a larger number were fined. However, we won two key demands—the Chancellor’s resignation was announced in December, and the exclusion rule was rescinded.

This did not end the dispute though. The university authorities sought to stop the Student Representative Council from using its funds to pay the fines imposed on radical students who had been suspended. The fines totalled $3,000: a substantial amount, equivalent to about $40,000 today. Early the following year, the university sought a Supreme Court injunction barring four student activists from entering the campus. When we defied it, Fergus Robinson, Brian Pola and I were imprisoned for contempt of court. Rod Taylor evaded capture.

We were held indefinitely at Pentridge prison, a notorious high-security prison, without a criminal trial, the right to bail or appeal, or the opportunity to cross-examine witnesses. No fixed sentence was imposed. We would remain in prison until the university authorities asked the court to release us. The case raises lasting questions about freedom of expression, judicial power and the use of imprisonment to suppress political dissent.

That struggle forms the background to my memoir. Pentridge Prison closed in 1997, but the reality of life inside its bluestone walls should not be forgotten. The prison has been transformed into apartments, landscaped gardens, shops and fashionable cafés. Much of its brutality has been softened, repackaged or concealed by the redevelopment.

I wanted to recover that history by describing what it was like to be held at Pentridge as a political prisoner, first in D Division and then in A Division. Through observation and conversations with other prisoners, I also came to understand conditions in B and C Divisions and the notorious H Division, known as “Hell”.

The imprisonment of the “La Trobe Three” as we were called shows how fragile our freedoms can be. In writing the memoir, I also wanted to challenge the familiar, softened account of the youth rebellion of that era. The movement was about much more than sex, drugs, rock’n’roll and counterculture. Opposition to conscription, the Vietnam War and apartheid were central concerns. Many young people took their politics seriously; some sought revolutionary change as well as reform and were prepared to make personal sacrifices. Conventional accounts often leave that commitment in the background.

My political engagement with Pentridge continued after my release. From 1973 to 1976, I played a leading role in the Victorian Prisoners’ Action Committee. We campaigned against brutality and degrading conditions and brought prisoners’ experiences into public debate. We organised …

author: AWSM
title: Why I Won’t Vote ~ A SYMPOSIUM #1
content:
Anarchy 37, March 1964, Why I Won’t Vote

Voting : “The instrument and symbol of a freeman’s power to make a fool of himself and a wreck of his country”

The saying that ” only a fool would put a loaded gun into the hands of an idiot ” is an especially apt analogy of government. An idiot (usually well-meaning) considers himself clever enough to run the affairs of a large number of people by taking a seat in parliament. A large number of people, acting like fools, vote for his party’s policy then spend the next few years grumbling about the results. The error in approach is that the voter thinks that he will get what he voted for. If he could vote for those who in fact control the country, say the Governors of the Bank of England, the directors of the industrial corporations and those behind the ministries, the illusion of democracy would be more understandable.

The real centres of power lie far beyond the people’s influence at elections. These remain constant whatever Party is ” in power “. In the terms of centralised ” democracy ” the only possible argument to justify voting is that marginal benefits may be gained. The state only incidentally attends to the well-being of its subjects. Its main concern is its power relation to other states, of which the most perfect expression is in war.

I am on the side of people anywhere who are prepared neither to live nor die for something that in the long run can only militate against survival and the conditions that make life worth living. Our immediate action must, by its nature, be to oppose that pathetic gesture, voting. It must be direct and direction. We can learn to live as free men and women only by organising against the condition we are in.

The Tenants Association, Consumers Association, and Direct Action in industry all provide opportunities for people to experience directing their own lives in positive ways towards positive ends.

Only by direct involvement in society can the individual hope to transform himself and his world. Freedom cannot be given, it must be taken; and the free society can only grow from experiments in the problems (ethical and organisational) of community.

Voting does not, and cannot, mean government by consent. By voting, one acts on the assumptions that certain men are fit to govern, and that a majority is necessarily right. Also should the state, acting in the name of a (frequently fictitious) majority, declare war, the individual loses the right to live, if he ever had it.

To me, voting is complicity with the State and a negative action, therefore I do not vote.

author: Sue Bull
title: Socialist Alliance registered with the VEC for the Victorian elections
content:
Socialist Alliance will be on the ballot paper for the Victorian elections on November 28, after its registration lapsed in 2019.

Sue Bolton, Victorian candidate for the seat of Broadmeadows and a veteran Merri-bek City Councillor said she was pleased that Socialist Alliance, which formed in 2001, was registered again.

“We will be on the ballot, with our name and logo, presenting progressive, pro-worker policies.”

Bolton has a stand-out record of working with residents and communities standing up for their rights. She has helped win a number of concessions from the state, including saving the outdoor pool in Fawkner, and winning Merri-bek City Council support to end contracts with companies supporting the Israeli military.

Socialist Alliance is standing a group of candidates in the Northern Metropolitan Region of Naarm/Melbourne and in Djilang/Geelong, who have a record of fighting with vulnerable communities for rights and services.

Its campaign platform is “Fighting for people, not the billionaires” and says the incoming Victorian government must prioritise the needs of ordinary people, before corporate profits.

It is calling for the public sector to be rebuilt, including 100,000 new public houses and a moratorium on building energy hungry mega AI data centres.

Socialist Alliance is running five candidates for the Victorian Legislative Assembly, including Bolton and Jacob Andrewartha in Pascoe Vale, and three in the Northern Metropolitan Region.

In Djilang, the party will contest all four Legislative Assembly seats and three for the Western Victoria Region.

Sarah Hathway, a former councillor for the City of Greater Geelong who is standing in Lara, said there are a number of micro far-right parties, some with progressive sounding names, which have also registered with the Victorian Electoral Commission.

“Having Socialist Alliance registered means workers have a real alternative to the right-wing hypocrites, such as One Nation,” Hathway said.

“These conservative parties blame immigrants for the cost-of-living and housing crises. They whip up racism to distract and confuse people from putting the blame where it really lies — on the billionaires, one third of whom do not even pay tax.”

Tim Gooden, the lead Socialist Alliance candidate for Western Victoria Region and a former secretary of Geelong Trades Hall said: “Workers in the two regions can now vote for candidates who have a proven track record of fighting with communities and are putting forward positive solutions for workers, rather than the hate which is being spewed by the big end of town.”

[Sue Bull is running for Socialist Alliance in the Western Region. For further information and to help out, get in touch with Socialist Alliance Victoria.]

author: Robert Narai
title: France’s student revolt
content:
Video footage shows tens of thousands of school students packed into Place de la République in Paris, chanting, “High schools in struggle! Youth on fire! The revolution is on the march!” It’s 6 October, and outside Lamartine high school, students hold placards that read, “More class hours than sleep” and “8am to 6pm, are we students or in police custody?”

“We are protesting because we deserve the right to have a good life”, Lyna tells 

Red Flag

 via text from the Parisian suburb of Saint-Denis. She is a 16-year-old 

lycéenne

 (high schooler aged 15 to 18) at Paul-Éluard; her parents are Algerian immigrants. Lyna says many young people like her have lost faith that school will lead anywhere. Meanwhile, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu’s budget proposes €54 billion in public spending cuts and the abolition of 1,588 teaching posts. Combined with police who treat young people from the 

banlieues

 (working-class suburbs) like 

racaille

 (“scum”) and a growing far right, it has created a disaffected layer of young people.

“There are cockroaches and rats everywhere”, Lyna says of her classrooms. “We have classes that go from 8am to 6pm. The police harass us on the streets because of the colour of our skin and the 

banlieue

 we live in. We, the children of the 

banlieues

, are abandoned and neglected.” Yet students in better parts of Paris have joined Lyna. “We know we’re privileged, but we support the other 

lycées

”, a student at a private Catholic school told 

Public Sénat

 at the 6 October demonstration.

“

Lycéens

, and even 

collégiens

 [ages 11 to 15], are fighting above all against the two-tier education system they are victims of”, says Arthur, a student at Lycée Charlemagne in Paris and member of the New Anticapitalist Party–Revolutionaries (NPA-R), via message. “On one side, there is pressure at every level to ‘succeed at school’ or you have no future. But on the other, everyone can see that it’s cash that determines ‘success’. Year after year, the number of students per class keeps rising, up to 35, and students go weeks, even months, without a maths or French teacher.”

How the revolt unfolded

The revolt began on 21 September, when about 200 students at Saint-Exupéry high school in Créteil, south-east of Paris, blockaded their school. Within days, the blockades spread across the Paris region, as students in poor and migrant suburbs linked their own conditions—including Parcoursup (an online platform that allocates places at public universities, which entrenches class and racial inequality)—to decades of funding cuts. Hundreds of thousands of students have since joined strikes and demonstrations against the government of Emmanuel Macron, and the revolt has moved beyond the demand for decent schools into a confrontation with austerity, police violence and racism. On 29 September, more than 300,000 people marched in a public sector strike against the budget, carrying signs reading “70 billion euros for the army, nothing for education”. By 1 October, the Interior Ministry reported actions at more than 1,000 schools.

In each blockaded school, daily mass meetings (“assemblies”) decide the next day’s action, and the disempowerment of ordinary life is turned on its head. Arthur says debating the questions the movement raises gives students ownership over it. “The government sought to break the movement by discrediting high school students as rioters ‘manipulated by La France Insoumise’ [France Unbowed, the left-wing party led by Jean-Luc Mélenchon]”, he says. 

“Some students target the police, and rightly so, which has sparked debate: how can the division sought by the government be avoided? What is certain is that in the assemblies we all agree not to be divided, to denounce police violence, to demand the release of all arrested students, and to say what the placards in Lyon say: ‘The burning of garbage only scares the garbage’.”

And as the revolt spreads to every kind of high school, Arthur asks, “How can we maintain the working-class character of the movement and its demands, which was its initial strength, without it dissolving into a kind of ‘everyone together’ mentality?”

National coordination has emerged across the assemblies: 200 delegates from 71 schools met on 10 October and called actions for 13, 15 and 17 October. “No way our struggle is going to be stolen by others!”, Arthur says.

State repression

The demonstrations have been met with fierce repression from the police. By 8 …

author: Cas Smith
title: Land Forces weapons expo protested in a time of genocide
content:
Around 2000 anti-war activists took to the streets on October 6, in a strong rebuke to the weapons’ manufacturers displaying their wares at the Land Forces International Land Defence Exposition and Western Australian Labor, which welcomed it.

The rally, one of the biggest in recent years, began at Yagan Square near Northbridge, before marching through the city to Elizabeth Quay, close to the Perth Convention Centre.

A “security area” had been set up around the expo venue, which included the Elizabeth Quay train station and several sections of surrounding streets.

A new law, the Land Forces (Special Powers) Act 2026, gave police the “ability to establish checkpoints, cordons, and roadblocks, while also searching people, bags, and vehicles, and issue lawful directions for a 10-day period”, until October 10.

Alongside this, several activists had been told they were banned from the security area, and could face fines of up to $36,000 and three years in prison if they challenged this.

The media coverage of these repressive security initiatives — to which WA Premier Roger Cook had allocated $11.5 million — may have encouraged people to come to the rally, which was hosted by WA Anti-War Collective, Stop AUKUS WA, Nuclear Free WA, Independent and Peaceful Australia Network (IPAN), Friends of Palestine WA (FOPWA), Students for Palestine WA, Right To Protest WA and Extinction Rebellion Western Australia.

It included several creative aspects, including a flash mob dance to the tune of the Temptations’ song “War” and a performance by Drummers for Climate Action.

Noongar Elders Uncle Headley Hayward and Uncle Herbert Bropho gave the Welcome to Country. Adrian Glamorgan (Independent and Peaceful Australia Network and Stop AUKUS WA), Danica Scott (Stop AUKUS WA and Freiends of Palestine WA), Greens MLC Sophie McNeill, Rojin Didari (Students for Palestine WA) and Berlin Guerrero (Migrante and International People’s Struggle) addressed the protest.

Sam Wainwright (Stop AUKUS WA), who MCed the rally, said Labor’s decision to roll out the red carpet for weapons manufacturers indicated his priorities.

“[Land Forces] comes in the context of a worldwide increase in military expenditure, including a 50% increase in military expenditure by Donald Trump. It comes in the context of the genocide in Gaza, and a climate emergency,” Wainwright said.

“It poses the question: What is the real response of our rulers to what are known as the ‘poly crises’ of capitalism. Is it not repression at home and war abroad?”

It was particularly horrific that weapons used in Gaza would be on display at the exhibition, Wainwright added.

“For the last three years, we have begged this federal government to stop sending arms to Israel and to cancel bilateral military ties, because it’s the one thing you’d do if you were serious about stopping the genocide.

“Labor won’t, because it has committed to making Australia one of the 10 major weapons exporters in the world. Roger Cook has said he wants to make weapons exports the number two industry in WA. The place of Israel in the military industrial complex means deepening bilateral military ties with that state.”

Elbit Systems and Rafael were among the Israeli weapons companies featured at Land Forces, alongside Lockheed Martin, which constructs the F-35 fighter jets used in much of the destruction of Gaza.

author: Ridah Hassan
title: Manosphere making classrooms toxic
content:
“I had male students threatening to rape the female students consistently. They would play ‘rape marry kill’ and used my own name frequently in their ‘game’.”

“Students saying ‘good girl’ to teachers.”

“Less respect for female staff vs male in behaviour—even with the same approaches they instantly listen to males more. More inappropriate jokes—racism, homophobic and sexist jokes with little consequences. Visible [and] audible dismissal/rejection of female staff to their faces when they appear to take classes.” 

These are quotes from a Monash University report which has cast light on the disturbing sexist conditions faced by teachers and students in primary and secondary schools across the country. 

Duty of Care: Teachers’ experiences of sexism, misogyny and sexual harassment in Australian schools

 is based on the testimony of 2,600 educators and reveals the breadth and depth of the crisis. 

A common theme in the report is the lack of respect male students show female teachers. This includes frequent interrupting, ignoring of instructions, mocking and mimicking, speaking disrespectfully and refusing to accept responsibility when challenged about inappropriate behaviour. Physical aggression and intimidation were also reported, along with threats of more serious physical and sexual assault. Male students frequently make “derogatory comments toward females focusing on appearance and worth”, “jokes about gender roles e.g. the kitchen”, “inappropriate sexualised remarks about female bodies, including specifically about peers and/or staff” and “[making] sexual noises in the classroom” while female staff are trying to teach.

This behaviour is contributing to the burn-out of teachers in a profession already facing shortages due to poor pay and unmanageable workloads. One respondent put it clearly: “Being the front line and bearing the brunt of misogyny is exhausting and erodes self-worth”. According to the report, 77 percent of teachers say that sexism and misogyny have a “negative” or “very negative” impact on their wellbeing, and more than 50 percent of female teachers report that they either “occasionally” or “frequently” consider leaving the profession because of it. And the situation is getting worse—both primary and secondary teachers reported that gendered violence on the part of students had increased significantly in the previous twelve months.

Given adult teachers are feeling undermined, threatened and belittled by male students’ behaviour, the impact on teenage girls should be cause for immediate action. According to the report, “Younger students are comfortable using misogynistic language without thought e.g. calling girls in class a ‘slut’ ‘whore’ because they won’t share a highlighter”, and “Women/girls in class are okay with being treated with misogyny as this is seen as ‘normal’ now. They do not retaliate and internalise, making emotional regulation hard”. Another teacher observed: “Female students are scared to speak out and express their opinions in class with males who chastise them. I am noticing students are very hesitant to participate in discussion these days whereas it used to be female students being quite eager to share ideas and answer questions. Female students appear angrier than in the past as well”.

Male students direct sexist and misogynistic language towards their female peers freely, entrenching a toxic gender divide among students. Again, the statistics bear this out, with 80 percent of respondents agreeing that the behaviour is having a negative impact on student wellbeing. In observing and being victim to male students’ sexism—including constantly disrupting learning and making spaces hostile—girls are being socialised to accept dehumanising language and treatment and to make themselves small targets by withdrawing and accommodating to the selfish and anti-social behaviour of boys. 

And though there are undoubtedly some who are willing to challenge their peers’ appalling behaviour, it is an unacceptable environment for female students to be expected to navigate every day, while at the same time trying to do the actual tasks of deciphering Shakespeare or learning calculus. It is well established that students learn best when they feel safe, supported and respected. This is currently not the case for female students at Australian schools.

author: @ndy
title: Yeah Nah Pasaran #300 w Emma Hagberg on ‘Comrades, Not Friends’ & The Revolutionary Front : October 8, 2026
content:
This week on Yeah Nah Pasaran! we talk to Emma Hagberg. Emma is the author of Comrades, Not Friends: The Revolutionary Front, Antifascism, and Class Struggle (PM Press/Working Class History, 2026), translated by Gabriel Kuhn and with a preface by Tomas Rothaus (both of whom have been previous guests of the show).

According to Hagberg, RF had ‘a strong collective identity, the view of fascists as class traitors, and the critique of an autonomous left that often had no place for working-class people’; Comrades was originally published in Swedish as 18.6 – Kamrater, Inte Vänner (B.E.L Publishing, 2024) and is also available in a German translation.

The Revolutionary Front (RF), 2001–2015, was the most militant organization on the left in recent Swedish history. Staunchly working class, the first generation of RF members engaged in numerous street battles with Swedish fascists. When the fascists retreated from the streets, RF attacked them in their homes. The police cracked down on the organization in 2013, raiding the apartments of several alleged members at the crack of dawn. The courts handed out prison sentences of up to six and a half years. Two years later, the organization folded.

author: Peter Boyle
title: NSW Parliamentary Friends of the Kurdish people launched
content:
NSW Parliamentary Friends of the Kurdish People was launched in NSW Parliament House on October 13. It has an initial membership of 11 MPs, including co-chairs Abigail Boyd (Greens), Anthony D’Adam MLC (Labor) and secretary Tim James MP (Liberal).

Gulfer Olan, co-chair of the Federation of Democratic Kurdish Society Australia, said this was “an historical milestone”.

Boyd explained that it took seven years and the hard work of many people to get to the Parliamentary Friends of the Kurdish People officially established. “I resonate with the spirit of the Kurdish community, your commitment to grassroots democracy, your commitment to gender equality and economic equality, your love of nature, the environment.”

D’Adam said: “We are one in commitment to democracy and human rights, the right to self-determination and the right to cultural autonomy... [this is] another marker of the status that this community now holds in Australian society as an important part of our multicultural community.”

He added that it is “a very important thing to acknowledge our multicultural society where people aren’t asked to surrender their culture and become part of a monoculture”.

“We are all Australians and we’re able to maintain our cultural identity and that’s something that’s really important. It’s important that we defend that at this time when, as we know, there are dark forces rising in our community that are threatening those very values that we hold here.”

Parliamentary Friends of the Kurdish People

Federation of Democratic Kurdish Society Australia

author: Anneke Demanuele
title: Westsiders campaign against AI hub
content:
I met Anthony and Samantha on Holden Road in Plumpton, 40 kilometres west of Melbourne’s CBD. We’ve parked our cars at the Melbourne Renewable Energy hub gate, behind which a huge expanse of land could become home to a hyperscale data centre owned and operated by Syncline Energy. 

The surrounding area is a green wedge, meaning that it should be protected from industrial and urban sprawl. There’s a free-range egg farm, rolling fields, some houses and a few horses. Samantha, who is campaigning against the development, lives five minutes away in Diggers Rest and learned to ride a horse right here. In fact, one we are looking at is called Betsy and is the very same horse. 

A 

petition

 against the AI hub raises concerns about environmental destruction, including “endangered ecological vegetation communities, biodiversity corridors, areas of Aboriginal cultural heritage sensitivity and conservation efforts”.

The Plumpton plan is still awaiting approval from the state government. If it gets it, the site will host a

 

350-hectare AI hub

, which the 

Age

 reports is the size of 175 MCG playing fields. The facility will have a maximum power draw of 2.5 gigawatts, more than the entire output of the Loy Yang A coal power plant. Loy Yang A provides around 

30 percent of Victoria’s power

. It would use more power than every other data centre currently operating combined. 

“It’s such a blatant display of profit over people”, says Anthony, who has also been campaigning against Syncline’s plans for months. 

Their campaign group started after a community meeting of 150 people in Sydenham. “Anthony and Ella produced these awesome pamphlets, so we’ve been doing lots of letterboxing”, Samantha says. “We also hosted an information night [and] we’ve got a day of action coming up. We also attended the Senate inquiry as witnesses.” 

The Senate inquiry held hearings in Yarraville last month. The inquiry has heard from residents, local politicians and data centre CEOs. Local testimonies include stories of monolithic structures bearing down on residents, diesel emissions and pollution, drone surveillance, and concerns about fire risk.

“The Plumpton site will have huge amounts of lithium-ion batteries, and we feel like this hasn’t been assessed or regulated enough”, Samantha says. Lithium-ion batteries can trigger thermal runaway, releasing toxic fumes and a self-sustaining fire. Because data centres need 24/7 power, they often rely on diesel or gas generators. This increases the risk of uncontrollable fires. “The combination of lithium batteries and diesel is a pretty nasty sort of fire”, a member of Fire Rescue Victoria 

told the ABC 

in June

. 

The Plumpton group is one of many across Melbourne, mostly in working-class areas. The wealthy areas of Melbourne are unlikely to be high on the list of potential sites for the centres. In fact, Belinda Dennett, CEO of the data centre lobby group, said she wouldn’t want to live near one. Samantha describes her as “AI in human form”. Anthony is frustrated that communities have no say in whether centres get built. “It’s so clear that the system is not set up for a democratic decision”, he says.

Samantha says those living near the site don’t have much idea what is coming to their doorstep: 

“Last time I checked, there’s about 80 residents around here. And none of these guys knows about it. It will be in full view of their backyards, and they almost don’t want to believe me; they think I’m almost a conspiracy theorist. But it’s going to be built here, and they haven’t been notified”. 

That’s why Samantha and her co-organisers have been hosting outreach meetings, and doing the letterboxing and door knocking. They want to inform their neighbours what is coming to their communities and fight it together. 

According to Samantha and Anthony, Syncline’s CEO is a “schmoozer”. At the Senate hearings, he said his company has done a “bad job” at community outreach. He’s trying to turn that around and convince locals the AI hub will benefit them. 

“He is very good at convincing people that this will benefit them, without explaining how”, Samantha says. Anthony and Samantha feel the campaign has put pressure on Syncline, which is now trying to win support for its plan by claiming it will create new jobs. But those in the campaign aren’t fooled.

They also aren’t fooled by the Labor government’s Sustainable Data Centre Action Plan. The government promises that data centres won’t be built near …

author: Unknown
title: Fransa: Öğrenci isyanı toplumsallaşıyor, 800 bin insan Cumartesi sokaktaydı
content:
Fransa'da eylül ortasında başlayan lise protestoları, 17 Ekim Cumartesi günü Paris'ten Akdeniz kıyısında Marsilya'ya, Orta Batı'da Limoges'da kitlesel yürüyüşlere dönüştü. İçişleri Bakanlığı ülke çapında 110 gösteri düzenlendiğini açıkladı. Gösterilerin çoğu barışçıl geçerken bazı kentlerde yağma, kundaklama ve polislerle çatışmalar yaşandı.


İsyanın sınıfsal coğrafyası


Hareketin ilk merkezlerinden biri Seine-Saint-Denis. Burası, Paris'in kuzeydoğusunda işçi sınıfı nüfusunun yoğunlaştığı yoksul bir ilçe. İsyan, Saint-Denis, Aubervilliers ve Sevran'daki liselerde öğrenciler öğretmen eksikliği, bakımsız binalar, kalabalık sınıflar ve eğitimde bölgesel eşitsizlikler nedeniyle dersleri boykotuyla  başladı. Paul-Éluard ve Le Corbusier liseleri öne çıktı. Öğretmenler ve veliler de eylemlere katıldı.


Öğrencilerin itirazı yalnızca okul binalarıyla sınırlı değildi: Yoksul mahallelerde eğitime ayrılan kaynaklar ve yükseköğretime erişim koşulları da hareketin gündemine girdi.


Piketty: “Macronizmin alacakaranlığı”


"21. Yüzyılda Kapital"in yazarı iktisatçı Thomas Piketty, 17 Ekim'de

Le Monde

'da yayımlanan yazısında öğrenci hareketini şöyle değerlendirdi:


“Bugünkü lise ve üniversite öğrencileri hareketi, Macronizmin alacakaranlığına işaret ediyor.”


Piketty'nin aktardığı hesaplamaya göre 2017-2026 döneminde yükseköğretim bütçesi nominal olarak artsa da enflasyon ve öğrenci sayısındaki yükseliş nedeniyle öğrenci başına reel kaynak yaklaşık yüzde 20 azaldı.


Piketty, araştırmacı Asma Benhenda'nın verilerine dayanarak eğitimdeki bölgesel eşitsizliğe dikkat çekti:


"Paris ve varlıklı Hauts-de-Seine'deki öğretmenlerin yaklaşık yüzde 10'u sözleşmeli ya da mesleğe yeni başlamış öğretmenlerden oluşurken, yoksul Seine-Saint-Denis ve Val-de-Marne'da bu oran yüzde 50'ye ulaşıyor.”


Kaynak yetersizliği savunmasına “Fransa hiç bu kadar zengin olmamıştı” diyr karşılık veren Piketty sonucu bir cümleyle özetledi: 


“Sorun yalnızca bir bölüşüm sorunu.”


Sendikalar öğrencilerle buluştu


Öğrencilerle ilk örgütlü dayanışmayı eğitim emekçileri sendikaları kurdu. Eğitim, Öğretim ve Araştırma Sendikaları Federasyonu (FSU), Genel Emek Konfederasyonu (CGT), İşçi Gücü (FO), Fransız Demokratik Emek Konfederasyonu (CFDT), Ulusal Özerk Sendikalar Birliği (UNSA) ve SUD-Solidaires'in eğitim örgütleri ekim başında öğretmen açığına, eğitim bütçesine ve okul koşullarına ilişkin ortak eylem çağrılarında yer aldı.


17 Ekim'de katılım eğitim sektörünü aştı. CGT ve sendikal birlik Solidaires, üyelerini öğrenci ve emekçi gösterilerine çağırdı. CGT ücret ve emekli aylıklarının artırılmasını, hayat pahalılığıyla mücadeleyi ve kamu hizmetlerinin korunmasını öne çıkardı. Genel Sekreter Sophie Binet, kaynakların büyük servetlerden ve şirket kârlarından sağlanmasını savundu. Solidaires işyerlerinde grevlerin örgütlenmesini istedi.


Köylü Konfederasyonu (Confédération paysanne), gelir güvencesi, gıdaya erişim ve iklim adaleti talepleriyle katıldı. Akaryakıt fiyatları ve geçim sıkıntısına karşı harekete geçen Sarı Yelekliler de yürüyüşlere katıldı. Öğrenci örgütleri USL, UNEF ve Öğrenci Birliği çağrıları destekledi.


Ancak 17 Ekim'e bütün konfederasyonlar ortak genel grevle katılmadı. Eylem tatil günü yapıldı ve  CFDT ve FO ülke çapındaki ağırlıklarını 5 Kasım eylemine koyacaklarını açıkladılar. 


Gösterilerin yoğunlaştığı merkezler ve şiddet olayları


Paris'te Cumhuriyet Meydanı çevresi başlıca buluşma noktasıydı. Lyon, Nantes, Rennes, Marsilya, Lille, Toulouse, Bordeaux, Strasbourg ve Montpellier'de yürüyüşler düzenlendi. Boyun Eğmeyen Fransa (LFI) lideri Jean-Luc Mélenchon Paris'te gösteriye katıldı; komünistler ve Yeşiller de çeşitli kentlerde gösterilerde yer aldı.


Paris'te bazı mağazalar yağmalandı, araçlar ateşe verildi. Limoges'da belediye binasında yangın çıktı; Marsilya ve Lille'de belediye binaları zarar gördü. Lyon'da bir turizm bürosu kundaklandı; Bordeaux ve başka merkezlerde mağazalara saldırılar bildirildi.


Bununla birlikte, şiddet olayları yüz binlerce göstericinin katıldığı eylemlerin belkemiğini oluşturmuyor. İçişleri Bakanlığı yaklaşık 400 gözaltı açıkladı; bu sayı, yağma ve kundaklamaya karışanları ifade etmiyor. Önceki günlerde polisin gözaltına aldığı protestocu sayısı bundan birkaç kat yüksekti.


İçişleri Bakanı Laurent Nuñez saldırılardan radikal aşırı solu sorumlu tuttu; suçlamasını doğrulayan bağımsız bir genel bilanço açıklamadı. LFI lideri Mélenchon yağma ve tahribe katılmama çağrısı yaptı. Önceki gösterilerde bir …

title: Marcha Federal Universitaria: reclamo masivo, represión y resistencia en Plaza Congreso
content:
Masiva fue una vez más la marcha al Congreso para exigir el cumplimiento de la Ley de Financiamiento Universitario y rechazar también el DNU 70/2023, exigir el desendeudamiento y la prórroga de la Emergencia en Discapacidad. La jornada, marcada por

la falta de quórum

 en la sesión legislativa, terminó con un operativo represivo de las cuatro fuerzas federales y la Policía de la Ciudad que dejó al menos 550 afectados por gases y balas de goma, entre ellos numerosos trabajadores de prensa, incluidos integrantes de nuestro medio, y seis detenidos. La resistencia activa de los manifestantes se sostuvo pese a la represión.

author: Amy Goodman
title: Inside the Worker Resistance in Silicon Valley’s Tech Oligarchy
content:
Longtime tech worker organizers discuss early victories in the movement — and the repression that followed.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

Longtime tech worker organizers Clarissa Redwine and JS Tan’s new book, Against Tech Oligarchy: Worker Resistance in the World’s Most Powerful Industry, draws on the authors’ experiences at major tech companies to chronicle the rise and fall of the tech worker movement, its early victories, and the repression and slide to corporate control that followed.

“Over the course of the 2010s, what we saw was that the tech industry wasn’t quite the industry that it had promised to its workers and to the public. Rather than making the world more open, more democratic, we saw it really be the culprit of misinformation,” says Tan, who was pushed out of Microsoft after raising objections to the company’s ties to fossil fuel companies.

Silicon Valley’s slide to the right was influenced by corporate backlash to labor’s demands, explains Redwine, who was fired from Kickstarter for union organizing. She says she hopes to inspire a new generation of tech workers to organize “within these tech oligarchs’ own empires, to stand up and push back.”

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org, The War and Peace Report. I’m Amy Goodman.

If you work in the tech industry, your boss might not want you to tune in to our next segment. It’s about a remarkable new book called Against Tech Oligarchy: Worker Resistance in the World’s Most Powerful Industry. It’s written by longtime tech worker organizers Clarissa Redwine and JS Tan. Drawing on their own experience organizing at high-tech companies, they chronicle the rise of the tech worker movement, its early victories, and the challenges it faces today as tech titans consolidate their economic and political power, while tech workers face mass layoffs.

Clarissa Redwine helped unionize Kickstarter, where she was fired amidst a union-busting campaign before workers went on to win union recognition. JS Tan is a former Microsoft software engineer who publicly challenged Microsoft’s work with the Pentagon, with ICE and with fossil fuel companies, including its use of cloud and AI technologies to help Chevron expand oil extraction.

Their new book comes as tech companies embrace artificial intelligence, workplace surveillance and increased automation. At Meta, for example, a new initiative will collect workers’ mouse movements, keystrokes and some screenshots to help train AI models to replace them in the future. In response, Meta workers reached out to United Tech and Allied Workers, a branch of the Communication Workers Union, to discuss unionization efforts and how best to resist.

Clarissa Redwine and JS Tan join us now.

We welcome you both to Democracy Now! It’s great to have you with us. Clarissa, let’s start with you. First of all, explain what Kickstarter is and how you got the experience you did, and then how you tried to unionize your workplace, though it ultimately did get unionized.

CLARISSA REDWINE: Yes, it did. Yeah. So, I joined the tech industry in a moment where there was a lot of optimism for what tech could do for society. And Kickstarter was especially idealistic, where the reason the platform exists is to give communities a tool for bringing projects to life, cultural projects, but also technology. And, you know, in 2016, when I joined, there was a moment where tech management and workers felt aligned and united against the Trump administration. But as the years went by, we saw, over and over, tech companies capitulating, becoming complicit in the rise of the alt-right. And there came a moment at Kickstarter where we had the same experience.

So, there was a moment where Breitbart wrote an article saying that a Kickstarter project was inciting violence. This project was a comic book called Always Punch Nazis, which they did not like. And management decided, rather than stand up to Breitbart and this push from the alt-right, that they would cancel the project. And I and my co-workers demanded that we keep this project on the site. And that moment of collective action was transformative for myself, but also my co-workers, where we saw the promise of collective action. And after that, we decided we wanted structural power in the workplace. We wanted …

author: Julius Gavroche
title: The Encampment Movement against Evictions and Gentrification
content:
from the

CrimethInc.

 collective, 15/10/2026


A Report from Madrid and Barcelona


On September 23, 2026, Spanish authorities violently evicted Maricarmen Abascal, a disabled 87-year-old woman, from her home in Madrid following her long judicial struggle with a real estate company named Urbagestión. She had lived there for 70 years, but could not afford the latest rent increases. In response, 10,000 people took the streets in protest that day. Three days later, a much larger demonstration established an encampment in the Puerta del Sol square, which had been the site of the

15-M movement

 in 2011, itself the trigger for the

Occupy

 movement in the United States.


Maricarmen Abascal passed away on October 7 as a consequence of the stress resulting from the eviction. Protesters have continued to occupy the squares in many cities across the Iberian Peninsula. A general strike has been called for November 11.


Here, our correspondents in Madrid and Barcelona offer a view from within the movement against evictions and gentrification that has spread across Spain and Catalunya.


Anti-fascists gather to defend the housing encampment in Madrid’s Plaza del Sol, 2026.


The housing movement in Spain has a long and complex history. For any period that we might choose as a point of departure, there always exists a prior precedent that could serve just as well—so where we begin depends on how we wish to make sense of what is happening today, how we wish to narrate this story that is still being written in the streets. What follows, then, is an attempt, however insufficient and incomplete, to tell this story, in hopes that you can learn or be inspired by something from it and, in this way, become part of this story and build upon it wherever you live.


We could perhaps begin with the

15-M movement

, which erupted a decade and a half ago as part of the sequence of uprisings that unfolded across the globe in 2011. Encampments spread across Spain much as they have today, full of people clamoring for “

real democracy

.”


Whereas elsewhere, repression often put these movements to an unresolved end, in Spain, this movement culminated with the formation of several far-left political parties, including Podemos, as well as strong municipalist movements in Madrid, Barcelona, and other cities. Today, these parties lie in ruins, while the municipalists have largely lost whatever power they once held. Ultimately, much like

Occupy Wall Street

 and the Arab Spring, the true legacy of this sequence remains ambiguous, contested, and open to interpretation. Perhaps the 15-M movement is not the beginning of the story we’re telling, but simply the ruins from which the current one is being told.


Riot police are covered in eggs and paint while attempting to evict a building in Barcelona, 2021.


The movement that is now swelling across Spain emerged as a result of strong and stable union-style organizations that operate apart from the official institutional structures that are otherwise so present and influential in political life here. These organizations were built to tackle the housing crisis using horizontal and grassroots power, while simultaneously driving widespread and popular mobilizations like those we are witnessing today. These unions are novel in that they don’t involve questions of work directly, but rather address the conditions in which we live. The movement’s most significant antecedents lie in the creation of organizations such as the PAH (Platform for People Affected by Mortgages), the first chapter of which was founded in Barcelona in 2009. Like the more recently created housing organizations, the PAH groups practice what we call “social unionism.”


The premise is simple: an individual problem like a person facing the threat of losing their home is transformed into a collective issue addressed through shared political action. A variety of union-style tactics soon began to emerge, leading to the halting of many imminent evictions.


A group of thirty or so people assembles in front of an apartment in the historic city center as the sun is rising. People cling to one another tightly, locked arm in arm, crowding in front of the door of the building’s entrance while several vans of riot police pull up and park nearby as scheduled. There’s an announcement from a police loudspeaker to the effect that people must disperse, but no one does. Eventually, the cops move in, struggling to pull each person away one by one …

author: Unknown
title: Karabulut: Existing trade unions cannot even protect their own members
content:
Low wages, precarious employment conditions, and increasing obstacles to trade union organizing shape the working lives of millions of people in Turkey. According to the Ministry of Labor and Social Security, only 2.5 million of approximately 17.6 million registered workers are unionized. This means that around 86 percent of officially registered employees are not members of a trade union.


Özgür Karabulut, chair of the Revolutionary Construction and Road Workers’ Union (Dev-Yapı-İş), which is affiliated with the Confederation of Progressive Trade Unions of Turkey (DİSK), sees this as the result of policies that favor employers and systematically hinder workers’ ability to collectively assert their rights. Speaking to ANF, he also criticized traditional trade union structures, arguing that many are no longer capable of representing the interests of their own members.


‘Workers are at the mercy of employers’


Karabulut described working conditions in Turkey as increasingly precarious. He said millions of people were affected by unemployment, low wages, and a lack of social security. The fragmentation of employment into different working arrangements and contractual relationships further complicates efforts to organize collectively, he noted.


“Even the most fundamental right, the right to receive wages, is being violated. Under the pretext of the economic crisis, hundreds of workers are no longer even receiving their salaries regularly. Workers now have to fight not only for new rights but also simply to ensure that their wages are paid,” Karabulut stated.


Protests by workers whose wages have sometimes remained unpaid for months are now taking place in almost all industrial zones and at numerous construction sites. Those who resist these conditions or attempt to organize in trade unions face the threat of dismissal and repression. Karabulut also holds state institutions responsible for this situation. He argues that existing laws designed to protect workers are not consistently enforced, while companies that violate labor rights often face no effective consequences.


Traditional trade unions face criticism


Karabulut’s criticism also explicitly targets established trade unions. He argues that many have confined themselves to defending existing rights rather than securing new gains. Even this defensive strategy, he says, has increasingly failed.


“Traditional trade union structures are not even capable of protecting and advancing the rights and interests of their own members. They are even less capable of offering solutions to workers who are completely unorganized and left at the mercy of employers.”


Karabulut also traces the causes of this development to the history of Turkey’s trade union movement. “Following the military coup of September 12, 1980, hard-won workers’ rights were severely restricted, resilient trade unions were dismantled, and employer-friendly organizations were promoted. This created a trade union landscape focused more on controlling social conflicts than on securing collective rights.”


According to Karabulut, the consequences are still being felt today. “In many workplaces, there is now little difference in wages and working conditions between unionized and non-unionized workers. Just because a building bears a sign reading ‘Workers’ Union’ does not necessarily mean that the organization actually defends workers’ rights,” he said.


Karabulut added that some trade unions now operate more like corporate human resources departments than independent organizations representing workers’ interests.


New forms of labor struggle emerge


Despite the difficult circumstances, Karabulut sees signs of a new direction within the labor movement. Increasing attacks on wages and labor rights are prompting workers to seek new forms of organization rather than relying exclusively on established trade unions.


“When existing structures can no longer provide answers, workers will develop forms of struggle and organizational mechanisms that go beyond these structures,” he explained.


Karabulut emphasized the need for a fundamental democratization of trade unions. He argued that unions must abandon employer-friendly practices and once again become organizations that independently represent collective interests and actively engage in labor struggles.


He also opposed limiting trade union activities to collective bargaining and economic demands.
