author: Kodao Productions
title: Peso dives to new record low
content:
The Philippine Peso dove to a new record low on Thursday, breaching past the P63 threshold per US dollar for the first time in history. The Peso-Dollar exchange rate closed at P63.15 per US greenback. The previous record was P62.925 per US dollar set exactly a month ago on September 15.


The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) cited a stronger US dollar, shifting expectations around US Federal Reserve rate cuts, and regional market pressures brought about by the prolonged war in the Middle East as the reasons for the dive.


The Philippine currency had lost P5.21 to the US dollar since the US-Israel led war against Iran started in February 28.


The new record low happened as the BSP played conservative in defending the peso against the volatile foreign exchange market, choosing to preserve its reserves and intervening only when movements become sharp and disorderly.


The BSP primarily uses the country’s Gross International Reserves to stabilize the Philippine peso against foreign exchange volatility and to service foreign debt obligations.


The Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), meanwhile, said electronic products and petroleum products, such as crude oil and refined fuel are two top importations that drain the country’s foreign exchange and import outlays.


Much of the country’s reserves come from remittances from its millions of workers abroad, such as 2.4 million overseas laborers in the Middle East. There are about a million Filipinos in the UAE alone, contributing approximately P380 billion or $6.06 billion every year.


Local economic think-tank Ibon Foundation said that a record-low Philippine peso paired with high global oil and import prices creates a “double whammy” that aggressively drives up domestic inflation and worsens economic strain for Filipino households.


The PSA recently reported that the inflation rate in the Philippines was at a whopping 7.2 per cent last September, a sharp increase from 6.1 per cent last August.


Philippine oil industry sources have already announced a gasoline price increase of up to P4.30 per liter next week. #

(Raymund B. Villanueva)

author: To be a name
title: In Gaza, even thinking has become a struggle
content:
I have thought carefully about how to write about my life in Gaza. Even speaking about what we experience requires caution. How can I tell the truth about my reality without putting myself at risk?

This question alone says something about what it means to live here.

My days have become a series of moments. in which survival takes priority over everything else.

At night, the sound of surveillance drones makes it difficult to think about anything beyond the possibility that we could be next. Even when the sky grows quiet, peace feels unreal. At night, closing my eyes no longer feels different from opening them.

Our homes are destroyed, yet we still hope to recover even one small belonging from the rubble.

We want something to carry from our past into a future we cannot imagine.

Sometimes, the movement of rats among the ruins makes us wonder whether danger has returned. Even animals seek shelter in the remains of our homes, while we cannot safely retrieve the things that once made those homes ours.

Then comes the daily search for drinking water.

In 2026, finding clean water should not be the greatest problem occupying a person's mind. Yet we wait in line, hoping to receive enough to get through the day. We think about studying, working, resting and finding moments of happiness, but every ordinary activity competes with the demands of survival. Even water becomes a calculation.

After a bombing, another family may enter the records of the dead. Their loss might become a headline for a few seconds, or pass almost unnoticed.

But those who knew them will remember their names, their voices and the lives they lived. Human beings should never have to meet an unspoken threshold of tragedy before their deaths are considered worthy of attention.

I see people carrying grief that no words can fully express.

I see destroyed homes, displaced neighbours and parents trying to comfort hungry children. I see people who have lost their work, their security and loved ones, yet still find reasons to smile. Their smiles do not mean the suffering has disappeared.

Sometimes, they are simply a way of remaining human.

Then, from far beyond Gaza, we see people raising Palestinian flags and speaking out against oppression and genocide. Their solidarity reminds us that we are not alone. It gives us a moment to feel pride, connection and hope.

We do not ask the world merely to witness our deaths. We ask it to recognise our lives: Our right to study, to find clean water, to enjoy ordinary moments, to protect our families and to imagine a future without fear.

I write not only for myself, but for the millions whose daily struggles may never become headlines.

Thank you to those who have not forgotten us. Your solidarity cannot undo our losses, but it reminds us that humanity has not abandoned us — and that we are still here, trying to live.
